Sony's Japanese 4K Blu-ray lineup is disappearing, raising questions about the future of standalone disc players

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sony may be preparing to abandon the standalone 4K Blu-ray players, and the signs are becoming harder to ignore. According to a report by Forbes, its last remaining model in Japan, the UBP-X700K, was marked as unavailable on October 22, with local retailers reportedly told not to expect another shipment— a development that has raised questions about the future of Sony’s dedicated followers. Sony's U.S. website has also listed the player as ‘out of stock’.

So, is Sony really done making 4K Blu-ray players? That isn't clear. The company is yet to announce a worldwide withdrawal, and its responses to questions about the reports leave that possibility open. When asked by Forbes whether Sony is leaving the market, its UK operation replied: “This information has not been publicly announced by Sony. We are aware of the recent media reports, but prefer to refrain from commenting on speculation.”

There is an important difference between what is happening in Japan and what buyers can still find elsewhere. The UBP-X700K remains listed on Sony’s U.S. website, with Best Buy offering it for $329.99 at press time, which means Sony 4K buyers haven’t missed their chance yet. However, Amazon is no longer selling the player directly as a new product. Finding one could be harder if the company decides not to restock.

This is not the first time Sony has stepped away from physical media. In January 2025, the company stopped producing blank recordable Blu-ray discs, later announcing in February that it would also end its production in Japan. In July 2026, Sony announced it would stop producing physical PlayStation game discs from 2028— although it remains unclear if the next PlayStation console will have a disc drive. Notably, the PS5 Pro launched without a built-in disc drive, but customers who want to play physical games can purchase the optional drive separately.

However, if Sony ultimately leaves the market, buyers will still have alternatives. Panasonic remains the biggest name in dedicated 4K Blu-ray players, although its products are not that cheap. Currently, the Panasonic UB154 lists on Amazon for $289.99, while the UB820 goes for $649.99, a steep climb from its original $499 launch price. The higher-end UN9000 is retailing at $1,299.99 on Walmart. Buyers could also consider gaming consoles such as a disc-equipped PS5, which is listed at $649.99, or the Xbox Series X, priced at $799.99. Both can play 4K Blu-ray movies, but neither supports Dolby Vision when playing discs.

Sony’s move, if true, would add it to a growing list of manufacturers that have dropped the Blu-ray hardware. In 2018, Oppo stopped producing players while Samsung ended plans for new U.S. Blu-ray players a year later. Other companies include LG, which dropped the business in 2024, with French company Reavon halting production in 2025.

But it's important to note that 4K Blu-ray demand has not collapsed in the same way as the wider physical disc market. Figures laid out by the Digital Entertainment Group show that overall U.S. disc sales declined by roughly 9% in 2025. Spending on 4K discs, however, climbed by 12% over the same period, before climbing another 18% in the second quarter of 2026. That said, for existing Sony owners, there is no reason to panic just yet. A player that works today will continue playing the discs already in a collector’s library — and there is no evidence that Sony plans to push an update that would stop existing players from reading movies.

#10319. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

Passive candidates answer when a message is specific, short and clearly about them. This is a nine-step playbook, and each step shows how to do it in Pin. The method works in any tool. For a shorter version, see Pin's 7-step guide to sourcing passive candidates.

A passive candidate is a working professional who isn't applying for jobs but might say yes to the right conversation.

Gallup's fourth-quarter 2025 panel sizes the pool. It found that 51% of U.S. workers are actively looking (11%) or watching for opportunities (40%).

The practical reading: only 11% of workers are actively looking, so most of the market isn't on a job board, and about half is paying attention.

Write the brief as outcomes and skills, not a title. Use five lines:

Skills-based pools are larger. In Pin: paste the job description, add a job listing link, upload two or three ideal résumés, or import the role from your ATS. Pin asks clarifying questions about the brief, such as "Is remote considered?" Answer them. They are the parts of the brief you hadn't written down.

Samsung isn’t holding back when it comes to the iPhone Duo’s messy start. In new ads, the company mocks iPhone Duo’s “crackgate” with a push for customers to buy the Galaxy Z Fold 8 instead, and there’s not an ounce of subtlety here.

Following the debut of Apple’s first foldable, an unfortunate trend has emerged among early buyers. A number of users found that their display “cracked” with the display panel dying in the center, all in the exact same way, implying there’s a flaw within Apple’s hinge design.

In an ad for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 on Instagram, Samsung says that “folding is nothing new to us” and that “we know a thing or eight.” It cuts right to the chase: “Switch to Galaxy Z Fold8.” The attached imagery then depicts the iPhone Duo’s well-known screen “crack.

It's kind of funny that Apple had 8 years to copy the competition, and still failed spectacularly in such a serious way. The hinge section in question either suffers from material failure (metal breaks when it shouldn't) or its a design failure where the hinge simply breaks under a certain pressure (that a foldable should survive).

Either way this doesn't bode well for Apples QA.

That one was posted to Samsung Canada’s account, while another ad from Samsung Malaysia further takes that up a notch:

Feeling a little FOMO seeing all this talk about durability… oops, we’ve just been busy folding and getting on with our day

Samsung Australia similarly poked fun at Apple’s durability woes with a post about “how life sounds when your screen doesn’t break when opening your phone.”

Another post from Samsung Saudi Arabia puts the iPhone Duo crack on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 before revealing it’s just a wallpaper.

A federal judge rejects xAI’s mobile-turbine exemption argument, allowing the NAACP’s Clean Air Act lawsuit over Colossus 2 to proceed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX has suffered a setback after losing in a lawsuit aimed at stopping the Clean Air Act requirements on the turbines powering xAI’s Colossus 2 data center in Southaven, Mississippi. According to a report by CNBC, a judge rejected the company’s motion to dismiss the case on Friday, October 30, allowing the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) to proceed, rejecting xAI’s argument that its turbines fall under the ‘mobile sources’ category that exempts it from air permitting requirements.

The case, brought in April 2026 by the NAACP and represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center (SELC) alongside Earthjustice, targets xAI’s operation of a gas-fired power plant to supply electricity to its facility in the Greater Memphis area. SpaceX owns and operates xAI, implicating Elon Musk's wider aerospace and technology company.

According to court documents, NACCP accuses xAI and its subsidiary, MZX Tech, of installing 27 gas turbines in Southaven last year without obtaining the required permits. The applicants also argued that the company’s equipment has been polluting the environment through nitrogen oxide emissions and fine particulate matter, which can contribute to breath-related hazards to residents. The SELC particularly says the plant could emit over 5,00 tons of nitrogen oxides, 400 tons of fine particulate matter, and 47 tons of formaldehyde — a cancer-causing chemical — annually.

The judge also rejected xAI’s attempted classification of the turbines as mobile equipment, holding that the company did not qualify for exemptions under applicable regulations and that the turbines were not exempt from Clean Air Act permitting requirements. Just two weeks earlier, SpaceX suffered another setback after the same court rejected a separate Department of Justice lawsuit that argued against the case proceeding.

“This decision is another important victory in our effort to hold xAI accountable. The courts have repeatedly rejected attempts by xAI and the DOJ to dismiss the NAACP’s Clean Air Act case, affirming our right to pursue justice for communities impacted by pollution. Our position has been clear: xAI cannot operate gas turbines without the required permits. Now that the motion to dismiss has been denied, we look forward to continuing to defend our position in court,” Abre’ Conner, NAACP Director of Environmental and Climate Justice, said. SpaceX is yet to comment on the ruling.

Colossus 2 installed 59 natural gas turbines in July, immediately sparking concerns from residents about emissions and the impact on nearby communities. The Memphis facility plans for about 860,000 Nvidia GB300 GPUs across four Colossus buildings —but it could be more — with Musk stating, “There will be a total of around 1.2M Blackwells at Colossus 2 by end of year”

Elon Musk just gave a massive update on Colossus 2 in Memphis, and the scale of what's being built is absolutely insane Two buildings already packed with GB300s, two more are coming online within weeks, and it is heading toward roughly 860,000 NVIDIA GB300s Here's the breakdown: • Macroharder: 220,000 GB300s, 800-gig NICs, configured for training • Minihard: 220,000 GB300s, same training configuration • Gun Range: 220,000 GB300s, tracking to be operational by the END OF NOVEMBER • Spam: ~200,000 GB300s, configured for inference, targeting DECEMBER That's roughly 860,000 GB300s across these four buildings Spam is designed for inference, which needs much simpler networking and less than HALF the fiber of the training buildings. And yes, the building once housed Hormel products Elon personally walked the entire Colossus 2 site around midnight and again the next morning to check progress Building by building, SpaceXSI is assembling SI compute at a speed no one else on Earth can matchOctober 31, 2026

In August, the company stated that it would remove its unpermitted turbine generators and replace them with a larger permitted power plant — but that could take at least a year. The latest setback adds to a string of lawsuits surrounding the gas-powered infrastructure used to power xAI’s data centers. In June, the DOJ had asked the court to dismiss the NACCP’s lawsuit, arguing that Colossus 2 supports crucial national security operations. That request was, however, rejected. More recently, SpaceX started manufacturing turbine blades in-house to fast-track generator production for its xAI data centers.

#10311. Motorola Signature 27 specs detailed in new video, including Tandem OLED display

Ahead of its launch next week, a new video offers a closer look at the Motorola Signature 27 as well as confirming some key specs.

A video hands-on from Danny Winget on YouTube offers a closer look at Motorola’s upcoming flagship, and only makes its arrival all the more enticing.

There are several key specs mentioned in the video, with the most interesting being the “Extreme AMOLED Duo” display which makes use of Tandem OLED technology. Tandem OLED isn’t a new idea, with the tech stacking multiple layers of diodes on top of each other to improve contrast and brightness. Tandem OLED can be found on Apple’s new “PROLED” MacBook Pro, as well as 2024’s Honor Magic 6 RSR. But Motorola’s use of it in the Signature 27 is certainly nice to see, especially given the other spec shared. 12,000 nits of brightness. That rather insane figure is apparently the peak brightness on this new flagship.

Hardware shots of the phone also show the textured backs on the two color variants as well as the curved glass around the display.

I think it’s a interesting phone with a good camera system. But it also depend on the price. Anyway nice to see Motorola compete in the flagship space again.

The battery capacity isn’t revealed, but Winget says that it is “sizable.” Similarly, the vapor chamber is described as “40% larger” but a point of comparison wasn’t given.

It’s all shaping up for a powerful flagship in every sense of the word. Motorola has confirmed that Signature 27 will launch on November 5, and I don’t know about you, but I’m only getting more excited about it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has taken to X, the social network that he owns, to mock OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's stance that it's "quite terrible" for home computer users to have DRAM in their machines. Altman made the claim during an appearance on the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, noting that it would be better for DRAM to be used in AI data centers instead. Mocking the point, Musk shared a meme on X that referenced a movie in which a German WWII officer appears to be hunting for people hiding sticks of DRAM.

Altman's stance has already drawn plenty of ire across the internet. "From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said during the YouTube interview. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that."

The people deserve to have their RAM too! https://t.co/q6dwauALw4November 1, 2026

OpenAI does, of course, offer some open-source models, but it makes its money from models hosted in data centers, which it can charge users to access at home. With that in mind, it's perhaps unsurprising that Altman would rather people not have home computers that are capable of running local models, negating the need for cloud-based alternatives. However, Altman's comments are ill-timed — computer enthusiasts and average users alike are facing increased prices across the board, whether buying DRAM kits themselves or computers as a whole. As chipmakers retool factories to produce components for AI data centers rather than the consumer market, prices have skyrocketed on everything from DRAM kits to the storage used in devices of all shapes and sizes.

Even Apple, a company previously thought immune to component price increases, hiked prices across its lineups earlier this year. Its recent iPhone launches saw a price increase across the board, too. Beyond Apple, Lenovo said in June that it didn't expect prices to return to pre-2026 levels anytime soon, if ever. Makers of DRAM, Samsung and SK hynix, have also warned that AI-driven memory shortages will last until 2027 and beyond.

As the perceived demand for more AI data centers shows little sign of slowing, the demand for the components that power them will similarly maintain levels that put all other technology at risk of price increases and limited availability.

#10308. How Applicant Tracking Systems Read Resumes: 7 Checks Developers Should Make

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A resume that looks perfect on screen can look like a pile of scrambled text to a program. Applicant tracking systems (ATS) and hiring tools do not see your layout. They extract text from a file, guess where the sections are, and store what they find. If that step fails, the best experience in the world never reaches a human reader.

This matters whether you are sending your own resume or building a tool that processes thousands of them. This article walks through seven checks you can make with a few lines of Python, including one script you can run today.

A resume is a document with no guaranteed structure. One person writes "Work History", another writes "Experience", and a third uses a two-column layout that reads out of order. Any tool that processes resumes first has to turn this into predictable fields: contact details, sections, dates and skills.

Thinking in terms of a target schema helps. SitePoint's article on JSON schema design for document AI shows how the structure of the labels you define determines whether a document pipeline works. The same idea applies here: decide which fields you need before you write any extraction code.

Do not judge a resume by how it looks. Judge it by what comes out when you extract the text. SitePoint's walkthrough on building a JSON dataset from PDF documents describes a pipeline that extracts text from PDFs and then cleans up common extraction artifacts. That cleanup step exists because raw extraction is rarely tidy. Read the raw output first, and note what is broken.

PDF files store where characters are placed on a page, not what they mean. The pypdf documentation on extracting text from a PDF says this directly: there is no semantic layer, spacing is hard to get right because text is absolutely positioned, and pypdf is not OCR software, so it will never extract text from images.

Two practical results follow. A resume saved as a scanned image has no extractable text at all. And fancy layouts such as columns, text boxes and tables can come out in the wrong order.

Once you can extract text, a short script can catch the common failures. This one reads a PDF and reports whether it contains text, whether an email address is found, and which standard sections are missing:

Run it on a resume and look at the result. If has_text is false, the file is probably an image. If sections are missing, check whether your headings use unusual names. A passing result does not prove that every ATS will read the file the same way, but a failing result is a clear warning.

Different tools parse differently, so one script is only one opinion. A resume writing service such as ResumeCroc lists a free ATS resume checker among its tools, which is a quick way to see how another tool reads the same file. The linked page is a commercial service page, and every ATS behaves differently, so treat any checker as one data point and compare it with your own extraction results.

Most extraction problems come from layout. Single-column pages, standard headings, plain fonts and real text instead of images give parsers the best chance. Avoid putting contact details in headers or footers, since some tools skip them. If you are building a parser, test files with columns and tables on purpose so you know how your tool fails.

Create a folder of sample resumes: a clean one, a two-column one, a scanned one and one with unusual headings. Run your check against all of them whenever you change your parsing code. This turns "it seems to work" into something you can verify, and it makes regressions obvious.

Do all applicant tracking systems read PDFs the same way? No. Parsers differ in how they handle layout, headers and tables, so test more than one file format and more than one tool.

Is a Word file safer than a PDF? Not necessarily. Both can parse well or badly depending on layout. Test your own file instead of assuming.

Can a script guarantee my resume will pass an ATS? No. A script can find obvious problems, such as missing text or headings, but each hiring tool has its own rules.

Hiring tools read text, not layout. Define the fields you care about, extract the raw text first, understand what PDF extraction cannot do, automate basic checks, compare with an outside checker, keep formatting simple, and test against a small set of sample files. The script above is short, but it moves the question from "does it look right" to "what does a program actually see".

As we near the launch of Motorola’s return to the flagship space, it’s becoming clear that the company is ready to fill a gap left by the departure of OnePlus, though there’s one very obvious difference between the two.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. The Motorola Signature 27’s launch is coming up fast and, with it, the first truly exciting flagship the company has launched widely in quite some time. There have been a handful of high-end Moto devices in recent years, but this is the first one in quite a while where it seems Motorola is holding nothing back.

Between a powerful Snapdragon chip, top-tier cameras, and rumors of a massive battery, this is shaping up to be something special. Of course, all-out flagships like this aren’t uncommon in some parts of the world. Oppo, Honor, and other Chinese brands have been building devices like this for years but, especially in the US, they’re just completely lacking, especially now that OnePlus is dead. While OnePlus flagships in more recent years have not quite risen to the same bar as Oppo’s, they’ve been the best equivalent in the States and, now, they’re just gone.

Motorola is stepping up in a big way here, and seems to be the closest many are going to get to a OnePlus replacement.

It’s fitting, really. As much as I’d love to have Google Pixel step up its game here, Motorola’s Lenovo backing and long history in the smartphone space more than earns its spot as a proper flagship smartphone maker. The problem, really, is just going to boil down to pricing.

OnePlus was well known for top-tier specs, of course, but it built its brand on doing so at a lower price point. Even in its final days where prices were creeping higher than ever, a OnePlus flagship was still priced equal to or less than most competitors. Motorola Signature 27 does not seem to be trying to recover that part of OnePlus’ reputation based on early pricing leaks. RAMageddon surely isn’t helping matters, but Motorola’s return to the flagship space is not going to come cheap from the sound of it.

Another sore point for Motorola is in software updates, but it’s not like OnePlus was really doing that well in that regard anyway. Things are moving in a better direction with Motorola moving up to 7-year commitments on certain devices, but there’s still room for improvement and quite the poor track record to make up for.

With the launch of Motorola Signature 27 mere weeks away, I’m personally very excited to see what the company has in store. What do you think?

You’d think that Android foldables effectively doing all of the R&D for Apple’s first foldable would prevent any major issues, but apparently that’s not enough. While the scale of the problem remains unclear, Apple’s iPhone Duo is cracking for many in the same place, suggesting there’s a manufacturing problem in play. It’s not quite an OG Galaxy Fold debacle, but it doesn’t feel far off either.

Google’s latest frontier AI model has been announced in Gemini 4 Carbon. The company says it makes major leaps forward for coding and other purposes and outranks the competition but, like Argon, it’s not immediately available.

After being announced earlier this month, we reviewed the Fitbit Edge this week and the tracker is also now on sale. While it feels like an awkward middle child between the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, owners of prior Charge trackers will likely appreciate the upgrades it brings to the table.

Anthropic's recent move to have Claude Code deny video game cloning and possibly reverse engineering efforts has come under heavy fire from the software development community. Hot on the heels of Friday's report on the matter, an Anthropic employee responded to the tweet with the purported rule update with a direct statement confirming that the firm added guardrails to Claude Code to prevent game recreation.

In the full tweet, which you can read below, Addy Osmani says that "[Anthropic] added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against [its] usage policy." He goes on to state that work on original games is meant to continue working, and that Anthropic is iterating on the rules to try and "strike the right balance."

We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way.October 30, 2026

There's no telling what those sentences might be, though given Osmani's choice of words, it's possible that said sentences are indeed what X user Chasm posted a screenshot of: "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original."

In our previous report, we had already linked to recent issues raised at Claude Code's own GitHub repository, comprised of users complaining that the AI assistant was refusing to work on their games or on reverse-engineering tasks. As far as we can ascertain, it appears the game-related blocking is limited to the combination of using Claude Code and the Opus 5.5 model. Should that prove true, then users should be able to sidestep the limitation by calling upon Opus using another harness like Ollama or forwarding specific requests through a wrapper of some sort.

Regarding the blocking of reverse engineering, we have received direct confirmations. The first comes from our own alumnus Jarred Walton, who was trying to run checks on the software he's developing. He notes that such work had been performed with no issue until yesterday, October 31, and that switching to Opus 4.8 let him continue his work.

Walton theorizes that Anthropic may have added a new rule to Code specifically for reverse-engineering. Considering that timing, plus the fact that other reports of refusals all popped up around the last week, may indicate that the company could be fiddling with cybersecurity-related rules in the same manner as they are for video game-related content.

We also received screenshots from a staffer's direct acquaintance, who asked Opus 5.5 (via Code) to try and reverse engineer a product activation, a request that likewise triggered safeguards. Meanwhile, notices that Claude Code appears to block reverse-engineering continue to mount, now with a Redditor allegedly having their account suspended, and then reinstated, over using Opus 5.5 and Reverse Engineer Anything. The company has an ongoing Cyber Verification Program, in which only approved entities get access to the full set of frontier models' cybersecurity capabilities.

Rosstat acknowledged suffering cyberattacks but denied leaked data claims.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Russian Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat) admitted that its servers were hit by coordinated cyberattacks between October 29 and 31. However, it denied claims that tens of terabytes of data had been leaked, as asserted by hack groups like the Belarusian CyberPartisans and Silent Crow. Rosstat stopped publishing annual cause-of-death statistics in 2024, but the hackers say that the huge new 23TB data haul includes data on Russian wartime losses marked “for official use only,” reports The Moscow Times. A new chart shared by the hack groups using the data suggests that as many as 50,000 Russian soldiers are killed every month.

Rosstat is very much like the U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics in the United States, or the Office for National Statistics (ONS) in the UK. It isn’t a big juicy military infrastructure target, but if accurate war casualty figures can come from the claimed exfiltrated data haul, then it would be a considerable win for Ukraine and its supporters.

Today @cpartisans and SilentCrow took down Russia's Federal State Statistics Service — the nerve center behind every socioeconomic number this regime produces. Full breakdown below 👇 https://t.co/wUKfyUi6y6November 1, 2026

As we mentioned in the intro, both the Belarusian CyberPartisans and Silent Crow claim to have snagged lots of sensitive data from the Russian government thanks to this breach. The former’s tweet includes evidence and a breakdown. “Entire IT infrastructure wiped: Domain controllers, databases, servers, virtualization, document workflow, workstations, admin consoles, VPN,” notes a follow-up post about the Rosstat hack attack. “Systems destroyed: STATEK, CSOD, Demography, SED, ESSO, OFSN, internal employee surveillance, StatRegister, websites and more.”

This is a developing story with the Belarusian CyberPartisans promising to share more sensitive information from Rosstat after they have picked through it. The Rosstat website was reportedly defaced with hacker messages and logos. Rosstat remains inaccessible at the time of writing.

We spotted an interesting graphic shared by the Belarusian CyberPartisans, which included the Silent Crow logo. A chart indicates that over the last two years, between 25,000 and 50,000 Russian soldiers were killed every month. The October 2026 figure is just a smidgen under 50,000, if this data leak news is genuine.

These same hacking groups have claimed responsibility for the likes of the disruptive Aeroflot IT systems hack, and a state real estate company hack with two billion records, both in 2025. “Both groups are designated as extremist and banned in Russia,” notes the report.

#10299. How to Quickly Check What Your HTML Code Looks Like in a Browser

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Writing HTML is one of the main parts of building a website. It is mainly responsible for webpage structure and content.

A small error can result in layout problems. Oftentimes, you don't notice these issues until you preview the page in a browser. A quick way to ensure that your layout looks the same as you want is to preview your HTML code.

In this blog, we’ll show you easy ways to check how your HTML code will look in real time. So keep on reading till the end.

The following are two easy ways to check how your HTML code will look in real time.

This is a simple way to preview your HTML. You don't need a web server to preview your HTML code. You have to follow the following steps.

Open a code editor or simply Notepad on your device. Create a new file and paste your HTML inside it.

Step 2 - Save the File With an HTML Extension

After adding your HTML code in Notepad, save the file as index.html. You have to ensure that the extension is .html, not .txt.

If you are using Notepad on Windows, click on “File” and navigate to the “Save As” option and click it. Then enter index.html as the filename. Make sure that Notepad doesn’t save it as a text document.

Locate the saved file on your device. Double-click to open it in your default browser. The browser will render the HTML elements to show the headings, paragraphs, and buttons on the page, as you can see in the image below.

This is how you can create a simple file to preview your HTML before deploying it. If you see any errors, you can correct them in your file and preview it again.

However, it is worth considering that HTML may not show the complete website behavior alone. The final result can also depend on JavaScript, external CSS, or other resources. You should check those files as well.

This method provides an easy way to preview your HTML code. It involves using a specialized online HTML viewer. This approach is even quicker and doesn't even require you to create a local file first.

Step 1 - Open the HTML Viewer Open your web browser and search for an HTML viewer. You may see multiple tools in the search results. Select one that allows HTML preview online. For demonstration purposes, we are using HTML Viewer by minifier.org.

Once you’ve selected the tool, open it. Navigate to its input box and paste your HTML code into it. We are using the same HTML code from the first example.

You can also upload your file or paste its URL into the tool. After entering your HTML code, click on the “View” button to preview your HTML code.

In the screenshot above, you can see the tool showing the HTML preview on the right side. This tool also gives you the option to edit your HTML code and see the results in real time through the “Auto-update” option.

If the auto-update option is checked, you can see the changes in real time as you edit the code. This makes editing much easier, as you can modify the code and preview the changes immediately without returning to your original file. It also allows you to verify how your layout will appear on desktop, tablet, or mobile. You can check this by clicking on the icons provided in the top right corner of the tool. Once you are satisfied with the output, you can copy or download your edited HTML file easily.

This tool also allows you to test the HTML code of your game or video in real time, as you can see in the screenshot below.

These features make such specialized HTML viewers practical. These are quick and easy to use. However, the features shown above may not be available on all the tools. If you are specifically looking for such features, you can read the tool’s description for these features before using it.

HTML is one of the main components of a website. It defines the structure and content of webpages. Many users need to check how their HTML code will look in a browser to identify potential issues before deployment.

To preview your HTML code, you can use simple methods. One is to paste your code into Notepad and save it as index.html. Then open it in your browser to get a preview of your HTML code.

You can also use a specialized HTML viewer. Such tools can work by just pasting the code into the input box. Once you paste your code, click on the view button to get a preview of your HTML code. Some tools also offer various other features, such as editing, viewing games, and videos in real time.

Both of these methods work fine. The choice depends on the user's preferences and needs.

The Switch 2 is one of the first consoles to include microSD Express support, so you can use this Samsung P9 Express card's faster storage speeds compared to older UHS-I cards. Google secures approval for its Minnesota data center despite local protests, lawsuits, and power supply concerns

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google has secured approval for a proposed data center in Hermantown, Minnesota, following a unanimous vote by the city council, MPR News reports. The decision, reached on Friday, October 30, clears a major hurdle for the company following at least two postponed meetings and hours of public opposition, though the project still faces lawsuits and a separate inquiry into its electricity supply. The proposed development could cover just over 200 acres in a rural residential area outside Duluth with three data center buildings spanning approximately 1.66 million square feet.

The council approved a development agreement, a special use permit, and provisions for decommissioning the site if construction is abandoned or the facility eventually closes. The meeting, which was capped at 85 people and offered a livestream, ended shortly before midnight, with some criticizing the attendance restriction. Council member John Geisler, however, clarified the move, noting that the decision concerned local land use application rather than the wide debate over artificial intelligence or big technology companies.

“What we've done tonight is not about AI. It's not about big tech. It's not about software. It's about a project here in Hermantown, a land use application, and agreements that are associated with that,” Geissler said.

The approval comes at a hefty price for Google, with the company being forced to make several changes during the approval process. The company changed its initial plan of putting up four buildings to three, capped their height at 33 feet, and agreed to monitor nearby private wells —but each building would still be larger than six football fields. Google also agreed to withdraw an earlier request for up to $80 million in property tax breaks. The revised arrangement is now expected to generate about $3 million in annual property tax for the city, with a separate decommissioning agreement valued at $210 million in place.

Supporters point to those provisions as evidence that Google had responded to local concerns. Opponents, however, argue that the changes did not address the important questions of whether such a colossal development belongs in the area. The dispute echoes other data center battles within local communities, with Alabama residents being unable to halt a 50MW Bitcoin mining facility in August, despite local moratoriums, exposing gaps in the state's zoning rules. In September, a proposal for a 1,300-acre data center in Pennsylvania by NorthPoint Development also faced resistance despite its developer offering $10,000 to thousands of nearby households. Key issues raised mostly by residents in both cases have been about noise and water consumption by such facilities and property values.

It’s important to note, however, that Hermantown’s vote does not mean Google can immediately begin construction. Three lawsuits filed by The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy and Stop the Hermantown Data Center challenge the city’s zoning process and ownership of the land, and are also demanding the project’s environmental review. The project’s environmental needs are also another pain point, given it requires about 500 megawatts, comparable to the combined demands of homes in Minneapolis, St. Paul, Duluth, and Rochester, as per the Citizens Utility Board of Minnesota. Google still needs approval from the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission on power consumption, despite its agreement with Minnesota Power.

The scale of demand is a recurring point of friction in data center proposals. Last year, the OpenAI Stargate facility in Michigan received approval for a 1.4-gigawatt power supply — construction, however, started in June 2026 despite objections from local residents. Google is also pursuing a separate data center project near Pine Island, close to Rochester. That proposal is now subject to a more extensive environmental review following a legal settlement.

Project takes a stock Qwen 3.5 4B and compiles a RISC-V CPU into its weights.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI engineer Divyansh Agrawal has revealed the Qwenputer. Described in its most basic terms, Qwenputer is an experimental blend of the stock Qwen 3.5 4B AI LLM with a 32-bit RISC-V CPU compiled and inserted directly into its weights. In use, Qwenputer can run processor arithmetic operations – or even run C and MicroPython code on its built-in CPU, eschewing any external runtime or tool use. Moreover, it can run Doom, albeit very slowly. You can see the Qwenputer running Doom on its RISC-V CPU by expanding the tweet below.

QWenputer by @divagr1925 is so cool! but... can it run DOOM? Ofc yes! E1M1 on the RISC-V CPU compiled into Qwen3.5-4B weights. will opensource too https://t.co/hEa46rD6CJOctober 29, 2026

The implementation of Qwenputer raises some interesting concepts and solutions. For example, the developer used Qwen’s Gated DeltaNet (GND) state as RAM, which Agrawal reckons is “a pretty neat trick.” They admit that using these ‘fast weights’ as RAM isn’t an original concept, but modifying Qwen 3.5 this way does seem to be a first.

Unlike traditional LLM creation, adding a ‘CPU’ doesn’t involve training. This RISC-V CPU implementation “is 11 transformer layers in front of Qwen's own, and none of their weights are learned: a compiler computes every one,” it is explained. Agrawal boasts that Qwenputer’s built-in CPU “passes the official riscv-tests, its programs match qemu, and it has run 18 million instructions free-running without a single error.”

The developer stresses that Qwen makes use of this ‘CPU’ to send instructions and read them back with no external tool or runtime calls. In practice, it works as intended. Use of the CPU inside Qwenputer provides exact calculations, overcoming the arithmetic weaknesses of many LLMs. Moreover, users can run code on the CPU inside the LLM, with C and MicroPython compatibility.

Not content with wedging a CPU into an LLM, Agrawal decided to also give it a filesystem. They describe this extension of the model as relatively trivial, since RAM is already in place. Indeed, the filesystem storage also uses the DeltaNet state. There are 1,024 slots holding up to 512 files. Moreover, this storage is persistent if you save the state at the end of a conversation with the LLM.

Due to its expanded resource use, Qwenputer has basically doubled the size of the underlying Qwen 3.5 4B LLM to almost 19GB. Thus, Agrawal recommends a workstation with 24GB of VRAM or more for testing Qwenputer in its current version. Efforts are being made to streamline coding in Qwenputer, as well as make it run faster.

The project is experimental. One gets the impression that Agrawal built Qwenputer primarily as an experiment to explore what is possible, rather than to solve a specific problem. Nevertheless, the creation of this custom LLM raises some interesting concepts and makes the mind wander regarding potential practical applications.

#10290. Gemini 4 Carbon lags just behind Claude in benchmark, but wins in value

Google’s new frontier model, Gemini 4 Carbon, brings some welcome improvements and while it doesn’t top the charts in a new benchmark, it does provide much more bang for your buck.

SemiAnalysis, an AI research and analysis firm, recently published its new frontier-level benchmark, GDPx which includes numbers for Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon model. The leaderboard includes every major frontier model from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta and details both the score and cost for each model.

The benchmark includes 206 tasks across finance, materials science, cybersecurity, software engineering, legal, biology, and several other domains (topics).

Topping the results is Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, but Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is very close behind. The difference between the two is relatively minimal, but the cost is the biggest factor to consider here. Where Claude’s cost came out to around $51 per task, Gemini was just over $16 per task. Gemini also beat the next model on the list, GPT-6 Astra, which scored lower while costing more than both at about $54 per task.

The report notes that taking out cybersecurity, biology, and alignment domains shuffles the results. Safety guardrails in Claude and GPT models puts GPT-6 Astra at the top of the list with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 outranking Gemini 4 Carbon. SemiAnalysis says that this better aligns with their “subjective impressions” of each model.

As for Google’s existing frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, it ranks in eighth place on both lists, beating Meta’s Muse Wonder, but below Wonder Full. Argon’s costs in this particular benchmark are only slightly lower than Carbon.

Both of Google’s models score better than OpenAI and Anthropic models when focused on cybersecurity, but do fall behind Meta’s Muse models, which the benchmark found to be the best “by a meaningful margin.”

Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28 and touted “significant gains,” but the public release date has not been confirmed just yet. It is “coming soon” for most customers. Google’s own benchmark, below, beat GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 in many aspects.

#10289. AI Testing Tools: Benefits, Limitations, and Best Practices

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every vendor says the same thing: buy our AI, and testing gets easy. Don't believe it. AI testing tools do help, though. Some teams save real hours with them, while others waste a quarter and a budget. The difference usually comes down to how they start.

They support your QA team by writing test cases, running them, spotting failures and suggesting repairs. Some tools read a requirements document. Others watch real users click around and then replay what they did. Playwright, for instance, now ships built-in test agents: a planner that explores your app and writes a test plan, a generator that turns the plan into test files, and a healer that runs the suite and tries to repair failing tests.

Old-school automation needs a person to write every script. Then a developer moves one button and the whole thing falls over. Somebody loses a morning to repairs, and QA engineers hate that part of the job.

Quality is the big worry. Generated tests can look clever and prove nothing. A tool might confirm that a checkout page opens and then mark checkout as covered, but opening a page is not testing it. Even Playwright's documentation says generated tests may contain initial errors and that you should review what the healer changes before accepting it. A person has to read the output every time.

Business logic is the next problem. The tool has no idea that your refund window dropped from 30 days to 14, and it cannot feel that a signup form is confusing. Intent lives in people's heads.

Coverage numbers can mislead. A dashboard says 90%, and the room relaxes. Meanwhile, the odd edge cases nobody thought of sit untouched. Bugs do not read dashboards.

Check fit first. Does it cover web, mobile and API tests, and does it work with your stack? Ask before any sales call, not after. Then test its honesty: when something fails, a good tool tells you why. A vague red mark costs your team time because nobody can verify it. Read the pricing page slowly, too, since some vendors charge per seat and some per test run.

Finally, throw your ugliest feature at it. Demos use tidy little apps, but your product has pop-ups, slow pages and odd corners. Watch how the tool handles those.

Expecting instant results. People switch the tool on and wait for magic. What they get is noisy reports and grumpy engineers. Some managers even cut QA headcount right away, which is a bad idea: somebody has to tune the tool and handle the cases it cannot. Good testers become more valuable, not less.

Skipping training. Your team needs to learn how the tool behaves. Two short workshops and a shared doc go a long way.

Trusting machine-written text without a second look. AI tools now draft test descriptions, bug reports and release notes too. If your team wants to know how much of a document was machine-generated, an AI-content checker such as ZeroGPT can give a rough signal. Treat the result as a hint rather than proof, because such detectors make mistakes and publish their own accuracy claims.

Agents are the obvious next step. Instead of running fixed scripts, they poke around your app like a curious user, clicking, typing and reporting anything strange. Early versions already exist, and they are rough but improving.

Editors will change as well. Your code editor may soon suggest a test the moment you finish a function, and some bug reports may arrive with a fix attached. The wall between development and QA is getting thin.

Yes, but carefully. AI testing tools will not replace your QA team. They take the boring work off testers' hands and spot patterns people might miss, but they still need a human to say "that result is wrong." Start small, measure what happens and keep your testers close to the tool. Do that, and you will ship faster without losing control.

#10285. Apple finally has a touchscreen MacBook. Why now?

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

The Windows world has had touch for over a decade. Is Apple getting in the right way?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Last week, Apple finally brought two new display technologies to the MacBook Pro: OLED and touch. For the former, it was just a matter of time; Apple has been using OLED in the iPhone and Apple Watch for years, and also just brought it to the iPad Mini. But touch has never felt like a sure thing. While many of Apple's most successful products have relied on touch: the iPhone, the iPad, the Apple Watch, and some late-stage iPods all featured touchscreens. But until now, it never made its way to Apple's laptops.

Former Apple CEO Steve Jobs' words are infamous: "It's ergonomically terrible," he said of touchscreen laptops in 2010, describing how "your arm wants to fall off" due to fatigue. "Touch surfaces want to be horizontal," he added.

Since then, touchscreens have become ubiquitous on Windows PCs and Chromebooks. Outside of the Touch Bar, which was ultimately reversed because Mac users were not fans, Apple hasn't had a real touchscreen on the Mac.

That changed, as the company announced 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros with "PROLED XDR" displays with, yes, touch support. The devices are also lighter than existing MacBook Pros, have updated speaker systems, and, yes, are more expensive.

Apple eschewed touch on its laptops for years. But it seems, however, that at least some Mac owners disagreed.

"Apple tends not to move to a new technology until it can bring to market a differentiated product," Tom Mainelli, group vice president of device and consumer research at IDC, told Tom's Hardware. "Based on all the demos they are showing here in LA, the drive for 'why now' is because they see a desire for touch from creators who use the Mac."

He added: "The more business-focused answer is the company is creating further segmentation in a mature market, offering a new, more premium tier to its pro lineup."

There's one last uphill climb that the touchscreen on the new MacBook Pro faces: the price. After all, the touchscreen is debuting on just the new, redesigned 14- and 16-inch models.

In time, touch will likely fall down the stack, to the cheaper MacBook Pro models, the MacBook Air, and possibly even the Neo. You may see a touch iMac at some point. That will take time. After all, the Mac is just getting OLED, too. That means it's unlikely we'll see mass adoption of touch on the Mac anytime soon. It still has to reach the most popular devices, and even then, it has to coexist with the old standbys, keyboard and mouse.

You could trace the touchscreen laptop back to 2008's HP TouchSmart tx2, which had a swiveling screen. The real touch revolution started around two other releases: The Microsoft Surface Laptop RT and the release of Windows 8 in 2012, which had a touch-forward interface and led to a flood of touch laptops.

Windows 10 came and went with more touchscreens, and by the time of Windows 11's release in 2021, touchscreens largely became the default for Windows laptops. On all but the cheapest devices, I tend to assume a Windows notebook has a touchscreen.

On Chromebooks, the 2013 Chromebook Pixel was considered premium because of its touchscreen. In 2019, I reviewed the Samsung Chromebook Pro and Plus, as Google first experimented with Android apps in Chrome. I remember sitting there poking and prodding the device, thinking that "if Android apps are going to be on Chromebooks, every single one needs a touchscreen." I was seven years too early.

When Apple introduced the MacBook Neo earlier this year, it shocked the industry on price and performance. But it did cut some features, like a backlit keyboard. But some companies that made competitors, such as Dell with its XPS 13, made a point to add that not only did it have a backlit keyboard — it had a touchscreen. (HP also kept the touchscreen with its OmniBook 5. Acer did away with it on the Swift Air 14).

In an interview with Steven Levy at Wired, Apple's chief hardware officer Johny Srouji said that "Ten years is a very very long time," and said that a lot has changed, from display technology to custom silicon to software architecture, which now "met our bar." In the same interview, Apple's senior vice president of worldwide marketing, Greg Joswiak, explained that most creatives have an iPhone or iPad and find it natural: "There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch."

This might betray my age, but in general, outside of tablets and 2-in-1 laptops, I don't make a ton of use of touchscreens on computers. It hasn't bothered me once in the past five years that my personal MacBook Pro doesn't have a touchscreen. In general, I agree with Jobs; The ergonomics aren't great.

There are other reasons you might skip a touchscreen. For a long time, they were thought of as battery hogs. The digitizer can add extra weight or cost. And operating systems haven't been designed with touch in mind.

Windows 11 was supposed to be more designed for touchscreens, having taken cues from the unreleased Windows 10X, designed for touchscreens and foldables. But Windows is Windows, and the underlying OS still feels best with a keyboard and mouse.

One of the best operating systems I've seen for touch is Googlebook OS, if only because it's so based on Android 17 that some parts make more sense with a finger than a keyboard and mouse.

For macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple has added system gesture APIs to make apps more likely to support touch. Apple says its own apps are ready, and in its press release, listed a number of other apps like the Microsoft Office suite, Zoom, Notion, Da Vinci Resolve, Adobe Lightroom, Blender, and Algoriddim DJay Paro.

But it also didn't remove the keyboard and touchpad. It's a Mac with a touchscreen, but not touch-first.

For creative professionals who need true accuracy, specialty tablets that work as peripherals will still be king.

There's one last uphill climb that the touchscreen on the new MacBook Pro faces: the price. After all, the touchscreen is debuting on just the new, redesigned 14- and 16-inch models, starting at $2,899 for the 14-incher and $3,399 for the 16-inch models, respectively.

In time, touch will likely fall down the stack to the cheaper Pros, the MacBook Air, and possibly even the Neo. You may see a touch iMac at some point. That will take time. After all, the Mac is just getting OLED, too.

That means it's unlikely we'll see mass adoption of touch on the Mac anytime soon. It still has to reach the most popular devices, and even then, it has to coexist with the old standbys, keyboard and mouse.

The Garmin Vivoactive 5 is down to its lowest price of all time in all four colors for a limited time, making this the least expensive Garmin you can buy today.

Garmin smartwatches are known for a lot of things. Extremely long battery life, epic health stat tracking, universal phone compatibility, and lots of training plans and tracked exercises. But they’re not known for being low-priced or particularly affordable. That is, until today’s Garmin Vivoactive 5 deal came along.

At just $169.99, this Garmin Vivoactive 5 deal brings the watch down to the lowest price it’s ever been. That’s a particularly excellent price since Garmin isn’t pushy with subscription costs the way some other brands can be. Buy your Garmin and use it. That’s the only real cost unless you need something very specific, and Garmin has several subscriptions for somewhat random things.

Garmin’s Vivoactive lineup is made for casual athletes who find themselves running every so often, go to the gym regularly (but aren’t trying to beat Olympic records), and just find workouts to be a healthy part of normal life. Garmin came out with a Vivoactive 6 earlier this year, which retails for $299, and only offers a few advantages that you might care about. And yes, it even supports proper messaging, images, and replies on Android!

Nvidia replaces potentially exposed SSH keys after detecting unauthorized activity on its Brev cloud platform

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Hackers have struck Nvidia again, this time targeting its BREV cloud development platform, with users reporting unauthorized activity between October 4 and October 20. According to a notification sent to affected customers, some accounts may have been exposed. The company said it had investigated the incident and identified unidentified activity on the platform, adding that information stored on the platform may have been exposed to malicious actors. The said information included the SHH key set up by Brev.

The company has already replaced the affected SHH keys and updated customer machines with new ones but says they found no evidence of improper use. “We are writing to inform you that Nvidia Corporation has experienced a security incident that may have affected the security of your data," the notification reads. “Our analysis determined that your information from our Brev network may have been affected. This SSH key has since been rotated, and your instances have been updated with the replacement key.”

However, the company fell short of explaining how the attackers gained access, or whether anyone attempted to use the compromised data. Moreover, it has not disclosed whether customer data or workloads were accessed. SSH is a protocol used to establish a secure connection between ‘virtual machines’ or remote computers working together. Developers or system administrators can use it to manage remote servers, transfer files, and execute commands without needing physical access to the machine—much like AnyDesk or TeamViewer, but now for developers. Brev uses SSH keys to help customers access these services in the cloud, meaning if attackers access these keys, they could potentially take control of a virtual machine, depending on its specific permissions and other security controls.

And now @NVIDIAAI Brev also got a security breach. At this point in time, every major tech company is going through some sort of security issues - CVEs, stolen keys/API, credentials of users 🥲 https://t.co/3VgUZriQ7lOctober 30, 2026

The incident comes as several firms hosting AI development services and cloud infrastructure grapple with mounting security incidents involving customer credentials. On October 30, cybersecurity firm Wiz released a blog dubbed ‘Black October’ for AI developer platforms. The firm identified at least nine platforms that have had security incidents during the month, including Zeabur, Fireworks AI, Lightning AI, Opencode, Warp, Northflank, among others. As per the firm, the incidents were recurrent, with researchers noting that “all public reports highlight targeted exploitation, explicitly hunting stored environment variables, with a focus on those granted AI access.” Wiz further shared two cases involving compromised Amazon Bedrock credentials where, in one, attackers generated about 800,000 API calls over 30 hours while another key was used to make roughly 1.7 million calls over 13 hours. The combined usage came to a staggering $100,000 at list prices.

Such incidents are not just restricted to Nvidia, with major US banks including JP Morgan, Morgan Stanley and Bank of America restricting Agents from accessing customer accounts earlier this month. Their primary concern is that automated assistants could veer off set instructions and initiate unauthorized approvals. Similarly, the CyberCartel hacking group has previously used Anthropic’s AI tool Claude and Grok’s XAI to conduct attacks on more than 400 Latin American institutions, mostly targeting banks and mobile payments services after attackers obtained customer login credentials. China-linked attackers have also been accused of using AI agents in a ConnectWise supply chain attack that left about 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants exposed, with some attacks reportedly reaching privileged access in under three hours.

Though updating compromised software may not be enough to eliminate an attacker’s access, Bradford Regeski, a threat intelligence analyst at RH-ISAC, has recommended extensive checks for customers in SHH-related incidents, asking users to “Isolate hosts that installed the compromised extension during the exposure window,” remove unauthorized SSH keys and persistence mechanisms, and rotate credentials and sessions.

#10280. AI wearables want to remember everything. What happens when we can’t forget?

A growing number of companies are pitching AI hardware products as a remedy for one of humanity’s oldest weaknesses: forgetfulness.

The latest such product comes from Amazon, whose Bee subsidiary introduced a $75 wristband called the Bee Frontier last month. The band, which looks a little like a screen-free fitness tracker, can record meetings and other conversations using two built-in microphones. Frontier owners can then access transcripts and conversation summaries on their phones or computers.

Amazon is also getting ready to sell a Bee phone accessory to keep track of your calls. The company’s pitch for these devices is that they will help you keep track of the many details that would otherwise fall by the wayside, all while safeguarding your privacy with encryption.

Amazon isn’t the only company looking to capture your work and family conversations. In September, Apple unveiled a new feature called Siri Recap for the latest Apple Watch models that can summarize conversations the watch listens in on. A new smart glasses brand called Vonder wants to keep track of your side of every conversation. And a number of work-centric AI recording devices promise to keep track of all your in-office conversations.

To be sure, these gadgets raise privacy concerns. But beyond the fear that any single conversation may be listened in on, there’s a bigger question to consider with the emergence of such devices: How will human interactions change if every word we utter may get sucked up by an AI-powered microphone, to be preserved for eternity?

LED lights alone don’t make devices privacy-friendly

To its credit, Amazon has been trying to address privacy concerns related to Bee products head-on. Audio captured by the devices is processed in real time and then immediately deleted. Transcripts and summaries are processed and stored in an encrypted private compute environment that even Amazon’s own employees can’t access. And any time a Bee device is used to capture a conversation, an LED turns on.

A number of other AI wearables, including Meta’s Ray-Ban AI glasses, also rely on LEDs to signal recording activity to bystanders. But privacy advocates argue that these lights are insufficient.

“That LED light might be known to some people to signify that a camera or a microphone is on and is being used, but not necessarily to every person,” says Electronic Privacy Information Center senior counsel Sara Geoghegan. “It’s small, and people might not notice it.”

Things can get especially dicey in states like California and Florida, which have two-party consent laws that make it illegal to record private conversations without the consent of other participants. Simply having a device signal that it is recording may not be enough to record others legally in those states. “I don’t think that a small LED light on someone’s glasses across from you is consent,” Geoghegan says.

What’s more, some Ray-Ban users have tampered with their LEDs to record others without their knowledge. This reportedly led Meta to remotely disable thousands of glasses.

By and large, companies rely on users of their devices to notify bystanders that they’re being recorded. That can be harder than it sounds, even for well-meaning owners. “Consent is perhaps impossible, if not much more difficult, to obtain from a crowd of people,” Geoghegan argues.

AI recorders could erode public spaces

Not everyone is as worried about the ability of these devices to record people without their knowledge. “I think consent is overvalued,” says Oxford University professor Viktor Mayer-Schönberger, who is instead more concerned about the broader impact of pervasive, AI-powered recording. “The ephemerality of public spaces has evaporated,” he warns.

People used to be able to go to a museum or a bar without worrying that anything and everything they said might get recorded and analyzed. “There used to be a sort of built-in forgetting in public spaces,” Mayer-Schönberger says.

If you made a bad joke or mispronounced a word, chances were that the people around you would forget about it soon after. AI may preserve that remark forever, leading him to wonder: What are the public spaces in which we can just be ourselves without having to worry about repercussions in the future?

Ubiquitous recording could ultimately cause people to retreat from public spaces, much as they frequently do in authoritarian societies. “In liberal democracies, engaging in public spaces is fundamental to the fabric of society,” Mayer-Schönberger says. “That retreat is actually what worries me.”

All of this is further complicated by the fact that some AI devices capture data even when they’re ostensibly not recording. Meta’s Ray-Bans, for instance, can be used to translate the remarks of your conversation partner. While doing so, their LED light stays off, as the devices don’t save any recordings to your phone’s camera roll. However, Meta’s servers may keep transcripts of translated conversations for up to a year if users don’t manually delete them.

The company’s new camera-free AI glasses don’t even have an LED light, making them virtually indistinguishable from regular glasses. “In the future, you will have to assume that everybody who wears glasses is actually recording something,” Mayer-Schönberger says.

AI gadgets require new social norms

AI device makers are aware of people’s privacy concerns, and a few have gone beyond LED lights to address them. HTC’s Vive Eagle smart glasses cease capture when a bystander says “stop recording,” and AI pendant maker Limitless even required audible consent from bystanders before recording their voices when it released its device in 2024. (The company has since been acquired by Meta, which hasn’t adopted this particular feature for its own AI gadgets.)

“Mechanisms and features that can obtain consent should be baked into the technology,” Geoghegan says. “Tech companies absolutely play a role in ensuring that the products they’re selling are safe.”

Mayer-Schönberger agrees that companies should play a more active role, but he also believes the public should have a say in how AI wearables are used. “They require careful negotiations within society of what is permissible and what is not permissible,” he says.

It’s a process he likens to earlier changes in how we behave in public: People used to yell at actors while watching a play, which seems unthinkable nowadays. Conversely, browsing your phone while spending time with others may have seemed strange not too long ago, but is perfectly acceptable to many people today.

“What is really important is that we start negotiating and we start trying things out,” Mayer-Schönberger says. Without public discourse, devices could remain unregulated until something bad happens, at which point regulators will inevitably overreach. “There is no quick fix, so it will be some relatively extreme regulatory theater,” he says. “Think about taking off shoes at airport security on steroids.”

A Redditor by the name of /u/antisocialnae describes their Asus TUF VG258QM 280Hz gaming monitor as "the best $280 [they] ever spent" after it blocked a bullet that passed through the wall of their home, nearly striking them directly as they were playing some "late-night Call of Duty." Asus has responded to the post with a promise to investigate, though no confirmation of a replacement monitor just yet.

It probably doesn't need explaining that the only reason the plastic-and-plastic monitor was able to stop a bullet is that it had already passed through the exterior wall of the home, and that monitors are generally not ideal for sheltering from gunfire.

But even still, it's a wonderful tale, especially given the TUF branding of the display. TUF technically stands for "The Ultimate Force", but most TUF gear is actually subjected to U.S. Department of Defense MIL-STD-810H testing protocols, including shock & drop tests, vibration tests, high-and-low temperature tests, humidity, sand and dust ingress, and more. That sand and dust ingress protection could be important given the sheetrock powder all over the back of his rig.

What Asus doesn't test for is bullet ingress, which would be quite a thing. While it wouldn't actually be that hard to build, it's difficult to imagine the circumstances where someone would specifically select for that when buying a display.

While these events don't seem to be all that common, we've previously covered a couple, including an event where a user's gaming PC deflected a bullet that came through the wall earlier this year. A few years ago, another user's Razer headset deflected a bullet, almost assuredly saving their life. For their part, /u/antisocialnae says that they've been meaning to buy a new display anyway, so this makes the perfect excuse. For now, they apparently have two other Asus monitors to game on.

Incredibly, the monitor actually still works aside from the damaged portion of the LCD. It makes a decent advertisement for Asus TUF monitors, which mostly miss our selections of the best gaming monitors — beaten by pricier rivals — not because of any problems with the quality. In fact, our last TUF Gaming monitor review scored very well and earned itself an Editor's Choice award. Of course, we also don't test for bullet ingress.
