#10277. Shadow ‘accidental landlord’ housing market supply could be looming, says giant institutional landlord

Want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox? Subscribe to the ResiClub newsletter.

Invitation Homes, one of the nation’s largest single-family rental landlords with 85,961 wholly owned homes, says the rental supply picture is improving recently in some markets that have been hardest hit by the multiple-year cyclical cooling that followed the pandemic housing boom. But on its Q3 2026 earnings call on Thursday, management flagged a wild card it’s keeping an eye on: “shadow [SFR] supply.”

Tim Lobner, COO of Invitation Homes, said single-family rental listings from large operators were down 13% year over year in August, including in the company’s three largest markets: Atlanta, Tampa, and Phoenix. Build-to-rent deliveries peaked in 2024 and are expected to keep slowing through 2027 and 2028, he said. And single-family housing starts are forecast to fall 7% this year and another 5% next year, he told analysts.

Invitation Homes says the wild card is so-called shadow rental supply. That includes “accidental landlords,” homeowners who list their homes for sale, can’t get their asking price, and list them for rent instead, along with unsold homebuilder spec homes that could end up in the rental market.

Here’s what Dallas Tanner, CEO of Invitation Homes, said on the company’s October 29, 2026, earnings call:

“In an elevated mortgage rate environment, it [higher rates causing some renters to stay put] is obviously beneficial for our renewals business, but it could bring additional [rental] supply pressure around [on the] new lease side. So we’ll be mindful of that . . . And what do the mom and pops do that are maybe sitting on a home they’re trying to sell? Does that then kind of come back into play as well? So it’s too early to tell on any of those from a supply-oriented story, but it’s something we’re mindful of and we pay attention to.”

And here’s what Lobner, the COO, said on the earnings call:

“The one area of focus, and Dallas talked about this earlier, was the mom and pop shadow supply. We’re trying to keep an eye on that. Too early to tell where that’s going to go with interest rates where they are. You know, as we look more broadly though at the housing supply, it’s interesting.”

Where accidental landlords are most common

So where are accidental landlords most prevalent? Back in spring 2026, ResiClub analyzed a Zillow dataset covering 50 major metros, which measured the share of rental listings that had been listed for sale for at least two weeks, failed to sell, and were relisted as rentals within three months.

While that data is a little dated now, the directional finding remains: Accidental landlords are most common in the softer pockets of the U.S. housing market.

Major metros with the highest share of accidental landlord rental listings:

  • Denver: 4.9%
  • Houston: 4.2%
  • Austin: 4.1%
  • San Antonio : 3.9%
  • Portland, OR: 3.7%

Major metros with the lowest share of accidental landlord rental listings:

  • Boston: 0.6%
  • Providence, RI: 0.6%
  • New York: 0.7%
  • Hartford, CT: 0.7%
  • Buffalo: 0.8%

ResiClub’s spring 2026 analysis found a fairly strong negative relationship (R² = 0.58) between how much a metro’s home prices have shifted since their 2022 peak and its share of accidental landlords. Put simply: Markets with bigger price corrections, like Austin, Denver, and San Antonio, are more likely to see sellers pivot to renting rather than accept what they view as an unfavorable price cut. We also found a strong relationship (R² = 0.65) between accidental landlords and how far active inventory has rebounded above 2019 levels before the COVID-19 pandemic. More listings mean more competition, and more homes that fail to sell.

Why it matters for local markets

The concern for Invitation Homes is pricing power on new move-ins. In Q3 2026, the company’s renewing tenants paid 4.3% more than on their previous lease, while incoming tenants paid 0.2% less than the prior tenant in the same home.

The weakness on new leases was concentrated in Sun Belt markets where rental listing supply has been elevated: Phoenix (-2.9%), South Florida (-2.6%), Tampa, Florida, (-2.4%), Las Vegas (-2.3%), Atlanta (-0.7%), Houston (-0.5%), Denver (-0.4%), and Dallas (-0.1%). Many of those places also have higher shares of accidental landlords. If those accidental landlord shares rise further, it could undo some of the rental inventory cleanup that’s taken place in some of those markets over the past year.

In most markets, accidental landlording remains fairly niche. Many homeowners need the equity from selling their current home to buy their next one, which caps how many can hold onto a home and rent it out (especially given the current affordability picture). On the flip side, homeowners this cycle are under far less financial stress than during the financial crisis of 2008-09, and many locked in ultralow mortgage rates, which allows some to rent out a home at or above their monthly payment while they wait for the market to improve.

If economic conditions worsen, some of those accidental landlords could eventually become “capitulation sellers,” returning to the for-sale market at lower prices.

While shadow rental supply from accidental landlords is a headwind, Invitation Homes argues current rent vs. buy math is a tailwind. The giant SFR landlord says that as of September, it was on average more than $1,000 a month cheaper to lease a home than to own one in its markets.

#10275. How will the 2026 midterms impact the stock market? Experts warn of ‘uniquely difficult’ year, despite history of post-election rallies

Historically, midterms have been good for business in the months following the elections. Over the past 70 years, U.S. stocks, for the most part, have made gains in the months between midterm elections and the end of the year—and since 1980, the S&P 500 index has gone up 13.7% on average in the year after the midterm elections, according to a CNBC analysis.

But 2026 could be different. As things stand, it remains “uniquely difficult” to predict how this year’s midterms will affect the market, according to the Pew Research Center.

Here are a few reasons why.

Going into the midterms, the markets see uncertainty

If there’s one thing the markets do not like, it’s uncertainty—and on the eve of the 2026 midterm elections, there is plenty of it.

From the markets’ perspective, it remains unclear if or how the war in Iran will continue to raise already soaring oil prices; how inflation will play out—either with or without an interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve; and how the tech sector will fare amid growing concerns about runaway spending on artificial intelligence.

From a political perspective, the elections have the potential to redraw the political map, with a number of seats in play, including 435 in the U.S. House of Representatives and 35 in the U.S. Senate.

There are also 36 state governorships, thousands of state legislative seats, and 145 state ballot measures that will be decided, according to the Taubman Center for American Politics and Policy at Brown’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.

“The 2026 election is among the most consequential in decades,” said Eric Patashnik, a political science professor and director of the Taubman Center. “Understanding how the U.S. political system works—and why our governing institutions are struggling to solve the problems Americans care about—has never been more urgent.”

With a number of races too close to call, it remains to be seen whether the Democrats will take back control of the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, and how the markets will react.

Could there be a rally? Or could we see stock drops in government-connected sectors such as defense, healthcare, cryptocurrency, and AI—as a Democratic sweep in one or both branches of Congress could empower the party to investigate U.S. companies? Even for experts, it’s impossible to predict.

#10273. Testing JSON-LD Like an API: 7 Checks Before Your Next Release

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A content editor changes an article’s headline. The page updates immediately, but its JSON-LD still contains the previous title. A redesign introduces a new author component while an old plugin continues publishing a different author name in the page source.

Neither failure necessarily produces a JavaScript error. Both leave machines and readers with conflicting descriptions of the same page.

For developers, the useful approach is to treat JSON-LD as a maintained output of the application, with a data source, validation rules, and regression tests. This guide uses a blog template to show how. You will need basic JavaScript knowledge and a modern Node.js installation for the runnable tests.

Requests for search improvements often arrive as broad outcomes: improve discoverability, clarify entities, or support answer engines. These need to become implementation requirements before development starts.

For example, AEO directory includes structured data within descriptions of broader optimization services. For an engineering team, the actionable deliverable is a page representation whose types, properties, and values can be checked against the published content. I personally used this , and adding this because this can help other developer's and designer for optimization and get higher search result's.

For a blog template, define these acceptance criteria:

Keep implementation success separate from search outcomes. Google’s AI features guidance says there is no special Schema.org markup required for its AI search features. Correct markup also does not guarantee rich results or inclusion in an AI-generated answer.

Avoid separate, manually maintained copies of the headline, author, and publication date. Both the visible template and metadata builder should consume the same published record.

Save the following as article-schema.mjs. The builder assumes an upstream content-validation step has already checked required strings, timestamps, and approved HTTPS URLs.

This is a deliberately small example, not a complete rich-result eligibility checklist. Add relevant images and other supported properties when the real page supplies them. Consult the Schema.org BlogPosting definition and Google’s Article documentation for their respective vocabularies and search guidance.

Use a consistent canonical-URL policy before building the identifier: normalize the intended hostname, trailing-slash convention, and query parameters. Do not generate a fresh UUID for the same article on every request.

SitePoint’s guide to implementing JSON-LD on modern websites covers embedding approaches across common stacks.

Valid JSON is not automatically safe to insert into a raw HTML script element.

A CMS value containing can terminate the element at the HTML-parser level, even when the value belongs to a JSON string. Concatenating a headline directly into a script tag is particularly risky.

Append this helper to article-schema.mjs:

JSON serialization handles quotes and backslashes. Replacing literal less-than characters prevents an embedded closing-script sequence from appearing in the resulting text. The Next.js JSON-LD guide documents this approach for script embedding.

Use the serialized result as the content of a script element with type="application/ld+json". Follow your framework’s documented embedding mechanism so the JSON is neither double-encoded nor inserted through an unrelated HTML context.

This helper is specific to JSON-LD script content. It is not a general-purpose HTML sanitizer, URL validator, or substitute for validating CMS data.

The tests should catch changes that would make metadata misleading or unsafe, not merely confirm that an object exists.

Save this file as article-schema.test.mjs beside the builder:

These are unit tests for the builder and serializer. They do not prove that a template embeds the script correctly or that the deployed page is eligible for a search feature. SitePoint’s explanation of unit, functional, and integration testing helps distinguish those responsibilities.

A passing builder test cannot detect a page component reading a different CMS field.

Add a browser-level check against a controlled article fixture. Inspect its visible heading, byline, dates, canonical link, and JSON-LD together. For this template, assert that the intended article entity appears once and matches those visible fields.

Do not assert that the entire page contains exactly one JSON-LD script. A site may legitimately publish organization, breadcrumb, and article entities separately. Instead, identify the relevant entity by its @id and detect conflicting definitions.

Include these failure cases in the test plan:

Prefer generating metadata from the content loaded during server rendering or static generation when that fits the application. If it is injected client-side, inspect the rendered result and test navigation explicitly. Avoid making essential metadata depend on a user interaction.

No single tool establishes syntax, semantic accuracy, search eligibility, and content consistency at once.

Test both representative code samples and deployed URLs. A validator cannot confirm the truth of an author name simply because the property is syntactically valid.

Google’s general structured-data guidelines also require markup to represent the page accurately. Treat validation warnings as findings to investigate; do not add invented reviews, dates, or attributes merely to improve a tool’s output.

Ownership matters after the first release. Decide which application layer generates article markup, who maintains its mapping, and which publishing events invalidate cached output.

When an editor changes a headline, the visible page and JSON-LD should be rebuilt or refreshed together. Updating one while serving the other from an older cache creates a mismatch even if both implementations are individually correct.

Avoid setting dateModified to the current time on every deployment. A CSS update or infrastructure rebuild does not necessarily mean the article changed. Read the timestamp from the editorial record instead.

Before shipping a template change, run the builder tests, inspect one rendered page per affected template, and check representative deployed URLs. Keep a small fixture set that includes optional fields, long text, translated content, and script-like strings.

A reliable JSON-LD implementation has a traceable relationship with published content. When someone changes the page, its machine-readable description should change predictably—and the test suite should expose the cases where it does not.

#10272. The midterms’ biggest branding trend? Centrism

When Griffin Glaze, a graphic designer, got the job to design James Talarico’s campaign branding, she had just 10 days to do it. Talarico, a Texan who is running for a seat in the U.S. Senate, wanted something that looked unique and nonpartisan.

“A lot of what they were looking for was something that felt different,” Glaze tells Fast Company. The North Carolina designer came up with a visual identity inspired by hand-painted signage at Baptist churches, with texture and imperfection designed into its typography and asterisks for decorative Texas stars. Though they tried out different color palettes, they kept coming back to black and white because it didn’t feel linked to a political party.

“I think for him, it was really about finding something that could be healing, more of a bridge builder, that when people saw it, they weren’t immediately jumping to a specific party,” Glaze says.

Talarico (full disclosure: he’s a Democrat) isn’t alone.

Across the midterm campaign, candidates have branded themselves to play down their party affiliation, and for good reason. Gallup polling earlier this year found 45% of U.S. adults self-identify as independent, a record high. In an environment where both major parties and the president are unpopular, candidates would rather not be associated with any of it, and it’s showing up visually in their logos, mailers, and advertisements.

For candidates actually running as independents, the trend towards less partisan branding means designing the word “independent” directly into their logos. But Democrats and Republicans too have found ways to signal a break from their parties.

In the race for Iowa governor, neither campaign website mentions their party or President Donald Trump, and both candidates use green as their campaign color with logos designed to represent unity. The logo of Zach Lahn, a Republican, says “Iowa First,” while that of the Democrat, Rob Sand, shows shaking hands, above the tagline “Governor for All.”

In Arizona, Governor Katie Hobbs, a Democrat, uses a circular logo with the tagline “For Arizona.” Her state party organization sent mailers to unaffiliated voters that play up elements of her record that would appeal to both sides, like public safety, slashing red tape (for conservatives), and expanding the state’s school lunch program and canceling medical debt (for liberals).

Tropes that were once associated with Republicans have gone bipartisan this year. Democrats are using their own versions of logos like Trump’s, inspired by the so-called “MAGA box,” or adapting his “America First” slogan for their own states to communicate that they’ll put their state ahead of party.

Scott Sutton, president and CEO of the New Jersey print shop Burlington Press, says that while most of the design and print work he’s gotten this year has been extremely partisan, it often comes in the form of attacking the other side for being too extreme.

“We’ve had several Republicans reference socialism to attack their opponents, and equally harsh criticism from Democrats against MAGA,” Sutton says. Even in their attacks, candidates are moving towards the center.

Candidates who play up their bipartisan appeal are trying to inoculate themselves from attacks like this. To show how centrist he would be in office, Adam Hamilton, a Kansas pastor and U.S. Senate candidate, stands in the middle of the field in his 30-second spot “Smack Dab in the Middle” and says, “Here in Kansas, we’re smack dab in the middle of the country” as a metaphor for moderation.

“We’re proud of being in the middle politically too, and that puts us about a million miles away from the extreme politics of Washington that are tearing us apart and driving up prices,” he says, but at no point does he mention he’s a Democrat. The closing tagline of the ad is “Time for Something Different.”

Among advertising for Republican House and Senate candidates, mentions of bipartisanship, working across the aisle, or “both sides” are up 60% from 2024, according to data from the ad tracking firm AdImpact. Mentions of Trump are way down as Republicans seek to distance themselves from him and his agenda.

Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for a U.S. Senate seat from Michigan, practically sounds like a Democrat in a recent ad. It shows him seated in bar with a Canadian beer in front of him, saying, “Canada is not our enemy” and that if elected, he’ll “end this tariff war. Now.” Zach Nunn, an Iowa Republican running for reelection in a House district the nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates as “Lean Democratic,” touts his ranking as one of the three most bipartisan members of Congress as a selling point in his ad “Iowa Comes First.”

Nearly six in 10 Americans have unfavorable views of the Democratic and Republican parties, according to Pew Research Center. Candidates branding themselves to stand apart from them this year are just taking their cues from voters.

A new website seeks to distill over 10,000 public comments across more than 410 local governments, and it's bad news for data center builders.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As more and more AI data centers are being built across the United States, the backlash is starting to gather pace. Following the recent news that Amazon canceled plans to build four new facilities after a public outcry, a new website seeks to detail how sour public sentiment on the subject has turned. American Sentiment is operated by Prophecy Gov, an AI startup based in San Francisco, and it has turned 10,202 public comments at 417 local government meetings from 2026 into a scrollable collection of facts and figures that will give data center builders nightmares, revealing that more than 90% of public comments on data centers are negative.

The website notes that, while public comments don't always match the country's true sentiment, it's clear that the discussion around data center buildouts has reached a "fever pitch" of late. That's something borne out by the data, which takes in 48 states and 417 local governments, with 906 public meetings tracked. Of the 10,202 comments, 90.5% were negative, with just 7% saying positive things about the potential for a new data center being built in their backyard. The remaining 2.5% simply asked questions about the subject. A staggering 73% of meetings had no data center supporters whatsoever. Even those who did support the prospect of a data center being built found themselves outnumbered 6:1, according to the stats.

Predictably, a range of concerns were raised in opposition to data centers, with water use being the most common. In May this year, it was reported that a single AI data center project had consumed 29 million gallons of water. It used so much water, in fact, that local residents noticed a drop in water pressure as a result. A month later, Microsoft claimed its new AI data centers use as little water annually as a restaurant. Beyond water consumption, the impact on local quality of life and the lack of transparency around the project made up the top three complaints. These concerns aren't offset by the benefits of building such facilities, with many people saying that they didn't believe that the claimed benefits would ever come to fruition. Perhaps surprisingly, AI and its potential negative effects weren't mentioned in 4/5 of the comments. Just 21% made any mention of AI as a whole.

Members of the public called out some of AI's biggest players when arguing against data centers, including Google, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft. Concerns also turned personal, with SpaceX/xAI CEO Elon Musk by far the most mentioned during meetings, followed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Notably, Palantir's Peter Thiel was third, ahead of Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos when discussing Amazon.

At a time when the United States may seem more divided than ever, the lack of desire for local data centers appears to be a thoroughly bipartisan issue. Red and blue counties oppose the prospect at almost exactly the same rate, although rural counties raised different issues than urban and suburban ones. The former most commonly worried about the impact on a community's character, farmland, and property rights. Commenters in urban and suburban areas raised the issues of transparency, government distrust, air pollution, and utility bills more often. Pollution is one issue that has been raised previously — a report earlier this month warned that U.S. data centers could wipe out 15 years of progress in greenhouse gas emissions.

There was one group of people largely in favor of new data centers, however. 79% of commenters who said they were union workers were in favor of data centers. Conversely, just 3% of property owners and 3% of residents agreed. Even just 40% of data center workers were in favor of actual data centers, according to the figures.

#10269. Major League Baseball’s new look pays homage to the sport’s history

Major League Baseball has a new look, courtesy of an all-star lineup of type designers.

In 2020, after MLB moved to its new headquarters in New York City, it reached out to Mother Design, the branding and design agency behind work for brands like Cadillac, Tripadvisor, and the scented water bottle Air Up. The league was looking to expand professional baseball’s fandom and talent, and it wanted its visual identity to feel unified.

Beginning in late 2022, Mother Design started building out MLB’s new brand architecture, which was introduced beginning in 2024 on a rolling basis. The league’s famous silhouetted batter logo, designed in 1968 by Jerry Dior, was left untouched, but MLB’s wordmark was updated to fit into larger visual system that’s now complete.

As part of the multiyear brand refresh, the agency tapped five type designers or foundries chosen for their individual specialties to build out a one-of-a-kind font book that shows up across the league, from its Ballpark app and venues to social channels and special events.

Each font in the brand—MLB Franklin, MLB Clarendon, MLB Flare, MLB Block, and MLB Script—was chosen because it’s a style that was present in baseball in the early 20th century in some form or another.

“It’s ensuring that we’ve got these visual cues and these letterforms that have been part of our visual vernacular for longer than any of us have been alive,” Mark Sloan, Mother Design’s New York City head of design, tells Fast Company. “How do we make sure that we carry that forward and we honor that tradition, but that we build them in a way that is prepared for retina screens [on smartphones] and extremely small spaces as well as emphatic, large moments. That’s really the crux of it.”

The typographers for the project were purposefully enlisted. MLB Script was designed by the Bay Area foundry OH no Type Co., which was selected for its attention to unexpected quirky details. The variable typeface includes flags, the horizontal stripe from a word’s final letter that underlines the word and looks quintessentially baseball.

MLB Flare has a handlettering style designed by the Uruguayan foundry Tipotype. The aim is to feel warm and charming, and to reflect and honor the cultural connection between baseball and Latin America.

“There is a long tradition of Latin American players in MLB, so the Latin influence is naturally part of the game,” Tipotype’s cofounders, Martín Sommaruga and Vicente Lamónaca, say in an email. “The Latin community also has a strong presence not as a distinctive feature, but as a fundamental part of the sport itself.”

The type designer Nick Sherman designed a customized version of MLB Franklin, a classic American grotesque-sans serif used on scoreboards that could be seen in stadiums during the recent World Series. MLB Clarendon is similarly a customized version of a classic slab-serif font found throughout baseball history, to which the type designer David Jonathan Ross gave added flexibility in weights and widths.

Skye Dillon, a type designer who specializes in sports branding and designed the 2026 MLB All-Star Game style guide, designed the octagonal MLB Block. It’s based on letterform found on jersey names and numerals and lettering at venues like Ebbets Field, the now-vanished ballpark where the Dodgers played when they were based in Brooklyn.

Research for the brand refresh included books, baseball cards, ticket stubs, felt letters, and individual clubs’ venues, history, and ephemera. The goal was to find visual through lines that go back the furthest but still feel relevant, as if they were designed today, says Sloan, Mother Design’s head of design.

Baseball is rich with typographic inspiration, from jersey lettering and numerals to logos like the interlocking NY monograms for the Yankees and Mets. Sloan compared baseball to “a visual history of the country itself,” and says it’s arguably responsible for keeping a lot of typographic styles alive and relevant in pop culture.

“If you look at something like baseball script, for example, it’s something that as Americans, it’s in our visual consciousness,” Sloan says. “It sort of comes in and out of fashion in the world of branding, but it’s always been in fashion in baseball.”

The 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 launched at a price of $120 in January 2025.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Raspberry Pi boss Eben Upton has officially announced price rises for some 16GB products. Specifically, the price of the 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 is being raised by $80 to $385, and the 16GB Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 will go up by $40. In a glimmer of better news, the price of the Raspberry Pi 500+ all-in-one desktop, which also features a 16GB model, is being held, but it was already rather pricey.

Upton framed the decision to raise prices as being due to “the steep rises in the cost of memory over the past two years.” He explained that other computer makers have had to make similar decisions recently. That sounds fair, and he added that Raspberry Pi had been doing what they could to minimize costs passed on to customers.

The price rise of the headline 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 to $385 is effective immediately. As is the $40 increase to the CM5 16GB variant. Of course, both these 16GB devices have seen prior increases in price since being launched at $120 and $135, respectively.

Some moderately good news was that there would be no price increase today for the Raspberry Pi 500+ 16GB all-in-one keyboard wedge computer. Upton didn’t mention that this is already rather expensive at $485, though.

Indeed, there have been several waves of price increases affecting Pis since the components RAMpocalypse began. Only a month ago we saw a similar cost-of-memory post by Upton on the official blog, this time accompanied by news that there were price increases being implemented for the 2GB Raspberry Pi 4 and Raspberry Pi 5 models. Prices of both rose by $12.50, to $67.50 and $77.50, respectively. Perhaps this price gulf between the 2GB and 16GB Pi 5 helps highlight the heavy impact of RAM pricing even more clearly than today’s blog. 1GB devices haven’t seen price rises recently.

The price rises, and comparison in prices between high-and-low memory density models makes it all the more important “to make sure you’re not paying for more memory than you need,” indicates the Raspberry Pi blog about the latest price increases. Sadly for the Pi business, hobbyists and makers already seem to be moving away from the full-sized Pi and CM products for many DIY projects.

Higher pricing is affecting all sorts of computer products, but it might have a particular impact on Raspberry Pi’s business. Generations of this device were explicitly designed around a strict budget constraint, and very famously stuck to a $25–$35 target price for many years.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Now the core Raspberry Pi business is being squeezed by simpler microcontrollers at the low end, where the use of Picos and ESP32 boards have become increasingly popular for small projects. At the other end of the market, with some Pis approaching $400 or $500, makers start to eye entry-level x86 SBCs and mini PCs. Even a cheap mini PC can be powerful with a stronger CPU, GPU, NPU, and more. Mini PCs can win on flexibility and expandability too, and there’s a wide variety to choose from capable of running the most popular and capable OSes and applications.

#10266. Personality is the new fuel for marketing

Through the annals of advertising history, the gospel of brand building has been written around a single capital letter: P.

The classical four P’s of price, product, place, and promotion were drilled into marketing minds in college. The major brand totem, P for positioning, is where companies spent millions defining razor-thin functional benefits, establishing category ladders, and staking claim to owned territory in the consumer’s mind. The last decade’s reverence has been for the all-guiding P for purpose, where brands raced to solve global crises, writing manifesto after manifesto, making very similar-looking ads to save the world (and sell products).

Now, the pendulum has swung again. While some would argue that positioning could feel cold and analytical, and purpose maybe grew lofty and detached, the new imperative for business growth is infinitely more human. This might arguably be at a time when consumers want something more human and real.

ENTER THE ERA OF PERSONALITY.

Personality is the new fuel for supercharging commercial growth. It is no longer enough for a brand to stand for an ideal or a functional benefit; it has to show up as a living, breathing entity with a voice, a soul, a vibe, and a belief system. Needing a distinct perspective on the world and attitude that consumers can feel part of, co-create with, and ultimately believe in, is key.

Adzooma research suggests that 57.5% of consumers buy brands with strong, distinct personalities. Meanwhile, according to the Future Proof report from The Daily Aus, only one in five feel positively about a brand when it relies solely on describing itself as “purpose-driven.” With information overload in this attention economy, and perhaps if we dare say it, as a small rally against AI, we are seeing consumers gravitating towards brands that make them feel something real. And this shift is creating commercial velocity for those brands that are determining how to win in this moment.

Duolingo transformed its green owl mascot from a simple app icon into a slightly unhinged, self-aware cultural icon with a living and breathing point of view in the world. It scaled fandom, deep commercial impact, and drove 1.7 billion views.

And e.l.f. Beauty delivered 30 consecutive quarters of business growth by being a bold disrupter with a kind heart. Its product and personality ecosystem goes hand in hand, allowing its community to feel, live, and be the DNA of its brand. 

Poppi unleashed a personality that shaped a new category with a distinctive and fresh POV, provoking a $1.95 billion acquisition by Pepsi while getting over 1 billion views on TikTok on the journey.

Liquid Death, one could argue, was the early creator of this movement. It brought personality to water with a living content machine that unleashed who they were in the world, stimulating a 6-year CAGR of 122% since its 2019 launch.

So how do brands develop a new weapon beyond expected corporate tone guidelines and build a personality and world that is rich, deep, and drives growth?

It starts by rethinking how personality operates.

4 PILLARS OF BRAND PERSONALITY

To build a personality that flexes and wins across a community-led world, brands must become the masters of four fundamentals:

1. How you speak (voice and fluidity): Stop trapping your brand inside rigid, 50-page tonal guidelines. In a fast-moving culture, your voice needs to flex. It’s about codifying the rhythms and rules of how your brand talks so that it retains unmistakable recognition whether responding in a social media comment or running a Super Bowl ad.

2. How you look (visual identity): We live in a visually driven culture where brand lust is dictated by design. Craft a signature look, and be clear on your distinctive brand assets, but be fluid with it. You can play and flex how you show up for different audiences while still always looking and feeling like yourself.

3. How you feel (vibe and energy): Define the energy your brand brings to the room. Brands that possess a clear “vibe” can react, improvise, and play in real time alongside their communities, and become magnetic to the consumers they want to attract.

4. How you act (real-world behavior): Personality is proven through action, not empty claims. When a brand uses its core belief system to do bold, unexpected things in the real world, it turns passive consumers into passionate advocates. This is where personality breathes life back into purpose.

    BE A CATALYST

    If you can unlock the awesomeness of your brand, the final shift you need to make is changing how you behave as a brand leader. Unleash a new personality within yourself.

    For decades, marketing leadership was defined by brand guardianship. Leaders were trained to protect the brand identity, enforce rigid guidelines, and shield the company from risk.

    But in a world driven by fast-moving communities, creator economies, and real-time culture, protection is passive. Guardians end up building polished, potentially lifeless museum artifacts that can trigger a brand’s demise.

    To succeed today, leaders must shift from being guardians to being catalysts.

    A catalyst doesn’t lock the brand in a vault. A catalyst ignites the brand’s personality, empowering teams and communities to play with it, flex it, and bring energy, empathy, and humanity to everything it touches. They live, breathe, and become the brand.

    So stop playing it safe, be comfortable in the chaos, and embrace the fluidity of what can help you win. Find your authentic voice. Rise above the sea of sameness. Unleash uniqueness. Let your brand’s personality lead the way to fuel your next phase of growth.

    Chris Kay is the international CEO of 72andSunny.

    #10264. Election Day is unfolding across America after a surge in early voting for the midterms

    The final day of voting in this year’s midterm elections arrived Tuesday against a backdrop of uncertainty after a year in which President Donald Trump has tried to interfere in how states run their elections and sown doubts about the outcome should Republicans lose.

    Millions of Americans already have cast their ballots, with early voting turnout on pace to eclipse that of the last midterm elections. In contrast to the president’s continued rhetoric about election cheating, voting so far has unfolded with relatively few problems.

    Trump has spent months trying to use the power of the presidency to put his thumb on the scale of this year’s elections, which will determine whether his party keeps control of Congress.

    His Justice and Homeland Security departments have been involved in a massive hunt for voters who are not U.S. citizens, at one point engaging in a made-for-the-cameras predawn operation that led to more than two dozen arrests in California. The Department of Justice was planning its largest-ever effort to monitor Election Day polling places, countered by an even larger effort among Democrats and allied groups, and at the president’s urging had sued to block certification of Alaska’s results if the outcome of the Senate race favored Democrats.

    At the same time, Trump’s constant false claims about widespread voter fraud led election officials and Democratic groups across the country to plan for the possibility of immigration agents at voting sites or federal officers seizing voting machines. His administration has insisted that no armed federal officials would be guarding the polls on Election Day.

    Courts have blocked the Trump administration’s efforts to influence elections

    In the run-up to Tuesday, none of the steps Democrats most feared had come to pass, and the Republican administration’s legal maneuvers had been largely blocked by the courts.

    One of the Trump administration’s most high-profile attempts to interfere in state elections was turned away Monday night by the U.S. Supreme Court, which rejected its push to force California to set aside thousands of ballots as part of its search for noncitizen voters. In another Monday night ruling, a federal judge said the Trump administration must stop sending voter lists of alleged noncitizens to election officials.

    Even the administration’s own record of arrests and charges has demonstrated what research and state investigations have made clear for years — that instances of noncitizens casting ballots are extremely rare.

    Monday’s rulings followed another defeat for the president at the Supreme Court less than two months ago, when it rejected his attempt to limit mail balloting through changes at the Postal Service. That directive was included in one of two executive orders Trump has signed during his second term that attempted to federalize certain aspects of elections, even though the Constitution gives the states, and sometimes Congress, the authority to set election rules.

    Voting begins smoothly with some weather disruptions in the Southwest

    The first polling sites opened at 6 a.m. EST Tuesday in a handful of states — Connecticut, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Missouri, New Jersey, New York and Virginia.

    Heavy rains and flash flooding in a swath of the Southwest were expected to make it harder for some voters to reach polling places in parts of Colorado, Arizona, Utah and New Mexico. Election administrators in the Navajo Nation announced changes to several of its polling locations, and in Utah’s rural San Juan County, voters were being allowed to vote electronically on Tuesday because some of them may not be able to reach polling places.

    Election administrators and voting rights advocates have been advising voters casting late absentee ballots to use drop boxes or deliver them to polling places in person rather than mail them. The advice came after concerns emerged that recent changes in U.S. Postal Service operations could result in postmarking delays that would mean mail ballots could not be counted. Late-arriving ballots or late postmarks disenfranchised tens of thousands of voters in California, Oregon and Washington, which mail ballots to all voters, during this year’s primaries.

    Trump hasn’t committed to accepting the election results

    The most significant disruptions ahead of Election Day were the Trump administration’s attempts to interfere. Voting rights groups, Democrats and the Justice Department have been exchanging a flurry of legal filings over alleged noncitizen voters, federal election monitors, federal intimidation of election officials and other concerns. They reveal how Trump’s attempts to expand federal control over state-run elections — combined with high-stakes races — are resulting in court battles that could extend past Election Day into ballot counting and certification of the results.

    Election law experts said Trump’s lawsuits go beyond historic norms, but they said the administration’s legal arguments were unlikely to convince the courts.

    Trump also has ramped up his own equivocations about whether the election will be legitimate, as he has in the past. A week before Election Day, when a reporter asked him if he would accept the results, he offered a qualified answer.

    “I will if they are honest,” he said.

    Associated Press writer Geoff Mulvihill contributed to this report.

    —Ali Swenson, Associated Press

    Creality’s K3 is a solid entry into the swelling tool changer market, but without the lid and TPU Kit ready at launch, we’re left wondering what else this machine is capable of doing. The overly large spool holders impose a frustrating limit on the brands of filament you can use. Still, this is a good printer for fans of the Creality lineup who only need PLA or PETG.

    Top hat and TPU printing kit not available at launch

    Spool holders are too large for many 3rd party spools

    Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

    Creality has finally caught up with the tool changer fad, presenting us with a speedy, four-nozzle system named “KliTek” mounted on a Creality K3. Tool changers are the way to go, since they do not compromise speed for color and eliminate the need to waste your filament in the form of “printer poop.” The K3 is still programmed to create a purge tower on multicolor prints, but this is a small fraction of the filament wasted using any type of AMS-style color system.

    The new KliTek nozzle system supports printing with different-sized nozzles in the same print, which sounds more useful than I actually found practical. Users will also be able to blend colors in Creality Print, a trick picked up from Snapmaker’s open-source Full Spectrum. This method creates the optical illusion of new colors by stacking very thin layers of filament.

    The tool-changing system works very well and never dropped or misplaced a tool during the review. Creality has tucked 37 sensors inside the printer, with 12 dedicated to the nozzle swapping process alone. No, I’m not going to name all of them, but they do work. I didn’t get a single bad print during the review, even when running at higher speeds.

    However, the K3 looks suspiciously like a Snapmaker U1 clone, departing from the black and grey aesthetic of the K1 and K2 3D printers. It has conveniently placed, side-mounted spool holders that are a tad too large for many 3rd party brands of filament. We’re not sure if they’re trying to herd us towards a walled garden of Creality plastics, or if they simply didn’t check out all the options.

    Unfortunately, the Creality K3 needs a lid for printing high-temperature filaments, and this “tophat” was not ready at the time of the review. Creality says the top hat will be packaged with a TPU Kit to enable the printing of super soft materials.

    The K3 is currently on preorder with a price tag of $849. The competition for affordable tool changers is pretty stiff, and Creality hasn’t brought anything new to the table, which is keeping the K3 off our list of the very best 3D printers you can buy. But if you’re a fan of the Creality ecosystem, it’s a welcome addition to the fleet.

    260 x 260 x 260 mm (10.23 x 10.23 x 10.23 in)

    PLA/PETG/PCTG/TPU/CF and GF filled (up to 300 °C)

    Double-sided Textured PEI steel flex plate (up to 100 °C)

    482 x 420 x 536 mm (18.97 x 16.53 x 21.10 in)

    The Creality K3 comes with everything you need to assemble and maintain your printer. The included tool kit has hex keys, side cutters, grease, and a nice nozzle cleaner. There is also a paper copy of the quick installation guide and a 200g spool of white Creality filament.

    Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

    The Creality K3 has four tools, each with a built-in ceramic heater, nozzle with a hardened steel insert, and filament path. The KliTek system supports printing with different nozzle sizes and different materials in the same print. Like the Prusa/Bondtech INDX, the extruder and cooling fan are mounted on a single toolhead.

    The rest of the Creality K3 shares its design with the K2. The printer has a solid metal frame clad in white plastic and a glass door with dampened hinges. The motion system is Core XY, with a linear rail for the X axis and linear rods for the Y axis. The bed rides on four linear rods driven by 2 lead screws belted to a single stepper motor on the bottom of the printer. Parts cooling is provided by a blower fan in the toolhead and a large side-mounted blower fan mounted on the left side of the case. The stock Creality K3 comes with an open top, so chamber cooling is not an issue. Unfortunately, this makes the printer rather loud.

    The Creality K3 has a 720p camera located at the top right of the printer, which does a great job providing print monitoring from the device tab in the slicer and the Creality Cloud app. There is also an AI camera that monitors for build plate detection, foreign object detection, and spaghetti detection. There were no false positives during the test.

    We did not get to review the special TPU kit, which will allow the machine to run super soft TPU, which is becoming quite trendy for those interested in printing shoes. The kit will replace the CFS Nano material handler with a CFS Flex and add dry boxes for the filament and a special high-flow nozzle. The kit will be bundled with a lid/ tophat with ventilation and air filtration.

    The Creality K3 arrives with some assembly required. After removing the packing material, you need to remove the four screws securing the bed for shipping, and there is a nice reminder to do this when first firing up the printer.

    The spool holders twist into the printer’s side panels and are numbered to match the filament slots. Two PTFE guide brackets, also numbered, need to be secured to the rear of the printer with M4x6 screws, as does the bracket for the CFS Nano. There is a communication cable that runs from the rear of the printer to the CFS Nano as well.

    The tool cables attach to the top of the printer with 2 M4x12 screws each, with the PTFE tubes running to the CFS Nano. The toolhead communication cable is attached with M3x5 screws on the toolhead and M4x8 screws on the right side of the printer. Attaching PTFE guide tubes from the side brackets up to the CFS Nano completes the assembly.

    The Creality K3 does an excellent job calibrating and bed leveling as part of its initial self-check. Bed leveling can be repeated at the start of each print.

    Loading filament into the Creality K3 is pretty simple. Filament is inserted into a port on the side bracket, which guides it up to the CFS Nano, which does the rest. The filament waits in the tube until called for by a print job. It is then loaded into the tool.

    To unload, the tool is selected from the printer’s screen. The printer then cuts the filament and retracts it out of the tool, and it can be manually pulled out of the CFS Nano the rest of the way.

    All four filament slots can read RFID tags in the spools to load information for Creality-branded filament. For other filament brands, the printer will beep to remind you to manually enter the filament type and color.

    The latest version of Creality Print 7.3 is available from Creality.com. It is based on the Orca Slicer and Ultimaker Cura Engine. The default settings worked well, and there is a new AI assistant mode, which is still labeled as beta. At the time of the review, the only thing missing for the K3 was a button to map the filaments into the slicer. The button is still there for the earlier K-series printers in the slicer. The slicer does have filament mixing for more color combinations.

    A link at the top of the page will take you to Creality’s AI Creation tools and Creality Cloud, Creality’s online file-sharing service. If you don’t like the Cloud, you can export files from the slicer and either move them to the printer with a USB stick or move them over your home network by accessing the printer’s FLUIDD interface. To access FLUIDD, you need to find the IP address of your printer and type that into a browser window, followed by:4408 with no spaces.

    The Creality K3 comes with a 200g spool of white Hyper PLA. If you want more colors and materials, you should check out our guide to the best filaments for 3D printing for suggestions.

    For the first print, I was going to run a pumpkin fidget toy, so I grabbed a spool of Prusa orange and was really quite cross when it didn’t fit on the preposterously large spool holders. I decided right then to mod the spool holder with the Creality Pika scanner. I took the scan into Tinkercad and reduced the diameter of the spool holder, then ran the new spool holders in Inland basic white using a .2 layer height and an average print speed of 170mm/s. The print took 8 hours and 34 minutes to complete. I do not usually mod printers while reviewing them, but Prusa Orange is perfect for pumpkins.

    Below is the original spool holder (left) and the modded version (right).

    For my second print, I did a pumpkin fidget toy I found on MakerWorld using Prusa orange PLA, Elegoo green PLA Pro, and Polymaker black HT-PLA Pro. I used a .2 mm layer height and printed with an average speed of 160mm/s; the print took a little over six hours. It came out nice without a hint of overextrusion. I liked it so much I decided to print it again scaled up to 200%. Using the same settings, the larger print took 16 hours and 28 minutes and is also very nice with a good fidget action.

    For PETG, I printed a plate of 3 flexy geckos I found on Creality Cloud using Prusa Carmine Red, Prusa Sky Blue, and Bambu Lab basic white PETG. Using a .2mm layer height and running at 180mm/s, the print took 5 hours 45 minutes to complete. The geckos are smooth and clean, plus all of the links work perfectly with no stringing or overextrusion present.

    The Creality K3 did not have its special “flex” CFS at the time of review, but I decided to try TPU anyway. I printed some omni wheels for a Death Racer we’re working on in both hard TPU for MFS from Inland and some 95A Inland rainbow TPU. The stock CFS Nano had no trouble pushing these, and the toolhead extruder had no problem with it. It did well. Trouble came when I tried some 90A TPU from Bambu Lab. I’d stick to the harder stuff until the TPU kit is ready.

    I did get good prints with the black TPU for AMS and the rainbow 95A filaments. The prints are omni-wheel rollers from the Deathracer project of Michael Baddeley. Both sets of eight rollers were printed at a .2mm layer height at an average speed of 50mm/s and each took a little over 4 hours to print. There was a tiny bit of stringing, but otherwise the rollers are perfect.

    The Creality K3 is a terrific printer that should become more capable with accessories like the tophat and TPU kit in the future. The oversized spools are a little annoying, but easily fixed. The only thing I worry about is Creality’s track record of releasing a printer, then introducing a better “pro” or “max” model within four months. I wouldn’t be surprised if we get a six- or eight-color K3 variant before next spring.

    At its prelaunch price of $849, it’s $100 more than a similarly equipped, slightly larger Snapmaker U1, which is a tough place to be. It is also the same price as the fully enclosed Flashforge Creator 5 Pro, which we didn’t review, but we did check out the budget model Flashforge Creator 5, which is currently available for $699.

    MORE: Best Budget 3D Printers for Beginners

    Denise Bertacchi is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware US, covering 3D printing. Denise has been crafting with PCs since she discovered Print Shop had clip art on her Apple IIe. She loves reviewing 3D printers because she can mix all her passions: printing, photography, and writing.

    #10261. ‘Blue tsunami’ watch: 4 ways to track the midterm election results today

    Election Day 2026 is here. By the end of today (Tuesday, November 3, 2026), the balance of power in Washington is almost certain to have shifted. But the big question is, by how much?

    Voting in the 2026 midterm elections across the country is now underway, and most political analysts say it could be a blowout for the Democrats, with polls showing that voters are broadly concerned about the economy—especially inflationary pressures and rising gas prices.

    What do the latest polls say?

    The latest CNN Poll of Polls shows that 52% of voters prefer Democrats for Congress, compared to 43% preferring Republicans. NBC puts it at 52% for Democrats and 44% for Republicans.

    As Axios reports, election forecaster Nate Silver says the Democrats have a 95% probability of winning the House and an 80% probability of winning the Senate. More than just a “blue wave,” Silver says today’s election could be a “blue tsunami.” 

    What is the makeup of Congress right now?

    Currently, the 100 Senate seats are made up of 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats, and 2 Independents (who caucus with the Dems).

    The 435 House seats are made up of 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, and 1 Independent (with two vacancies).

    To flip both chambers, the Democrats need to achieve just 218 seats in the House and 51 in the Senate—something polls show is within reach.

    However, historically, polling has underrepresented Republican support in some states. A lot of races will also ultimately hinge on voter turnout. That means nothing is certain until every last vote is counted.

    How can I track the election results live?

    If you want to track the 2026 midterm results as they come in, you can do so online in several ways, including:

    • Maps galore: News organizations love to visualize election data, especially using maps. To see individual states turn blue or red for their open House and Senate seats tonight, you can follow along online with interactive maps from the Associated Press, Bloomberg, CNN, Fox News, and 270toWin.
    • YouTube: Cord-cutters may still prefer live broadcast coverage of election results, and for them, YouTube is a great option. Several major news outlets will be streaming their election coverage live this evening, including ABC News, CBS News, Fox News, and PBS NewsHour.
    • Google: If you don’t feel like watching talking heads or seeing maps slowly turn blue or red, and instead just want a quick update, Google is your friend. The search giant usually embeds the latest election results at the top of search result pages when you type in related queries like “election results” or “Midterm results.”
    • iPhone: Apple’s iPhone supports Live Activities—widgets that live on your home and lock screen that update in real time. Today, Apple’s News app lets people opt in to display real-time election results on their screen—no manual action required to see the latest results. To enable the Live Activity election widget, open the News app, then tap the “Follow the 2026 midterms live” banner at the top of the screen.

    Polls begin to close at 6 p.m. ET tonight, so you can expect to see the first results shortly after.

    However, if you do plan on watching all the results, you could be in for a late night. The final polls in the country—those in Alaska—don’t close until 1 a.m. ET.

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    Learning how to create an app in ChatGPT starts with the Jotform App Builder plugin (listed in ChatGPT's plugin directory as Jotform Apps): install it, connect a Jotform account, describe the app, approve the requested action, and refine the result. The plugin creates a Jotform App containing pages, forms, and resources that can be edited in Jotform App Builder and shared with its intended audience.

    ChatGPT helps turn an idea into a clear request and supports revisions through conversation. The Jotform App Builder plugin performs the app-building actions, while the App Builder in Jotform provides the editor for closer customization.

    This no-code ChatGPT app builder workflow suits projects built around information, forms, and everyday tasks.

    "ChatGPT app development" can also describe coding projects. OpenAI's documentation on building plugins for ChatGPT describes a package of skills, an optional MCP server that connects to tools and data through the Model Context Protocol, optional UI, authentication, and publishing. The two routes differ like this:

    This article covers the no-code route. The result is a Jotform App; the workflow does not include writing and deploying a separate codebase.

    A Jotform App can organize pages, forms, and resources for customers, employees, members, or event attendees. The most useful first project has one audience and one clear purpose. Here are some examples:

    These are starting structures. A booking form, for example, still needs its availability settings checked. An ordering app needs its order process reviewed, and any payment setup requires separate attention.

    Setup starts with installing the plugin in ChatGPT and authorizing access to the intended Jotform account. Jotform's own how-to guide lists the steps.

    To create an app in ChatGPT, select the installed plugin in a new chat and enter a specific description. Include the audience, purpose, pages, and design direction.

    This gives the AI app builder a defined structure. The studio should then supply its real booking URL, approved resource links, contact details, and onboarding copy during review. It is important to review every generated form, link, and business rule before use.

    A good prompt explains who will use the app, what they need to accomplish, and which elements support that task. Visual preferences help, but purpose and content should come first.

    "Build an app for my business" leaves the audience, structure, and actions unclear. The design-studio example identifies a client audience, an onboarding task, specific pages, and a color scheme. Before submitting a request, define:

    Request the essentials to build a Jotform App around one process, then expand.

    The plugin supports follow-up requests in the same chat. Smaller changes make it easier to review each update and identify anything that needs correction. For the studio onboarding app, some follow-ups could include:

    Each request should be followed by a review of the result. A map needs the correct address; a gallery needs suitable images; a booking form needs appropriate fields and configuration.

    Select Edit in Jotform when you need closer editing. In Jotform App Builder, inspect every page, element, form, link, label, and visual choice. Replace the sample content and check that navigation follows the client's expected path. Third-party integrations require manual setup in the builder, so requesting a booking feature should not be treated as confirmation that an external calendar has been connected.

    Select Share App in the generated result to open the available sharing options. For detailed distribution and access settings, open the app in Jotform App Builder and use the Publish tab and Quick Share. Jotform's sharing guide covers each option.

    The builder supports copying the app link, inviting people by email, social sharing, and downloading a QR code. Choose the method that fits your audience: a client can receive a link, while event attendees may find a QR code more useful.

    Review access before distributing the app, because newly created apps are public by default. Check exactly what a visitor can open before publishing.

    Test the Jotform App as an intended user would, using fictional information first. Review it on both desktop and mobile before collecting real submissions.

    Creating an app with the plugin is free to start, and Jotform offers a free Starter plan, but app usage remains subject to your account's allowances. A Jotform support reply from 2024 describes Starter as up to five forms and 100 monthly submissions. These are account allowances, rather than a separate allocation for each generated app, and they may have changed, so confirm them on Jotform's current pricing page. Paid plans provide more submissions.

    Before you launch, compare expected usage with the current account limits. An onboarding app serving a few clients has different requirements from an event app collecting hundreds of registrations.

    The most common mistakes are unclear requests, oversized first versions, and sharing before testing. Each can be reduced by defining a smaller task and reviewing the result.

    This workflow is best for defined business tasks. Projects requiring extensive custom backend behavior need a separate assessment, such as the developer route described above.

    Before sharing, confirm that the app serves its intended audience and that its content, behavior, and settings have been reviewed. A short launch checklist helps keep the review consistent.

    Here are some frequently asked questions about the output, account requirements, and practical limits of the Jotform App Builder plugin.

    Yes. With the plugin installed and authorized, plain-language requests can generate and revise an app in ChatGPT.

    The plugin can create a Jotform App combining pages, forms, and resources. Follow-up prompts can refine its structure, content, and design.

    Customer portals, internal tools, event apps, business websites, directories, onboarding hubs, and booking or ordering apps are some of the suitable starting points.

    Yes. Setup requires signing in to Jotform and authorizing the connection.

    Yes. Further prompts support revisions in the same chat. Edit in Jotform opens the editor, and Share App provides sharing options.

    Yes. The workflow supports forms and requests for booking forms, maps, FAQs, and galleries. Check their content and configuration before use.

    A Jotform App is the finished app created and maintained through Jotform. A custom GPT configures a conversational assistant, while a plugin or application made with OpenAI developer tools involves a separate development workflow with its own build, authentication, and publishing steps.

    Understanding how to create an app in ChatGPT means keeping the roles clear: ChatGPT supports the conversation, the plugin creates and revises the Jotform App, and the Jotform editor handles closer editing and configuration.

    Start with a focused task, then review the content, permissions, and behavior. Test the complete experience with sample information before sharing it with the intended audience.

    #10257. How soon will we know who controls Congress? It could be a while. Here’s why

    The stakes in Tuesday’s election — which party will control Congress — are crystal clear. But when that will be known is impossible to say.

    The Associated Press will be calling races in all 435 House districts and the 35 Senate contests that are up for election this year.

    Control of the House depends on which party reaches 218 seats. Currently, 219 members caucus with Republicans, just one more than the minimum needed for a majority when all seats are filled. There are two vacancies now.

    The bar for the Senate is 51 seats for Democrats or 50 for Republicans, since Vice President JD Vance can cast a tiebreaking vote for his party. Republicans have a 53-47 edge in the Senate right now.

    During the last midterm elections in 2022, the AP called control of the Senate four days after Election Day, while the House call was eight days after.

    During the presidential cycle of 2024, there was a bigger gap between the two. Senate control was called the day after Election Day, with the House call coming eight days later.

    Some states consistently take days to count all their ballots. California, the nation’s most populous, has seen thousands of mail ballots dropped off on Election Day. In 2022, half the state’s votes were counted after Election Day.

    Other states like Alaska and Maine, which have key Senate races this year, use ranked choice voting.

    A candidate can win with more than 50% of votes in the first round, but if no one reaches that threshold then the candidate with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated and their votes are redistributed to the voter’s second choice. The process can significantly delay results.

    The AP does not make projections and will only declare a winner when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow the trailing candidates to close the gap.

    —Mike Catalini, Associated Press

    Owners of non-state data centers in Russia have been told to hold back 10% of their capacity, ready to aid the country's state-owned IT infrastructure should the need arise. That's the message from President Vladimir Putin, with the aim of quickly unlocking additional data center compute capacity in the future if it becomes needed by the state, reports Reuters.

    This comes as Russian data centers have become targets for Ukrainian drone attacks in recent weeks, causing huge amounts of damage and affecting state-owned internet services. In early October, drones struck Russia's largest data center in what was the second such attack in as many days. The huge 63-megawatt facility was so badly damaged that multiple modules had to be removed from service completely. At the time, users reported problems with Yandex Mail, Disk, Documents, Pay, and Market despite Yandex claiming that key services remained up and running. Two weeks later, Russia's finance ministry's data center was damaged after Ukrainian drones targeted the facility. It was reportedly home to Russia's tax databases as well as other state registry data.

    Now, Putin has told the Digital Development Ministry to inventory all available data center capacity and floor space at privately owned facilities throughout the country. A new government commission will be given the power to order the release of reserved data center capacity. Once ordered to do so, third-party data center owners will have 24 hours to comply. The temporary use of data centers located outside Russia has also been mooted, pending the approval of Russia's Federal Security Service. (FSB)

    It isn't just drones that have been targeting Russian data centers. On the same day that news broke of the country's plan to siphon data center capacity from third parties, the Russian Federal State Statistics Service admitted that its servers were hit by cyberattacks that saw 23TB of data stolen. It's reported that the haul includes new data on Russian wartime losses marked “for official use only.”

    Data centers have become a target for Russia, too. It bombed Ukrainian facilities in September of this year, resulting in the loss of internet connectivity for 100,000 households. At the time, a government official noted that Ukraine's internet network is highly decentralized before admitting that users should expect local disruptions to service.

    #10254. Apple just had its best year ever. So why is its stock falling?

    Yesterday, Apple (Nasdaq: AAPL) reported its fourth-quarter results, which closed out its fiscal 2026 financial year.

    On the surface, the results were exceptionally strong, with Apple exceeding Wall Street’s expectations on the most important metrics. But after announcing its results, AAPL shares fell, and today in early morning trading they are down. Here’s what you need to know.

    Apple’s Q4 beat expectations

    Wall Street had some lofty expectations for Apple going into its Q4 2026 earnings report. Analysts had a consensus expectation of Apple delivering $113.46 billion in revenue and earnings per share (EPS) of $2.00.

    Apple topped both.

    The company ended up reporting $114.5 billion in revenue and an EPS of $2.10. But things were even better: Its all-important iPhone revenue for the quarter was $57.58 billion, beating analyst expectations by more than a billion dollars, suggesting that, despite price hikes, demand for Apple’s smartphones remains strong. Mac revenue came in at $10.79 billion, also beating analyst expectations by more than a billion dollars.

    “Today, Apple is proud to report a September quarter revenue record of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent from a year ago,” Apple CEO John Ternus said, “with iPhone reaching a September quarter record and Services reaching an all-time high, capping off our best fiscal year ever.”

    Still, Apple shares fell after its earnings report, which was released after the closing bell yesterday. And today, the company’s stock price is down around 2% as of the time of this writing to $327.25.

    But why?

    Guidance matters more than results

    Investors love great, record-setting results. But if they love one thing more than results, it’s guidance showing the future is rosy for the company.

    After Apple reported its Q4 results yesterday, it also issued guidance for its current quarter, which is Q1 of fiscal 2027. The quarter is arguably Apple’s most important as it’s the first full quarter with the new iPhone on sale, and it covers the all-important holiday period.

    On the sales front, things look positive: Apple is forecasting a record Q1 revenue of $158.18 billion. However, revenue isn’t profit, which comes from the margins on its sales. And Apple’s reported gross margin guidance for Q1 wasn’t what investors wanted to hear.

    Apple said it expects gross margins for the quarter to be between 45% and 46%. As CNBC noted, analysts expected Apple to guide gross margins to 46.3%. Either way, those gross margins are expected to be well below Apple’s Q4 gross margins of 47.9%.

    The lower-than-expected gross-margin guidance seems to be the main driver of AAPL’s stock price drop today.

    Why are Apple’s gross margins expected to decline?

    But why are Apple’s gross margins expected to decline when the company has raised prices on most of its products in recent months?

    You can blame the so-called RAMageddon—the skyrocketing cost of memory, which AI hyperscalers are gobbling up to power their data centers, leaving consumer electronics companies like Apple forced to pay more for an increasingly scarce component that used to be relatively inexpensive.

    Apple chief financial officer Kevan Parekh told analysts that its expected lower margins for Q1 “includes primarily the impact of higher memory costs” in addition to “some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI,” the company’s revamped AI chatbot.

    The higher consumer prices but lower-margins discrepancy shows that Apple isn’t passing the full cost of higher memory prices onto customers; instead, it’s absorbing some of those costs to keep product prices rising even further, which could potentially put consumers off upgrading.

    #10253. Hate hearing your own voice? Blame your skull

    In the 20 years I’ve been a TV producer, media executive, and speaking coach, I cannot count the number of times I’ve seen people literally cringe upon hearing their own voice. Sometimes it’s a slight scrunch of the nose and sometimes it’s an audible sigh. Why do we hate our own voice? And what can we do about it?

    It’s not you, it’s biology

    You’re not that special. I don’t mean that rudely, but you’re actually a member of a very large club. The reason you hate the sound of your own voice is grounded in biology. In evolutionary terms, we have only been hearing our voice played back for a short amount of time. While humans have been around for hundreds of thousands of years, our recordings have not. Thomas Edison first recorded and played back his own voice just 150 years ago. (Fun fact: he sang “Mary Had a Little Lamb.”) Our body has not caught up yet to technology.

    It’s your skull’s fault

    Why do your friends not cringe at your voice, but you do? They hear your voice differently than you do. When we hear our own voice, there are vibrating sound waves hitting the ear drum and vibrations inside our skull due to our vocal cords. As they travel, the lower tones come through stronger. That makes us think our voice is deeper and richer than it is. When we hear our voice as it actually sounds, we’re not used to it.  

    How to get over it

    When you’re just starting to improve your speaking skills, it’s very hard to listen to recordings of your own voice. However, if you’re committed to improving, it’s essential. Every CEO I media train watches their TV segments back. Every coach I work with listens to the podcast they were a guest on. Every speaker I support watches their speech. We listen to it afterwards together. 

    Familiarity breeds like

    Familiarity often breeds liking because of a psychological concept known as the “mere exposure” effect. Listen to your voice back. I recommend starting with audio or video where you sound unrehearsed—on a zoom call or a friend asking you about something you love, like a hobby or a vacation. That way you’ll be hearing yourself as you actually sound.

    Analyze it

    Separate two aspects: your message and your delivery. Ask yourself: Do I like what I said in this video/segment/podcast? Then analyze it just for delivery. If this is too hard, read a transcript instead of listening to it. Now, listen to the recording. Listen for specific things, not a general “Ugh, my voice sounds weird,” which is unproductive. 

    Ask yourself: Did I have vocal range? Did I use uptalk, ending my sentences like questions? Did I bring the right energy level? Your answers will point the way to improvement. If you are feeling particularly brave, you can send a sample to a friend or trusted advisor.

    Voice memos are another great way to get more comfortable with the act of speaking on cue. You can send them to friends or clients. While you do this, use the wave form of voice memos or another app. Pay attention to your vocal range; you want a normal roller coaster, not high mountains.

    Just because you are not used to your voice doesn’t mean there is anything wrong with it. The sooner you can move past the judgment around your voice, the sooner you can focus on what you’re saying and how you’re using your voice to spread your knowledge, be seen as a leader, or, well, just chat.

    #10252. Google shuts down a sneaky malware backdoor on millions of Android TV and Google TV boxes

    Google has confirmed that an Android TV device maker snuck a backdoor for malware onto certified devices, which is leading to security improvements for the ecosystem as a whole.

    In a post today, Google confirmed that it has cut ties with “Videostrong,” a company that was manufacturing certified Android TV boxes. This is due to the company building in a backdoor that it could sell access to, including the distribution of malware. Google has taken legal action to block the domains and servers that “Videostrong” was using to control the XCPE botnet and malware modules and banned the company and its subsidiaries from selling certified Android devices going forward, or selling software to any other certified vendors.

    We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

    Synthient (via The Hacker News) compiled a list of potentially affected devices, with the focus being on the Mecool brand that has made some well-known Android TV and Google TV boxes in the past. Mecool has been rumored to be shutting down.

    Google somewhat admits that this was a failing on its part, as these devices were sold as “certified” Android devices with the implication that they were safe. The company explains that these bad actors “employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device’s first boot.” With that in mind, Google is updating its review process to protect users against this type of behavior, and Google reiterates that “a device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust.”

    Google’s shutdown of the domains and servers used to spread malware should leave affected Android TV and Google TV boxes safe to use – the company says that “taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices” – but owners may still want to consider alternate options.
