    Update 11/2/2026 3:00 PM ET: As it turns out, the ultimate parent company and holder of all Tachyum intellectual property is Cayman Islands-based Tachyum Ltd., which controls U.S.-based Tachyum Inc., which in turn controls Slovakia-based Tachyum s.r.o. that is responsible for the lion’s share of Tachyum’s development of the Prodigy universal processor. This means that while Tachyum Inc. and Tachyum s.r.o. can be declared insolvent and liquidated, Tachyum Ltd. can continue operations, establish new entities and continue developing Prodigy.However, the Cayman Islands company holding Prodigy-related patents is itself the target of liquidation proceedings. Therefore, the Slovak subsidiary’s bankruptcy cannot necessarily protect Prodigy’s intellectual property from creditors. If Tachyum Ltd. is liquidated, the control over the Prodigy patents could pass to court-appointed liquidators, who could sell them to repay creditors. While the current Tachyum management could buy Prodigy’s patents back cheaply, they would have to compete with other interested buyers and satisfy the applicable sale requirements. In any case, this could be the end of the road for Tachyum.

    Tachyum, the company behind the overpromised and overhyped universal Prodigy processor, has filed for bankruptcy in Bratislava, Slovakia, reports Forbes (as observed by @System360Cheese). The filing follows a court order initiating bankruptcy proceeding after the company repeatedly missed its development and production milestones — but there are still theoretical chances that development of the processor will continue.

    Despite eight years of development and numerous promises, Tachyum has yet to demonstrate working Prodigy silicon. Tachyum introduced Prodigy in 2018, targeting a 2019 tape-out and 2020 commercial availability. But the company repeatedly postponed the processor's launch, first to 2021, then to 2022, 2023, 2024, and eventually 2025.

    Meanwhile, Prodigy's specifications changed considerably along the line: The original 64-core design evolved into a 128-core processor manufactured on a 5nm-class process technology, then a 192-core chip with 16 DDR5 memory channels. In late 2025, Tachyum announced yet another radical redesign: a chiplet-based architecture with 1,024 cores, 24 DDR5 memory channels, and TDP of 1,600W manufactured using TSMC's 2nm-class node. The redesign would require substantial additional development work and would have delayed commercial availability until 2030 or beyond.

    According to court documents cited by Forbes, Tachyum Slovakia itself filed for bankruptcy on October 22, 2026, without waiting for a petition from creditors seeking to recover unpaid debts. The Bratislava III Municipal Court subsequently initiated bankruptcy proceedings after determining that the company's petition met the legal requirements. Under Slovak law, a company that voluntarily files for bankruptcy is presumed insolvent, according to Forbes, so technically Tachyum Slovakia is bankrupt.

    If the court formally declares Tachyum bankrupt, a court-appointed trustee will take control of the company's assets, which could then be sold to repay creditors. We do not know at this point what these assets are, but theoretically they may include intellectual property related to its Prodigy processor, patents, and other technologies in addition to hardware used for development. Unless Tachyum secures additional financing or finds a buyer that can fund further development, work on Prodigy could effectively end.

    Bankruptcy proceedings against Tachyum's Slovak entity do not necessarily mean that its affiliated companies elsewhere will also cease operations. Furthermore, the company's IP could survive under new ownership (if the company finds a buyer, or transfers IP ownership to another entity), which could theoretically let Prodigy development to continue. Nevertheless, the bankruptcy filing casts serious doubt on Tachyum's ability or intention to bring its long-delayed processor to market.

    Theoretically, Tachyum's owners could potentially use bankruptcy proceedings to shed the company's debts, acquire its intellectual property through another legal entity, and resume Prodigy development. There are other options too.

    Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

    Although most of Tachyum development activities are concentrated in Slovakia, Tachyum Slovakia is a subsidiary of the U.S.-based Tachyum Inc. according to Dennik N. If the American parent company owns the Prodigy IP, while the Slovak subsidiary employs engineers, conducts development, and accumulates debts, bankruptcy could enable the group to eliminate a substantial portion of those liabilities without losing its most valuable technological assets. In short, Tachyum's Slovak subsidiary could disappear along with much of its unpaid debt, while the American parent retains Prodigy IP and attempts to commercialize it somehow in the future. If the Slovak subsidiary owns the IP, the American parent could theoretically buy it from the bankruptcy estate and attempt to commercialize it eventually. Meanwhile, there is another complication: The American parent has reportedly faced pressure from its own creditors, some of whom have requested its liquidation, according to Dennik N. In this case, the destiny of the Prodigy IP is completely unclear.

    For now, the future of Prodigy may depend on who actually owns Prodigy's intellectual property — Tachyum Inc. in the U.S. or Tachyum Slovakia — and whether the American subsidiary continues to exist or gets liquidated. The answer could determine whether this bankruptcy represents the end of Prodigy or a restructuring of the Tachyum group with the aim to continue development.

    #10249. Midterm voters to decide on these key ballot measures, putting Trump’s agenda to the test

    A battle over abortion rights is playing out in several states Tuesday as voters decide 145 proposed laws and constitutional amendments, including some that could affect voting for future elections.

    The ballot measures provide a political undercard for a high-profile midterm election that will determine which party controls Congress, state legislatures and gubernatorial offices in many states.

    Some measures put President Donald Trump’s priorities to a public test by gauging support for his attempts to reshape congressional districts, limit transgender athletes in sports and strengthen voter identification requirements.

    Abortion ban faces an unusual redo in Missouri

    Two years ago, Missouri voters became the first in the nation to pass a ballot measure undoing an existing ban on most abortions.

    Now voters are deciding whether to repeal the 2024 abortion rights amendment and replace it with a new prohibition — this time allowing exceptions for medical emergencies and fetal anomalies, and in cases of rape or incest up to 12 weeks of pregnancy. The proposed ban was placed on the ballot by the Republican-led Legislature. Abortion rights advocates, led by national progressive groups, have greatly outspent abortion foes in a bid to defeat the measure.

    In three other states, ballot measures would create a right to abortion using standards similar to what was in place nationally before the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022 and opened the door to state bans.

    Ballot measures in Idaho and Nevada would block bans on abortion before fetal viability, usually considered after 21 weeks. Nevada voters already approved the measure once but have to do so a second time for it to become official. In Virginia, an amendment would ensure abortion is allowed for the first two trimesters.

    Redistricting measures could affect 2028 elections

    Nine states are using new congressional districts in the midterm elections after a rare spate of mid-decade redistricting encouraged by Trump.

    Missouri’s Republican lawmakers also had adopted new House districts designed to help the GOP win an additional seat. But courts ruled they cannot be used unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. If passed, the districts would take effect for the 2028 election.

    Voters in Democratic-led Maryland are deciding on a constitutional amendment that also could pave the way for new congressional districts in the 2028 election. Democratic proponents, backed by former President Barack Obama, have urged a “yes” vote as way to “stop Trump.”

    Some Democrats also want to redistrict in Colorado. But a citizen initiative on the ballot would prohibit any potential 2028 redistricting from favoring one political party and require approval from both an independent commission and the state Supreme Court.

    Transgender restrictions are proposed in several states

    Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Missouri, Nebraska and Washington are considering measures restricting transgender athletes or medical procedures. That comes as Trump’s administration has been pushing for restrictions impacting transgender people, especially youth.

    Most Republican-led states already bar transgender women and girls from female school sports teams. Citizen-led ballot initiatives propose similar restrictions in the Democratic-led states of Colorado and Washington. The Arizona measure would extend public school sports restrictions to private schools. And Nebraska’s measure would add existing restrictions to the state constitution.

    A second ballot question in Colorado would ban some transgender medical treatments for minors. The Missouri abortion amendment also would add existing transgender medical restrictions to the state constitution.

    Five state measures seek voter ID mandates

    Though Trump’s push for nationwide voter ID mandates remains stalled in Congress, citizen activists bypassed Democratic-led state legislatures to place new voter ID requirements on the ballot in California, Colorado and Nevada.

    Those measures would require government-issued identification — like driver’s licenses or partial Social Security numbers — to cast ballots. The Nevada amendment already won approval in 2024 but needs a second vote to take effect.

    Measures referred to the ballot by Republican-led legislatures in North Carolina and Ohio would enhance existing voter ID requirements by placing them in the state constitution.

    Six states consider citizen voting measures

    Ballot measures in Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia would reinforce current election practices limiting voting to U.S. citizens.

    Critics argue the measures are largely symbolic and unnecessary, because voting by noncitizens is rare and already forbidden in federal elections. But noncitizens are allowed to vote in some local elections in California, Maryland, Vermont and the District of Columbia.

    Two years ago, similar citizen voting amendments won approval in all eight states where they appeared on ballots.

    Elections themselves are up for a vote in some states

    A Massachusetts ballot measure would end separate party primaries in favor of open primaries where the top two vote recipients of any party advance to the general election. In Alaska, voters are deciding for the second straight election whether to scrap their system of open primaries and ranked choice voting.

    Proposed amendments in North Dakota and South Dakota would make it harder to amend their state constitutions by requiring 60% approval from voters instead of a simple majority. A similar 60% threshold is proposed in Utah for citizen initiatives that raise taxes.

    Meanwhile, a Missouri amendment would make it harder for lawmakers to change voter-approved citizen initiatives by requiring revisions to get an 80% vote in the state House and Senate.

    Colorado amendment would aid immigration enforcement

    Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts could get a boost in Democratic-led Colorado under a proposed constitutional amendment that would chip away at state laws restricting cooperation with federal immigration agents.

    The proposed amendment, placed on the ballot by conservative activists, would require law enforcement officers to notify the U.S. Department of Homeland Security when someone with an illegal or unknown immigration status is charged with a violent crime or faces a new charge following a prior felony conviction.

    Arizona measure would limit traffic cameras

    Voters in Arizona are deciding on a proposal limiting the use of traffic cameras to catch drivers speeding or running red lights. The Republican-led Legislature referred the measure to voters after Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vetoed a ban on the cameras.

    Hobbs said the cameras enhance roadway safety, but opponents contend they infringe on people’s privacy and point to instances of misuse by certain law enforcement officers.

    The proposal would bar new contracts for traffic camera systems starting in 2027 and require local governments to hold elections on whether to continue existing systems.

    About half the states, including Arizona, have communities that use cameras to enforce speeding or traffic signal laws, according to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.

    Associated Press writer Geoff Mulvihill contributed to this report.

    —David A. Lieb, Associated Press

    #10247. U.S. job postings rose sharply in September

    U.S. employers ramped up their job postings in September as stronger economic growth may be encouraging more hiring. Yet voters are headed to the polls Tuesday, largely gloomy over an economy beset by higher prices.

    U.S. job openings jumped to 7.5 million from a revised 7.19 million in August, the Labor Department reported Tuesday. It is the largest number of openings since May and up from a recent low of 6.9 million in March.

    The department’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) also showed that gross hiring—job gains before subtracting people who quit or lost jobs—rose and layoffs fell in September.

    The increases are a hopeful sign that hiring could improve, but the trend would have to continue for several months to suggest real progress. Hiring has been sluggish for nearly three years, though layoffs have also been historically low, a sign of meager “churn” in the labor market. Low churn means those who are employed are enjoying relatively high levels of job security, but it is much harder than normal for those looking for work to find a job.

    Still, the number of job openings now exceeds the number of unemployed, a sharp switch from a year ago when there were more people out of work than available jobs.

    “It’s an encouraging sign that despite all the headwinds right now with high diesel and gas prices and ongoing inflation problems, companies are slowly increasing their hiring,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said.

    Job openings rose the most in professional and business services, which includes high-paying jobs in engineering and accounting, as well as jobs in the temp industry. Manufacturers, shipping firms, and state and local governments also advertised for more workers.

    Nicole Bachaud, a labor economist at ZipRecruiter, cautioned that with inflation still high and interest rates having increased since the summer, companies may not be able to ramp up hiring by much in the coming months.

    “All of that added up together just makes it much more expensive to operate as a business and much more expensive to expand,” she said. “And so that will likely continue to be a downward pressure on hiring, until we see inflation really able to cool down.”

    The government will issue the October jobs report on Friday, which is forecast to show that employers added 65,000 positions last month, according to data provider FactSet. That would be an improvement from 29,000 in September. The unemployment rate is expected to stay at a low 4.2%.

    Typically, job gains of just 65,000 would be seen as a sign of a struggling economy, but with the giant baby boom generation retiring and immigration sharply reduced, the economy doesn’t need to generate as many jobs as it has in the past for unemployment to remain low.

    In September, layoffs fell sharply to just 1.64 million, the fewest since March 2025. The number of people quitting their jobs rose to 3.37 million, the highest in about 18 months, and up from 3.04 million.

    The rise in quits is generally a good sign because workers usually leave a job when they either have another lined up or when they are confident they can find new work.

    —Christopher Rugaber, AP economics writer

    #10246. AAWireless expands beyond Android Auto adapters with new cooled Qi2 car charger

    AAWireless is known for helping you convert a wired Android Auto connection into a wireless one, but the company is now launching a new product – an active-cooled Qi2 car charger.

    “AAWireless Charge” is a Qi2 25W wireless car charger that costs $50. The charger is compatible with MagSafe, Pixelsnap, and Qi2 in general, and supports up to 25W charging speeds on compatible phones.

    “Charge” also includes active cooling support with a built-in fan that the company says is “quiet” when active.

    While AAWireless adapters remain available on Amazon, “AAWireless Charge” is available solely from the company’s website.

    #10245. AI, DevOps and the Cost of Hosting: From Idea to Production for $0

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    An AI coding agent rebuilt my photo-collage app as a distributed system and deployed it to a free server. The hard part turned out to be hardware: one free ARM CPU, 538 collages created during load testing, zero failed jobs, and $0 a month.

    Like most developers, I have never been short of product ideas. Hosting them has always been the problem. I have tried shared hosting with SmartWeb, Azure free credits, Google Compute Engine’s free VM instances, SmartWeb’s virtual private servers, and Heroku dynos. None of them left me satisfied. The worst experience was a $200 charge for an AI address API on Google Cloud—for an application that never earned me a single kobo.

    I am not a cheapskate, but I learned quickly that one of the easiest ways to kill a potentially good idea is to get the finances wrong. An application has to stay online until it reaches a critical mass of users, and hosting an untested, unverified product on expensive hardware can be wasteful.

    Agentic AI coding has changed how quickly I can move from idea to production. Over about five weeks of intermittent coding—amounting to roughly three days of full work with Claude—my photo-stitching app went from an Angular 8 project that would not even build to a distributed system running in production.

    Along the way, Claude upgraded the front end from Angular 8 to Angular 22 and fixed the build on Node 24. It set up RabbitMQ with Docker Compose so the message broker configures itself on startup, and added real-time notifications over SignalR with a progress spinner. It fixed a crash loop caused by an unreadable iPhone photo. It redesigned the system so any server can process any job, with switchable database and file storage, direct browser-to-storage uploads, and photos resized in the browser before upload. It added reliability work that a team might debate for a sprint: a dead-letter queue, confirmed publishing, idempotent workers, recovery of stuck jobs, and automatic clean-up. It fixed the stitching so photos keep their proportions and borders are even. It wrote 41 automated tests and scrubbed leaked passwords and personal photos from the Git history.

    Coding, QA, DevOps, and production support used to be separate phases, often handled by separate people. Here they happened in one conversation. When code becomes this cheap to produce, the bottleneck moves. For me, it moved to hardware.

    To check what the AI builds, you have to run it locally. A distributed app means running the whole system locally: a web app, a background worker, a message broker, a database, and storage emulators. Because Claude adds features quickly, and each one can add another container, it is easy to exhaust a laptop’s RAM and CPU.

    My setup made this lesson concrete. I work on a MacBook Air, with Visual Studio in a Windows virtual machine. Docker cannot run inside that VM on Apple Silicon, so Claude ran Docker on the Mac and drove it from Windows over SSH. Later, my mobile connection started dropping large packets and broke uploads from the VM, so Claude moved the load testing onto the server itself. The software problems took minutes. The hardware and network problems took longer.

    Then comes hosting. Heroku looked like the easy route, but it has had no free dynos since 2022. The cheapest option is an Eco dyno at about $5 a month, plus about $5 for Postgres. That is affordable, but running it for an idea that has no users yet did not seem prudent.

    Claude suggested Oracle Cloud’s Always Free tier: an ARM server with up to 4 CPUs and 24 GB of RAM, free with no end date. I created a small instance with 1 CPU and about 6 GB. Claude wrote a production Docker Compose file and a one-command setup script: Caddy as the gateway, the web app, the stitching worker, RabbitMQ, and PostgreSQL, with data that survives restarts. My repository is private, so rather than put a GitHub token on a public server, it copied the code over SSH and deployed it. The last blocker was mine to fix: opening ports 80 and 443 in Oracle’s network firewall. Then the site was live.

    I did not want to guess, so I asked Claude to load-test the live server. Simulated users ran the full flow: upload two photos, wait for the real-time notification, and download the stitched collage.

    The server handled 64 people creating collages at the same moment without a single failed job: 538 collages, zero errors. Its ceiling was about 62 collages a minute—one per second. Beyond that, users queue. With 4 people creating at once, 95% of collages arrived within about five seconds; at 64, each person waited about a minute. If each active user makes a collage every couple of minutes, one CPU comfortably serves around 85 people at once, and a few hundred if they use it less often.

    The test also showed what runs out first, and it is not the CPU. Each collage stores about 5 MB, mostly the PNG output, so at full speed the disk would fill in under two hours. Switching to JPEG and shortening retention fixes that, and when traffic grows, three more free CPUs are waiting. That is the value of measuring before paying: I know what to change, and when.

    Oracle isn’t being charitable. Servers need applications to run—ideally ones that go viral—and the free tier is a play for loyalty. Oracle wants successful projects to stay and grow into its paid services instead of moving off the platform once they reach critical mass. It can also reclaim free instances that sit idle.

    I think the bet is smart, and it points to a bigger trend. AI-generated code still needs energy to run and hardware to host it, even when far fewer people work on each project. As more people turn ideas into working software, demand for compute will keep growing, and I expect hosting and data centres to become a very profitable business.

    For now, the combination works: Claude orchestrates the coding, QA, and DevOps, and Oracle’s free server keeps an idea online long enough to find out whether it deserves to grow.

    OpenAI plans community agreements and infrastructure commitments as it prepares to rebrand data centers amid growing public opposition

    When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

    OpenAI is reportedly preparing a major public relations campaign to influence how Americans view artificial intelligence, including a proposal to rename its data centers as “AI Compute Campuses,” Axios reports. The initiative comes ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections and forms a broader effort to influence the debate around AI before the 2028 presidential race. Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, noted that the midterms would be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028.” He expects AI to be a major issue for presidential candidates as the technology raises concerns over its impact on jobs, the economy, and the environment.

    The proposed terminology change by OpenAI has been ongoing since August as the company focuses on promoting safeguards for the powerful technology, which Lehane described as “speed limits.” The proposed AI compute campuses is particularly interesting as it comes as opposition to large data centers accelerates across the U.S. Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity and water, with nearby communities raising concerns about noise, air pollution, rising utility bills and limited public consultation. OpenAI hopes to address these concerns through community agreements and a different way of presenting the infrastructure. “Compute campuses better describe the role of the infrastructure we are rebuilding for AI," a company spokesperson separately stated. He added that these projects represent long term investments in computing, energy infrastructure, and skilled jobs.

    The latest proposal follows similar efforts by other technology companies to improve their relationship with communities hosting their infrastructure. In January, Microsoft announced a community-first approach, promising to cover electricity cost increases associated with its data centers, and invest in local infrastructure and jobs. However, while changing the name may be easier, changing public opinion may bring some headaches. A Redfin report in May found that 47% of Americans surveyed are opposed to having a new data center built in their community. Another report in August detailed how negotiations between developers and local authorities frequently take place behind non-disclosure agreements, leaving residents without access to important project information.

    The resistance has also affected actual construction plans. At least 19 Michigan municipalities have already moved to restrict new data center developments after OpenAI and Oracle’s $16 billion Stargate project went ahead with their project in Sanile township despite local opposition. Meanwhile, Amazon abandoned plans for four data centers in northern Virginia last month following community pushback.

    OpenAI is not alone in trying to reshape the language surrounding AI. President Donald Trump has previously pushed for terminology change, directing Federal agencies and urging AI companies to replace artificial intelligence with ‘super intelligence.’ Trump announced the change in late September arguing that the word "artificial" made the technology sound "fake." His administration subsequently instructed state department employees to use super intelligence or SI in official directives, websites, reports and policy documents.

    Some technology executives have also embraced the terminology. Nvidia CEO Huang has previously referred to data centers as "superintelligence factories" while Elon musk announced plans to rename his AI company SpaceXAI to SpacexSI last month. Meta, meanwhile, established Meta superintelligence labs in 2025, and Microsoft has also assembled a team focused on developing superintelligence. OpenAI’s proposed terminology will now face a more difficult test than simply finding a name as communities will still want answers about the raised issues. Lehane, however, acknowledged that public scrutiny is part of the process saying, “Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects.”

    #10243. Election Day could mean big things for your 401(k). Here’s what history tells us

    Whether or not Tuesday’s midterm elections deliver a so-called blue wave, one thing is for certain: More volatility will likely ripple through financial markets.

    Midterm years have been historically weak for the U.S. stock market, delivering annual gains of just 7.5% versus an average return of 12.4% during non-midterm years, according to figures compiled by global investment management firm BlackRock. And even though more money has been pumped into this year’s midterm campaign than any other in history—to the tune of nearly $12 billion—your 401(k) portfolio isn’t likely to benefit so much.

    Despite polling that points to Democrats gaining seats, nay the majority, in Congress, investors haven’t been positioning for such an outcome. Rather, a survey of more than 100 institutional investors conducted by Wolfe Research suggests that these key market players haven’t positioned themselves for any particular result, according to CNBC.

    “Investors seem to have a significant dose of skepticism about whether the final outcome is going to be quite as favorable to Democrats as the polling suggests,” Tobin Marcus, the firm’s head of U.S. policy and politics, told the outlet. 

    Likewise, veteran market strategist Ed Yardeni warns that the stock market hasn’t fully factored in a blue wave, as such an outcome could lead to “much worse” partisanship in Washington, D.C. “It could be a very cold shower for the market in terms of the gridlock,” Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, told Bloomberg. 

    Why history favors investors

    For long-term investors, the best course of action is to ignore election results and stay invested. BlackRock cautions that letting politics guide investment decisions has come at a significant cost in recent years. Since 2013, for instance, a $100,000 investment in the S&P 500 Index would have grown to nearly $400,000 at the start of 2026 if left untouched; by contrast, investors who moved money out of the market during that time frame based on their politics saw much lower returns.

    What’s more, any kneejerk reaction to the election outcomes may not be as dire as some people are warning. 

    JPMorgan’s trading desk puts the odds of a Democratic sweep at 66%, which would lead to a subdued knee-jerk response for the S&P 500. Instead, the less likely outcomes of Republicans retaining control of both the House and Senate (with odds of only 7%) or Democrats taking the House while Republicans maintain control of the Senate (with odds of 26%) could see stocks rise as much as 1.25%.

    Any dips or spikes in the stock market are likely to be short-lived. Since 1970, the S&P 500 has risen by an average of 14.1% in the six months following midterm elections, according to BlackRock. However, in scenarios where one party lost majority control of both the House and the Senate—as polling suggests could happen this year—returns averaged just 10.4% during that same period.

    HOW THE OUTCOME COULD AFFECT INVESTORS

    Complicating matters for this particular midterm election is the sharp rise in stock prices this year, fueled by unprecedented spending to support the AI buildout. Meanwhile, the Treasury market just suffered its worst quarterly sell-off since 1994.

    That’s meant a mixed bag for retirement savers as the classic 60/40 portfolio has delivered lackluster results this year. This allocation model, popularized by the likes of famed investor John Bogle, is made up of 60% stocks and 40% bonds. So far in 2026, the 60/40 strategy has delivered a return of nearly 7.1%, well below the 10.1% annualized return over the last 10 years, according to estimates by PortfoliosLab, a portfolio analytics and educational platform.

    A Democratic sweep of Congress could put more pressure on stocks—and particularly the high-flying AI stocks that have driven most of the market’s rally this year. That’s because Democrats are seen as being more likely to pump the brakes on the data center projects that are crucial to the AI buildout and, hence, the market’s continued gains. 

    Because of how central the AI trade has become to the overall market, investors will closely watch a few key governor’s races—particularly Texas, which Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has called the “epicenter of AI development.” A surprise loss for the incumbent governor has the “potential to spook” the stock market in the short term, as Wolfe Research’s Marcus told CNBC.

    On the other hand, if Republicans somehow manage to retain control of both the House and Senate, it would have the most dramatic implications for the bond market, according to Reuters. That’s because the Republican policy agenda could continue, further expanding the deficit and therefore pushing Treasury yields even higher. 

    But no matter what happens, Wednesday will at least bring an end to the deluge of political advertisements and texts to voters—as well as the pre-election anxiety that can grip markets, as Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at the wealth advisory network Carson Group, told CNBC. 

    “Once you are through it, it’s a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well,” he said.

    #10241. The next big subscription service could be sunlight. And it might cost $5,000 an hour

    A startup wants to fill the night sky with ultrapowerful beams of redirected sunlight. What could go wrong?

    According to astronomers, almost everything. Reflect Orbital’s plans to launch 50,000 satellites equipped with giant mirrors is akin to “a bullet in your head,” says one astrophysicist, citing threats to both the natural world and the future of astronomy.

    Selling the sun

    By offering “sunlight as a service,” Reflect aims to deploy a constellation of satellites to beam down 5-kilometer-wide solar rays on demand, ranging in brightness from “noon light to moonlight.”

    Reflect’s website suggests potential use cases such as powering solar panels, illuminating disaster zones and search-and-rescue missions, and lighting up worksites, cities, and events. But with a price tag of $5,000 for an hour of sunlight, the product would be prohibitively expensive for most customers—leaving critics to assume that only militaries and titans of industry are likely to make use of Reflect’s services, despite its altruistic branding.

    So far, Reflect hasn’t actually launched any satellites. In August, it received approval from the Federal Communications Commission to launch a single demonstration satellite (much to the chagrin of environmental groups, which urged the FCC to reverse its decision). But moving forward, Reflect won’t need to seek approval from the U.S. government at all: It recently booked two dedicated rocket flights with Skyroot Aerospace in India, which will be liable for any unintended consequences of satellites launched from within its borders under the Outer Space Treaty.

    The end of astronomy

    The prospect of messing with the day-night cycle immediately raised concerns with environmentalists and astronomers alike, who are already contending with an increasingly crowded night sky, thanks to spacecraft like SpaceX’s fleet of Starlink satellites.

    Gáspár Bakos, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told Sky & Telescope that Reflect’s plans for “sunlight on demand” are “essentially ignoring all the progress we have made for the past many decades in bringing awareness to and decreasing light pollution.”

    Bakos and other astronomers worry that the beams would cause light diffusion throughout the night sky, making it incredibly difficult for ground-based telescopes to view objects in space. Amateur astronomers would also be at risk of permanent eye damage if they happened to see one of Reflect’s beams through a telescope greater than 12 inches in aperture.

    Lighting up dark environments at night could also pose a threat to plants and animals that depend on the day-night cycle for biological regulation. That includes humans, whose own circadian rhythms dictate sleep patterns, hormones, and digestion among other bodily functions.

    Light bulb moment

    In an interview with Payload, Reflect Orbital CEO Ben Nowack responded to frequent concerns about his company’s plans. If astronomers are concerned about light pollution, Reflect will be sure to avoid getting in the way of their telescopes, he reasoned.

    “If there’s an astronomer or a place that doesn’t want to see light, and they have a really hard brightness requirement . . . we will make sure that we don’t serve customers close [by],” Nowack said.

    As for anxieties around the impact of life on Earth, Nowack chalks them up to a general fear of new technology. “Similar concerns and fears were brought up when light bulbs were introduced to the world, and people were worried about circadian rhythm and, like, is this godly?” he said. 

    Never mind the fact that Reflect’s beams of sunlight would be just a touch brighter than light bulbs, casting light for up to 30 kilometers from their targets. Each satellite would also appear in the sky as a point source four magnitudes brighter than the moon, according to a report by Bakos and his colleagues.

    “This is not a ‘concern’—this is like a bullet in your head,” Bakos said. “It’s the end of ground-based astronomy.”

    #10240. The Meta Quest 2 and Quest Pro are receiving their last OS updates soon. Here’s what you need to know

    The best-selling VR headset of all time (and its Pro-level cousin) will no longer receive OS updates after March 2027.

    Somehow, the Meta Quest 2 has been around for six whopping years, and Meta is finally bringing support for the headset to a close after March 2027. The far less popular Meta Quest Pro, which uses the same chipset as the Quest 2, will also see OS updates cease at the same time with OS v213. Meta will continue to deliver security updates through the end of 2027 to both headsets, according to an official Meta developers blog post.

    Meta says it will not be removing cross-play multiplayer functionality or blocking access to Quest 2 players, so any games that support the headset will continue to work after these dates, so long as they don’t rely on any new OS features introduced after March 2027. Developers have to give players a 6-month notice if support is ending for a game, so you’ll have ample time to decide what to do.

    That means the Quest 2 will receive just over 7 years of total security updates, while the Quest Pro gets two years less (since it came out in October 2022). The Meta Quest 2 remains the best-selling VR headset of all time, with around 20 million units sold over the lifetime of the headset. Meta says that Quest 2 owners can still play games throughout this time, although game support will likely dry up quickly after January 2028.

    The $599 Meta Quest 3 and $349 Meta Quest 3S, which debuted in 2023 and 2024, respectively, are the follow-ups to the Quest 2. The upcoming Meta VR Glasses, which will retail for $1299, feature a next-generation chipset, a significantly higher-resolution AMOLED display, and substantially lighter weight and smaller size than either Quest 3 model.

    Meta VR Glasses are expected to debut early next year, and with them, a new generation of OS development will take place. Since the Quest 2 uses a significantly outdated mobile chip at this point, it makes sense for Meta to cease new feature development for it and focus on newer, more capable hardware.

    Amazon’s closure email cites a verification process and offers no reason.

    When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

    AI creator Nick Saraev says on X that Amazon closed his account after he tried to buy seven Nvidia DGX Spark AI mini-PCs. The closure email cites a verification process and gives no reason. Epic CEO Tim Sweeney chimed in that his regular orders would go through, then get canceled before arrival, after he tried to buy two GPUs.

    Update: Amazon just closed my account.Buying even modest amounts of compute immediately puts you on a watchlist. Be careful!November 1, 2026

    Saraev puts it plainly that “Amazon just closed my account” and that “Buying even modest amounts of compute immediately puts you on a watchlist.” He was “4 orders deep,” and Amazon will no longer allow him to buy DGX Sparks.

    The shared screenshots indicate those orders were all canceled, with each stating, “Your order was canceled. You have not been charged for this order.” Although he does not give a unit count, the screenshots indicate he tried to buy seven DGX Sparks in total. All show the same listing, with 128GB of memory and 4TB of storage.

    Amazon’s support account did respond to his earlier post, about three hours before his closure post, offering a review. The shared email shows that Amazon had “made the final decision” to close his account after review; no reason was given. However, it did mention “previous attempts to verify your account,” and he says he did go through the verification process, but seven DGX Sparks is a significant amount that might draw suspicion. Either way, Amazon’s Conditions of Use reserve the right to “refuse service, terminate accounts” or “cancel orders in its sole discretion.”

    He’s not alone in running into trouble with the company. Sweeney says that “Amazon didn’t cancel my account but continued accepting all my regular orders and canceling them just prior to arrival dates, after I tried to buy two NVIDIA GPUs. Rather bizarre.” Nvidia GPUs are often used for local inference. Saraev replied that everyone would “appreciate a bit more transparency.”

    Also, in September, Dracones89 on the Nvidia developer forum shared that one Amazon account was hit with “suspicious activity locks” while trying to buy a pair of Asus GX10s; the user ended up with two DGX Sparks from Micro Center instead. Another X user, @PurzBeats, wrote, “They canceled the order when I tried to buy my 5090, twice.” This is a different trajectory than the OpenClaw days of Mac minis, when buyers faced long delivery waits rather than canceled orders or closed accounts.

    With local inference remaining of high interest to many, particularly AI influencers, the event is potentially disturbing, especially after recent comments about self-owned DRAM by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. While this time it was a guy who helps entrepreneurs and small businesses implement AI and claims 500K on YouTube and 700K on Instagram, the slope is slippery, although Saraev’s orders are hardly typical.

    The 128GB DGX Spark has an MSRP of $6,950, but it may be found at 20% or more over that: two Amazon listings showed $8,499.99 and $9,499.99 when we checked today, which would put seven at roughly $59,500 to $66,500. Both showed Prime delivery tomorrow, so the hardware is still on sale there.

    Hardware has been climbing in price, largely due to rising memory costs. As open-weight models have become more popular, so has local AI inference. The combination may make retailers uneasy, as you’re dealing with high ticket prices and there has been uncertainty about the safety of models as they have improved, with open-source AI agent tools reportedly being used in multiple recent cybersecurity incidents.

    Micro Center, a different retailer, required one buyer to sign an Advanced Computing Product Purchaser Declaration with photo ID, end user, and an install location, just for a workstation with an RTX 5090. This form specifically forbade exporting or reselling the hardware, which might give a little insight into Amazon’s reasoning, too. Amazon’s conditions also say customers “must comply with all U.S. or other export and re-export restrictions.” China and the U.S. remain locked in a fight over exports of AI hardware.

    Amazon hasn’t explained itself, but the attention this is getting may motivate a more detailed response. Right now, it’s a warning signal to users looking to buy significant amounts of hardware for AI work, at least from traditional online retailers. Brick-and-mortar stores, like Micro Center, may crack down further to prevent workarounds designed to export the hardware illegally.

    #10238. Taco Bell says it has a ‘magic formula’ for bringing customers back. Here’s what it is

    Yum Brands, the parent company of Taco Bell, KFC, and The Habit Burger & Grill, reported higher-than-expected third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, driven in part by KFC’s global expansion and higher revenue from its franchises.

    However, an outbreak of cyclosporiasis linked to tainted shredded lettuce at Taco Bell, which Yum considers its “growth engine,” affected the chain’s same-store sales, which dropped 4% in the U.S. for the quarter.

    Despite that, it appears consumers have not lost their appetite for Taco Bell. On Tuesday’s earnings call, Yum CFO Ranjith Roy said that looking ahead to the fourth quarter, same-store sales are up about 1%—and up 3% over the last four weeks—compared with the same period last year.

    Yum attributed the fast bounce back to a “magic formula” that included Tuesday weekly deals for loyalty members and limited-time offers.

    “Since the end of September, Taco Bell U.S. has been outpacing the [quick-service restaurant] industry on same-store sales growth,” Yum Brands CEO Chris Turner said in an earnings statement. “Taco Bell will continue building on this momentum, with differentiated value and innovation that resonate across all consumer groups. . . . [We] remain confident in our ability to deliver consistent earnings growth and create long-term shareholder value.”

    Shares of Yum Brands Inc. (NYSE: YUM) were down 0.2% in Wednesday afternoon trading.

    For the quarter ending September 30, Yum Brands’ reported revenue increased 3.8%, coming in at $2.05 billion, with earnings per share (EPS) of $1.56 adjusted, exceeding the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.47. Net income rose to $1.62 billion, up from $397 million at the same time last year.

    The company said the gains excluded the company’s recently completed divestment from Pizza Hut, which was acquired by LongRange Capital and Yum China Holdings Inc.

    #10236. Hinge is making a surprising change to its subscriptions. Here’s who stands to benefit

    Hinge users may soon have access to a more affordable subscription tier. The app’s parent company, Match Group, announced on November 2 that it’s testing a new feature geared toward women.

    During its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, Match Group said the new tier will give users more control through additional filters and custom location boundaries.

    “It’s designed for women in particular, but also for price-sensitive users,” Match Group CFO Steve Bailey said during the call. 

    Hinge currently offers three tiers: a free version with limits on filters and daily likes; and the more customizable Hinge+ and HingeX, priced at $89.99 and $99.99 for three months, respectively. 

    Tinder has similar subscription tiers, with Tinder Plus and Tinder Gold offering perks like unlimited swipes and top picks for around $25 and $35 per month, respectively.

    “Hinge is one of the highest-priced products we have. The revenue per payer, for example, at Hinge is almost twice that of Tinder,” Bailey said. “It also has one of the lower payer penetrations. Its payer penetration is only slightly more than half that of Tinder.”

    The company did not respond to Fast Company’s request for additional details about the new subscription tier. 

    The lower-priced offering comes as consumers grow increasingly frustrated with the dating ecosystem. In a February 2026 Harris Poll, 72% of Americans said romance feels more like a transaction due to dating apps, while 77% said dating has become a marketplace.

    Despite those sentiments, Hinge’s monthly active user numbers are up 12% year over year.

    While Tinder is still bigger, with around 8.9 million paid users, its base is shrinking, with its paid users down 4% from last year. Tinder has since leaned on a different strategy to keep users engaged, including facilitating in-person experiences to shift the focus away from swiping.

    Match Group owns a number of major dating platforms in addition to Match, Tinder, and Hinge, including OkCupid and Plenty of Fish.

    #10234. The 2026 midterm elections could change everything for Trump. Here’s what’s at stake

    The midterm elections have the potential to upend everything from politics to business to the stock market. But the person most impacted by Tuesday’s results could be President Donald Trump, and that, in effect, could determine the course of his final two years in office.

    On the political front, the battle to control Congress is key, with a number of seats in play, including 435 in the House of Representatives and 35 in the Senate.

    Should the Democrats gain control of the House (and, perhaps, even the Senate), the voting public will have broken the Trump administration and Republicans’ stronghold over Congress.

    “The midterms matter in general because they determine whether there is alignment between the executive and the legislative branches,” Harvard Business School professor Vincent Pons said in an interview earlier this year. “Oftentimes, voters vote against the party of the president. Some voters have a preference for divided government, to have checks and balances. If the Republican party was to lose the midterms, either the House or both the House and the Senate, it could have dramatic consequences in terms of circumventing the power of [the administration].”

    A Democratic upset could check Trump’s power, paving the way for a lame-duck presidency for the remainder of his term. A blue sweep could also give Dems the votes they need to investigate the president’s finances, his administration’s immigration policies, and bring another impeachment.

    In August, Michigan Democrat and Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed told CNN, “The first thing we’re going to do when [the Democrats] win this Senate seat? Hold Trump accountable. Then, on to the real work—taking on big corporations, taxing billionaires their wealth, and guaranteeing healthcare through Medicare for All.”

    Back in January, Democratic Representative Micah Lasher of New York posted a road map for Congressional oversight should the Democrats regain control of the House: “Check the Trump administration’s lawlessness by making clear that illegal activity and corruption will be investigated, and by spurring criminal prosecutions or impeachments; focus the American public on the illegal and corrupt activity that gets lost in the daily barrage of news and distraction out of the White House; and shape the narrative of the 2028 elections and help Democrats win back the White House and grow our majority.”

    In California, Democratic Representative Robert Garcia said he plans to look into the White House’s immigration policies, and “demand accountability” for the tactics used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement—the fallout of which would likely influence the 2028 presidential election.

    In July, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat, said, “When you put us back in charge of the United States House of Representatives, you’ll get a Congress that speaks up for everyday Americans and a Congress that stands up to an out-of-control president.” Jeffries emphasized that to beat Republicans, Democrats were focused on healthcare costs, bringing down the high cost of living, and ending the war in Iran.

    A divided Congress, with Republicans maintaining their majority in at least one branch, could result in major political gridlock for the remainder of Trump’s term, which could have major repercussions for business.

    If Republicans can hold on to their seats, that could empower Trump to accelerate his domestic agenda and policies on key issues like defense and AI—with those government-connected sectors seeing continued growth, and banks and cryptocurrencies retaining lighter regulation.

    #10231. Building a Human Review Pipeline for AI Search: A Practical Developer’s Guide

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    An AI search feature can return valid JSON, render correctly, and still give an unhelpful answer.

    Imagine a documentation assistant answering a question about an API's current authentication requirements. It retrieves an outdated page, summarizes it fluently, and displays a citation. Every technical component appears to work, but the user receives instructions that no longer apply.

    Automated checks are valuable, yet they cannot replace a clearly defined judgment about whether an answer solves the user's problem.

    This guide builds a human-review workflow for a hypothetical API documentation assistant. You will define a review rubric, validate submissions with Python, measure reviewer disagreement, and turn accepted judgments into regression cases. The Python examples use Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn; they do not require a model-provider API key.

    Start by identifying the failure you want to detect.

    A documentation assistant usually has several stages: receive a question, retrieve relevant documents, generate an answer, and present that answer with supporting material.

    Do not collapse these into a single “good answer” rating. A low score without a reason tells the team little about what to fix.

    SitePoint’s introduction to retrieval-augmented generation provides background on how retrieval and generation fit together.

    Preserve the exact question, answer revision, retrieved passages, document versions, and retrieval timestamp for each run. Store a snapshot manifest with stable passage IDs, source URLs, and content hashes. Reviewers should see the material supplied to that run, not today’s edited page. Keep the model and prompt configuration with the run so a later review can be traced to the behavior it evaluated.

    A useful rubric defines observable criteria and separates evidence support from task completion and source suitability. Give each review the same user task and expected API version. Otherwise, reviewers may judge different questions while appearing to disagree about one answer.

    For an answer about API authentication, use separate labels such as:

    Supported: every material factual claim is backed by the supplied evidence.

    Partially supported: some material claims lack support, while others are grounded.

    Unsupported: the answer's central instruction lacks support or contradicts the evidence.

    Cannot assess: the necessary evidence is missing, unreadable, or inaccessible.

    Define task completion independently as complete, incomplete, or cannot assess. For source suitability, use suitable, outdated, or cannot assess. An answer can faithfully summarize an obsolete page while failing the request for current instructions.

    Consider a fictional API migration: version 2 accepts X-API-Key, while version 3 requires Authorization: Bearer . If the supplied evidence contains only the version 2 page, an answer repeating X-API-Key can be supported by its evidence but still use an outdated source. If the evidence explicitly requires Bearer and the answer invents X-API-Key, label the answer unsupported. These are different engineering failures.

    Also establish what reviewers should do when the source is outdated. They may correctly conclude that an answer reflects its evidence while separately flagging that evidence as unsuitable for the user's current task.

    Start with a calibration batch covering clear successes, unsupported claims, missing evidence, and version mismatches. Have two reviewers label the same items independently, then compare their reasons. Revise ambiguous definitions before increasing volume; the batch is for improving the rubric, not estimating production quality.

    Keep a rubric version on every review. Labels produced under different definitions should not be mixed without checking comparability.

    A spreadsheet can help during exploration, but an engineering pipeline needs a stable record format.

    Pydantic can validate a review record before it enters the dataset. Install Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn in your project environment, then use this model:

    from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError

    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", strict=True)

    answer_revision: str = Field(min_length=1)

    completion: Literal["complete", "incomplete", "cannot_assess"]

    source_fit: Literal["suitable", "outdated", "cannot_assess"]

    rationale: str = Field(min_length=20, max_length=2000)

    Strict mode limits type coercion, and extra="forbid" rejects unexpected fields. The model checks shape and allowed values; it cannot establish that a judgment is correct. A minimum rationale length does not guarantee a useful explanation. The snapshot ID references a manifest, which can also record that retrieval produced no usable passages.

    On the server, resolve the item, answer revision, snapshot, and passage IDs against the stored run. Reject IDs that do not belong together. Obtain the reviewer identity from the authenticated session rather than trusting a submitted reviewer_id. Store a server-generated submission time and preserve review revisions instead of silently overwriting earlier judgments.

    Run this after the model definition. It accepts one fictional review and rejects both an unknown label and an extra field:

    "rationale": "The answer invents X-API-Key; p1 requires Bearer.",

    raise AssertionError("Invalid review was accepted")

    The expected error types are literal_error and extra_forbidden. Add separate integration tests for mismatched evidence IDs, unauthorized submissions, and retries. Use a database uniqueness rule or an idempotency key so a repeated request does not create a second independent review.

    More reviews do not automatically produce better evidence. If a task is ambiguous, scaling it can simply reproduce the ambiguity.

    The workflow needs clear eligibility requirements, examples, escalation routes, and acceptance criteria. Reviewers assessing API behavior may need domain knowledge that general writing fluency does not provide.

    If you work with an external AI-data contributor service such as Acquirox, define the task contract before assigning work: required expertise, permitted source material, output fields, and escalation rules. Keep ownership of the rubric, evaluation set, and acceptance decisions within the product team. Contributor capacity alone does not establish expertise in the API being reviewed.

    Pilot the actual task in the review interface. Track drafts, submitted reviews, items needing adjudication, and final decisions as distinct workflow states. Reviewer judgments should remain immutable once submitted; corrections should create a new revision with a reason. Keep adjudication separate from the original labels.

    For data involving users or contributors, document permitted uses, access boundaries, and retention. Remove credentials and unnecessary personal information from review material. An internal support transcript should not become a broadly accessible annotation task by accident.

    Distinguish annotation from usability research. A skilled reviewer can judge whether an answer is supported, but that does not prove a first-time user can understand the interface.

    SitePoint’s guide to choosing usability tests and participants offers related guidance on matching participants and methods to the question being investigated.

    The review interface shapes the data it collects.

    Label Studio is an option for configurable labeling interfaces and data import/export. If you use it, map exported annotations into the Review schema through an adapter; do not assume its export structure matches your application contract. A custom interface may be appropriate when reviewers need API-version navigation or passage-level citations.

    The original question and relevant user context.

    The evidence snapshot supplied to the model.

    Separate controls for support and task completion.

    A rationale field and an explicit “cannot assess” option.

    Display stable passage IDs beside the evidence and let reviewers attach those IDs to their rationale. Show the source version and retrieval time near each passage. Render retrieved content as untrusted text or sanitized markup, and never treat instructions embedded in a source document as reviewer instructions. Avoid loading executable third-party content inside the review panel.

    Avoid showing a preferred model name or a previous reviewer's verdict before an independent judgment. For pairwise comparisons, randomize answer order and include appropriate tie or neither-acceptable outcomes.

    Design for keyboard use, visible focus, readable text, and explicit selection states. Keep evidence and the answer accessible without requiring excessive horizontal scrolling.

    Start all judgment controls unselected and validate them on submission. Use labeled radio groups, an accessible error summary, and visible saving/submission status. A failed save should preserve the draft. Disable duplicate submissions in the UI, but enforce duplicate handling on the server as well.

    Practical check: observe a reviewer completing several borderline examples. Record where they pause, misinterpret a label, or cannot find the necessary source material.

    When two reviewers disagree, investigate before reducing their decisions to a majority vote.

    Different assumptions about the user's expertise.

    A genuine error by one or both reviewers.

    Preserve independent labels and store the adjudicated result separately. This allows the team to study ambiguity instead of erasing it.

    For two reviewers applying categorical labels to the same items, scikit-learn provides Cohen's kappa:

    from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score

    ("q1", "a1", "s1", "auth-v1"): "supported",

    ("q2", "a1", "s2", "auth-v1"): "unsupported",

    ("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "supported",

    ("q4", "a1", "s4", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported"

    ("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported"

    raise ValueError("Review sets must contain identical items")

    raw_agreement = sum(x == y for x, y in zip(left, right)) / len(keys)

    print(f"Raw agreement: {raw_agreement:.2f}")

    print(f"Kappa: {cohen_kappa_score(left, right):.2f}")

    This toy example prints raw agreement of 0.75 and kappa of about 0.64. Four items are not enough to assess a review program. In production, check for duplicate reviews before building dictionaries, use one rubric version per comparison, report unmatched items, and align all records by item, answer revision, and evidence snapshot.

    Kappa measures agreement beyond chance under its assumptions, not correctness. Inspect raw agreement, label frequencies, and the disagreement table alongside it. A single-category batch can make kappa undefined; report that limitation rather than substituting a reassuring score. Treat cannot_assess explicitly and report its frequency instead of silently excluding difficult cases.

    If both reviewers apply the same flawed rubric consistently, agreement can be high while the evaluation remains unhelpful.

    Once difficult cases are adjudicated, turn them into regression cases with explicit acceptance criteria. For the fictional authentication task: use version 3 evidence, cite the passage requiring Bearer, and do not invent a header. If version 3 evidence is missing, an acceptable response should explain the gap rather than provide confident instructions.

    Expected behavior or acceptance criteria.

    DVC can track larger datasets alongside Git. In an existing Git repository with DVC initialized and data/reviewed-auth.jsonl present, a minimal versioning step is:

    git add data/reviewed-auth.jsonl.dvc data/.gitignore

    git commit -m "Version authentication review cases"

    This commits metadata, not the dataset bytes. Configure an access-controlled DVC remote and push the data before expecting another machine or CI runner to retrieve it. Keep credentials and sensitive review material out of public repositories.

    Keep development examples separate from held-out evaluation cases. If developers repeatedly tune prompts against the same questions, those questions become less useful as evidence of generalization.

    Split related examples together where appropriate. Near-duplicate questions from one support conversation should not be scattered across development and evaluation sets.

    Use two evaluation passes. First, hold the evidence snapshot fixed to compare answer-generation changes. Then test retrieval against the intended document versions to detect stale or irrelevant sources. Record per-item outcomes and report failures by category; an overall improvement can hide a regression in version-specific or multilingual questions.

    SitePoint’s article on testing nondeterministic AI behavior provides further context for repeatable evaluation workflows.

    A correct answer can still fail in the interface.

    Users may overlook a caveat, misunderstand whether an operation has been performed, or miss that the evidence applies to an older API version.

    Pair answer review with practical usability tasks:

    Find the authentication requirements for version 3 and identify the source that supports them.

    Observe whether users complete the task and whether their confidence matches the available evidence.

    SitePoint’s overview of user research methods helps distinguish task observation from preference surveys.

    Turn interface failures into browser tests: a citation opens the expected document version, its passage ID matches the displayed evidence, missing evidence offers a recovery action, and a failed review submission preserves the draft. Verify that reviewers cannot access unassigned restricted items by changing an ID in the URL. These checks complement human judgments; they do not replace them.

    Do not use a fluent response as a substitute for a clear interaction. The interface should distinguish retrieved information, generated interpretation, and actions the application has actually completed.

    Start with one authentication task, a versioned rubric, and a small calibration batch. Use Pydantic for ingestion checks, Label Studio or a custom interface for review, scikit-learn for agreement analysis, and Git/DVC for dataset provenance. Add each tool only when it solves a concrete workflow need.

    At release time, run deterministic checks for schema, evidence references, permissions, and interface behavior. Compare candidate answers against adjudicated acceptance criteria and send new ambiguous failures back for review. Record the dataset revision and configurations with the results so another developer can reproduce the comparison.

    The purpose of human review is to produce evidence the team can act on. A smaller collection of well-defined, traceable judgments is often more useful than a large pile of ratings whose meaning nobody can explain.

    #10229. iPad Mini review: A pricey delight

    For a device with such a straightforward name, the iPad Mini has had many lives over its 14 years. Yes, it’s always been a small iPad. But at various times, it’s also been a cheap iPad with a lesser display, an iPad as technologically sophisticated as any you could buy, and a midrange iPad.

    Last week, Apple announced a new iPad—one of the remarkably large number of products the company introduced during what may have been its most productive October ever. It remains a small iPad. But the new version replaces the LCD screen of past versions with OLED, a technology previously available only in the iPad Pro. That’s one of several upgrades that take the new Mini to a tier of its own—not quite on the level of the iPad Pro, but in some respects above the iPad Air models the previous Mini closely resembled.

    The new iPad Mini also costs $100 more than its predecessor. That version went up $100 itself in June, when Apple raised many of its prices in reaction to the AI-induced RAM shortage. Now the Mini starts at an imposing $699 for the Wi-Fi version with 128 GB of storage, a 40% increase in a little over four months, and just $50 less than the cheapest iPad Air. (The basic, entry-level iPad also went up $100, but I still consider it a bargain at $449.)

    Even if the iPad Mini is no longer an impulse item for most of us, it remains the present-day iPad that reminds me most of Steve Jobs’s keynote introduction of the original 2010 iPad. In it, he outlined the need for the device and did much of his demo from the comfort of a cushy chair. That niche—bigger than a phone, more intimate than a laptop—is alive, well, and still evolving in the new Mini.

    The Mini’s roomy screen lets it do many things well that an iPhone can’t, unless it’s an iPhone Duo. Unlike its larger iPad siblings, however, it’s not trying to encroach on the traditional territory of a MacBook or other PCs. It’s a tablet in the category’s purest sense. (I am aware that third-party manufacturers have long made keyboard cases for iPad Minis and will surely offer ones for this model—I just can’t envision even that setup replacing anyone’s laptop.)

    Since the beginning, the Mini has been all about size, weight, and the pleasure of spending time with a device that you can hold for extended periods—in one hand, even—without it seeming to grow mysteriously heavier over time. It’s also been the easiest iPad to grab and take almost anywhere, maybe in a jacket pocket.

    After all these years, Apple is still finding ways to wring heft out of the new Mini’s design. Compared to the previous version, the most striking improvements are the 16% reduction in thickness and (for the Wi-Fi model) 13.8% reduction in weight. But Apple also shrank the display’s border by 25%, which allowed it to increase the screen size from 8.3 inches to 8.5 inches, even though the new model is slightly narrower. It’s about 45% lighter than the 11-inch iPad Air and 59% lighter than the 13-inch Air.

    Consequently, this tablet is a delight for tasks where more display real estate than a (non-folding) phone is desirable, but 11 or 13 inches may be overkill—long-form reading on the web or in an e-reader app, gaming, viewing and wrangling photos, lightweight productivity such as email triage. It’s also an extremely pleasant way to watch video, assuming you’re not trying to re-create the experience of watching a blockbuster movie in the theater. And its support for Apple Pencil Pro makes it a beguiling digital sketchbook when you’re out and about and lugging a larger iPad would feel like a burden.

    As for the new OLED screen, it delivers on the technology’s promise by providing deep blacks, rich colors, and peak brightness of 1,200 nits, compared to 500 nits for the previous model. Some people—such as Multicore’s Sam Byford—regret that the display doesn’t include Apple’s ProMotion technology, which uses a variable refresh rate to make scrolling and input smoother and more responsive. I don’t find its omission glaring. (The 256 GB and 512 GB versions do offer Apple’s glare-reducing nano-texture screen—previously exclusive to the iPad Pro—as a $100 option.)

    The new Mini is the first iPad to incorporate an audio system called Acoustic Display, which moves the speakers behind the screen. The resulting output sounds crisper to me than what I’m used to on my 13-inch iPad Pro. Just as notable, the new location allowed Apple to seal up the tablet, making it the first iPad ever to achieve an IP67 rating for water and dust resistance. It should be able to withstand being immersed in 3 feet of water for 30 minutes—a feature that makes sense considering it’s the iPad you’re most likely to take to the beach or pool, or use in a bathtub.

    Another change brings the iPad Mini in line with other current iPads: Its front-facing camera is on the tablet’s landscape edge rather than the portrait one. If you’re using a larger iPad in a keyboard case, that’s unquestionably the proper spot, since it centers the camera above the screen rather than putting it on the side, which can leave you looking shifty-eyed on video calls.

    I have always used iPad Minis mostly in portrait mode, so I’m not as sure the camera relocation is an improvement in this case. But it’s not an issue as long as you remember to rotate the tablet into landscape mode for FaceTime, Zoom, and the like.

    Despite the new Mini’s more upscale feel, Apple has stuck with a Touch ID sensor rather than equipping it with Face ID, which remains exclusive to iPhones and the iPad Pro. It’s built into the power button and, in my experience, works close to 100% of the time. But it requires more thought to use than Face ID, especially since the sensor’s location depends on how you’re holding the Mini. It’s the one area where using the Mini feels like less than a first-class experience.

    Then there’s the Mini’s processor, which I haven’t mentioned until now because so many of the tasks this tablet is well suited to don’t cry out for raw performance. (Fancy 3D games and on-device AI are exceptions.)

    Apple didn’t skimp: It chose the A20 Pro chip, a processor that is itself new, having debuted in September with the iPhone 18 Pro. The company touts benchmark numbers such as up to 60% faster CPU performance and up to 270% faster GPU performance than the previous Mini. That version used the A17 Pro, a chip that wasn’t new even when that tablet was released two years ago.

    Even if you don’t care how much faster a new iPad is than its predecessor, the fact that the tablet has Apple’s latest chip is a boon. It will extend the tablet’s useful life before it struggles to run new apps or is no longer supported by iPadOS updates. That may be more important for iPads than other devices: Anecdotally, at least, people tend to hold on to them for years.

    One other thing about the new iPad Mini is worth mentioning—not because it’s changed, but because it hasn’t. The tablet runs iPadOS 27, the latest version of the iPad’s operating system. That sports the same multitasking interface introduced in iPadOS 26—a Mac-esque world with floating windows, menus, and traffic-light-like buttons for expanding, minimizing, and closing windows. Even on the iPad Pro I use as a work computer for hours a day, I am not enthralled with the clutter and complexity it brings. On a Mini, actually trying to use these features feels like suffocating overkill.

    When setting up a new iPad Mini, you can avoid this experience altogether by choosing the “Full Screen Apps” option. That limits you to one on-screen app at a time, just like the iPads of yore. That, I suspect, will be plenty for a high percentage of users. If you expect to be one of them, you can stop reading now.

    Still, there is value in letting a Mini-size device do a certain amount of multitasking, particularly when you’re holding it in landscape orientation and performing tasks that involve multiple apps. As it happens, Apple just took a fresh shot at creating an interface tuned to this scenario.

    That would be the one offered by the iPhone Duo, whose 7.6-inch interior display is close enough in size to the iPad Mini that many people instinctively talk about the Duo as if it were a Mini you could fold up and put in your pocket. It offers far fewer options than iPad multitasking, but provides a more intuitive, foolproof way to perform the one form of multitasking that’s most useful on a small tablet: putting two apps side by side without letting them overlap or float.

    Now, the iPhone Duo is definitely an iPhone. It’s obvious why it doesn’t borrow iPadOS 26/27-style multitasking, which would be bizarre on a device so many people use for quick hits of information when they’re walking around. The fact that the Duo can’t run iPad apps may even be a stance on the company’s part: An iPhone with an iPad Mini-like interior screen size isn’t that close a relative of the iPad Mini after all.

    I do hope, however, that Apple is open to the possibility of the Duo’s influence rubbing off on future versions of iPadOS. The new iPad Mini’s hardware proves that the Mini is as relevant as ever. It’s still getting better at fulfilling the iPad’s original vision. The same should be true of the software it runs.

    Just 128MB of RAM is enough to boot Windows 11.

    When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

    NTDEV, the popular developer behind the Tiny11 project, has once again pushed the limits of just how little hardware is required to run Windows 11. In a video shared on YouTube, the developer claims to have successfully booted the latest Windows 11 26H2 on a system with just 128MB of RAM. Despite severe memory constraints, the heavily stripped-down installation manages to load the Desktop and File Explorer, access the Start menu, and even run the classic Notepad app.

    While it is an impressive achievement, the developer acknowledges that the system is "painfully slow," making this more of a technical experiment than a practical way to run Windows 11 on older hardware. According to Microsoft’s official requirements, Windows 11 requires at least 4GB of RAM, meaning NTDEV's latest experiment uses just 3.125% of the recommended minimum. The developer has not shared a detailed breakdown of every component removed or disabled to achieve the result, but the project builds on years of experimentation with stripped-down Windows installations.

    This is not NTDEV's first attempt at pushing Windows 11 beyond its usual hardware limitations. Back in 2023, the developer managed to get the operating system running with only 176MB of RAM by extensively trimming its system components, drivers, and background services. That experiment relied on an IDE storage interface to reduce the number of drivers required, and sacrificed the standard Windows desktop environment.

    Last month, the developer showcased another interesting experiment that squeezed an entire Windows 11 installation into a CD-ROM-sized ISO file. The experimental build created using the developer's upcoming Pico11 tool weighs in at 699,811,840 bytes and retains a functional Windows desktop. The stripped-down version of Windows 11 successfully boots into the desktop environment and runs basic applications such as Calculator, Settings, Notepad, and Paint. The test was conducted on a virtual machine with 4GB of allocated RAM, with the operating system using around 883MB.

    Such experiments are a great way to showcase just how much of Windows can be stripped away while still retaining some of its core functionality. At the end of the day, they are primarily technical demonstrations with the intention of exploring the limits of Microsoft's operating system rather than providing practical alternatives to a standard Windows installation. Stripping away essential components, drivers, and background services comes with significant trade-offs, including reduced functionality, compatibility issues, and severely degraded performance.
