    #10169. GLM-5.2: Built for Long-Horizon Tasks

    We're introducing GLM-5.2, our latest flagship model for long-horizon tasks. It marks a substantial leap in long-horizon task capability over its predecessor GLM-5.1 and, for the first time, delivers that capability on a solid 1M-token context. GLM-5.2's new capabilities include:

    Supporting long-horizon tasks starts with making long context engineering-usable: the model must maintain quality across long, messy coding-agent trajectories, not just accept more tokens. A 1M context is easy to claim, but much harder to keep reliable under real engineering pressure. To this end, we substantially expanded 1M-context training for coding-agent scenarios, covering large-scale implementation, automated research, performance optimization, and complex debugging. The result is a long-context system that is not only wide in scope, but solid in execution: a practical substrate for sustained engineering work.

    This capability is reflected in GLM-5.2's performance on three long-horizon coding benchmarks. FrontierSWE measures whether an agent can complete open-ended technical projects at the scale of hours to tens of hours, spanning systems optimization, large-scale code construction, and applied ML research. On this benchmark, GLM-5.2 trails Opus 4.8 by only 1%, while edging out GPT-5.5 by 1% and Opus 4.7 by 11%. On PostTrainBench, where each agent is given an H100 GPU and evaluated by how much it can improve small models through post-training, GLM-5.2 outperforms both Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5, ranking second only to Opus 4.8. On SWE-Marathon, an ultra-long-horizon software engineering benchmark covering tasks such as building compilers, optimizing kernels, and developing production-grade services, GLM-5.2 still has room to grow, trailing Opus 4.8 by 13% while remaining second only to the Opus series. Across all three benchmarks, GLM-5.2 is the highest-ranked open-source model, showing that its 1M context has translated into practical long-horizon delivery capability.

    On standard coding benchmarks, GLM-5.2 is the strongest open-source model, improving on GLM-5.1 by a wide margin: 81.0 vs. 63.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 62.1 vs. 58.4 on SWE-bench Pro. It also closes much of the gap to the closed-source frontier — on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (81.0) it lands within a few points of Claude Opus 4.8 (85.0) — while staying ahead of Gemini 3.1 Pro.

    GLM-5.2 also introduces effort level control, enabling users to explicitly balance model capability against task execution speed and computational cost. As shown in the figure, GLM-5.2 delivers substantially stronger agentic coding performance than GLM-5.1 at comparable token budgets, with its capability roughly positioned between Claude Opus 4.7 and Claude Opus 4.8 under similar token consumption. Moreover, the Max effort level allows users to allocate additional computation when higher performance is required in challenging tasks, further extending the model’s coding capability. This design gives users greater flexibility when using GLM-5.2 for coding tasks, allowing them to select the most suitable reasoning mode for different scenarios.

    To support 1M context length, in GLM-5.2, we apply IndexShare to reduce the computational cost of the indexer in DSA. Specifically, in GLM-5.2, every 4 transformer layers share a lightweight indexer. The indexer is placed at the first of 4 layers and topk indices are used for 4 layers. This reduces the computation of indexer dot product and topk operation in 3/4 layers. GLM-5.2 is trained with IndexShare from mid-training with 128K sequence length, outperforming GLM-5.1 on long-context benchmarks with less computation.

    We improve the MTP layer of GLM-5.2 for speculative decoding with two objectives: 1) Minimize the cost of the MTP layer as draft model; 2) Maximize the acceptance rate of speculative decoding.

    For the first objective, we also apply IndexShare on the mtp layer. In multi-step MTP, the indexer is placed on the first step and topk indices are used for all the following steps. However, different from the backbone, the input tokens of different mtp steps are different. As the following figure shows, if we reuse the topk indices of $h_4$ for $h_5$, $h_5$ can only attend to $h_1$ to $h_4$, but not $h_5$. We will show that the property can help us achieve the second objective, by eliminating the training-inference discrepancy in GLM-5.1's mtp layer.

    In the above figure we show the inference of a two-step MTP layer. In the first step, inference is consistent with training, with all the hidden states coming from the target model. However, in the second step, $h_{1:4}$ come from the target model and $h_5$ comes from the mtp layer. Therefore, the KV cache of $h_5$ is a mixture of $kv_{1:4}$ computed from the target model and $kv_5$ computed from the mtp layer. Instead, with IndexShare, the KV cache of $h_5$ includes only $kv_{1:4}$, all from the hidden states of the target model. For training, we reuse both kv cache and topk indices of the first mtp step. Note that the same as GLM-5.1, the parameters of different MTP steps are also shared. Furthermore, inspired by https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12370, we introduce rejection sampling for speculative decoding, and use end-to-end TV loss for training.

    The table below shows the ablation of techniques by acceptance length on the coding scenarios. In the experiment we use the backbone and training data of GLM-5.1. The number of MTP steps is set to 7 for both training and inference. Compared with the baseline, the acceptance length of the final MTP layer increases by 20%.

    As GLM-5.2 extends the maximum context length from 200K to 1M tokens, coding workloads are expected to shift substantially toward longer prompts. This shifts the primary inference bottleneck from computation to KV-cache capacity, long-context kernel overhead, and CPU-side overhead. Although the new GLM-5.2 architecture reduces per-token computational FLOPs, it does not proportionally reduce per-token KV-cache size. As a result, supporting longer contexts, higher concurrency, and higher token throughput under limited GPU resources becomes a central challenge for inference engine optimization.

    To address this challenge, we optimize the inference engine along three directions. First, building on LayerSplit, we introduce finer-grained memory management and parallelization strategies to increase KV-cache capacity and provide more usable cache space for ultra-long-context requests. Second, we optimize kernels whose cost grows with context length and better coordinate them with the cache transfer pipeline, minimizing the impact of cache transfer on both prefill and decode performance. Third, we optimize CPU-side cache management, request scheduling, and runtime execution paths to reduce bubbles in the GPU execution pipeline and improve end-to-end throughput. As shown in the figure, GLM-5.2 achieves an increasingly larger throughput advantage as context length grows, demonstrating stronger scalability in long-context inference scenarios.

    The agentic RL post-training of GLM-5.2 involves tasks at larger scale, across more domains, and with more complex execution patterns. Heterogeneous data and tasks need to be organized within a unified training process, while long-horizon interactions, tool use, sub-task decomposition, and multi-turn environment feedback all impose higher requirements on rollout and training orchestration. To support this process, slime serves as an integrated infrastructure layer from training to large-scale inference rollout. It supports multiple training and task organization modes, including white-box rollout, black-box rollout, compact trajectory, and sub-agent workflow, enabling the same system to scale to larger and more complex RL and OPD training workloads. In the post-training process of GLM-5.2, we used the slime framework to conduct parallel OPD training, efficiently merging more than ten expert models into the final model. The entire OPD training process took approximately two days, demonstrating high training efficiency.

    Agentic RL also places higher demands on system resources and inference infrastructure. slime provides a highly open and flexible interface to inference systems: the training side can connect to inference services in different forms, and flexibly adapt to different parallelism strategies, routing policies, PD disaggregation setups, and deployment patterns. At the same time, the configuration experience, scheduling strategies, and optimization paths accumulated during RL rollout can be reused and further refined in the production serving stage, allowing the training side and the serving side to reinforce each other. This creates a more direct path from post-training to production deployment. Together with flexible training-inference resource organization and KV-cache FP8, slime provides critical infrastructure support for GLM-5.2’s large-scale agentic RL training, further improving system efficiency, rollout throughput, and large-scale inference concurrency.

    RL for Long-Horizon Tasks. For GLM-5.2, long-horizon tasks produce substantially longer execution traces, and once a super-long trajectory is split by compaction into multiple sub-traces, different rollouts under the same prompt yield different numbers of trainable traces with highly variable lengths. We therefore move from group-wise optimization to a critic-based PPO formulation that learns from individual rollouts, relying on a critic to estimate token-level advantages rather than group-relative comparisons. This single-rollout formulation fits compaction naturally, as it places no constraint on how many traces a prompt produces or on their relative lengths: we bring compaction into training by including all compacted sub-traces as trainable trajectories, and apply a token-level loss to address their length imbalance.

    Anti-Hack in Coding agents. Coding RL is especially vulnerable to reward hacking because the reward is typically a verifiable pass/fail signal. We find that GLM-5.2 shows more potential hacking behavior than GLM-5.1. This makes the verification signal easy to optimize, but fails to actually improve the fundamental capabilities of the model. An agent can read protected evaluation artifacts, copy answer content from references or upstream commits, or directly fetch the target source in GitHub-related tasks. For example, the agent may download solution via curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ or even chained leakage like

    These behaviors inflate rewards and corrupt the training signal, requiring a clear mechanism to separate real task-solving from shortcuts. To address this, we introduce an anti-hack module for both RL training and evaluation. The detection process has two stages: a rule-based filter first catches potential hacks to maximize recall, and then an LLM judge checks the intent of these flagged actions to keep precision high. We use an online strategy that monitors the tool calls at each step. If a hack is detected, the system blocks the call and returns dummy information as the result. Importantly, this online guard allows the model to continue the rollout even after a hacked action is caught. By handling the specific invalid behavior instead of rejecting the entire trajectory, this approach helps prevent the training instability and model collapse that can happen when rollouts are abruptly stopped.

    Try GLM-5.2 in your favorite coding agents—ZCode, Claude Code, OpenCode, and more. https://docs.z.ai/devpack/overview

    Prefer a GUI? We offer ZCode —a desktop agent powered by GLM-5.2, with /goal for long-horizon tasks, SSH remote development, and mobile control. Special offer: use GLM-5.2 through Coding Plan inside ZCode and get 1.5x effective quota until June 30.

    The model weights of GLM-5.2 are publicly available on HuggingFace and ModelScope. For local deployment, GLM-5.2 supports inference frameworks including transformers, vLLM, SGLang, xLLM, ktransformers.

    Super impressive model and release, excited to try an Opus-level open model in open coding agents

    Can't wait for open models to shatter the closed once and bring back the good old pre-gtp-2 days of actually transparent frontier AI research and development.

    Intel Foundry last week made available its Intel 14A process design kit (PDK) version 0.9, an important milestone in the development of this next-generation manufacturing technology. The company says that the production node is reaching performance and yield maturity expected at this stage of development, and the results are backed by silicon validation. Intel plans to release PDK 1.0 in the first quarter of 2027, which will validate the technology's readiness for high-volume manufacturing (HVM).

    A process design kit contains transistor models, design rules, and other information that enables chip designers to develop products for a particular manufacturing process using electronic design automation (EDA) tools. The accuracy and quality of the PDK are crucial for modelling how chips will perform once manufactured, and the release of PDK 0.9 is particularly important because it provides customers with a representation of Intel 14A based on actual silicon measurements rather than on theoretical models or simulations. At this stage, customers can proceed with product development with greater confidence that the technology will meet their requirements when it comes to performance and power consumption.

    Intel says that PDK 0.9 lets customers develop designs intended to enter risk production around the time the process is certified, which — provided that PDK accurately reflects the characteristics of manufactured silicon — in many cases enables chip developers to greatly reduce the number of silicon revisions between initial tapeout and mass production. Of course, availability of PDK 0.9 does not indicate that Intel 14A is ready or even close to mass production, as the company expects to validate HVM readiness only with PDK 1.0, sometime in Q1 2027. Again, this does not mean that 14A will enter mass production in early 2027, as Intel itself expects to begin mass production using its 14A process technology in 2028, following risk production for its own products in the second half of 2027.

    "From a customer perspective, the PDK 0.9 gives customers the confidence to design products on Intel 14A, as the technology is reaching the industry-standard performance and yield maturity expected at this stage of development, supported by silicon-backed validation," said Ben Sell, corporate vice president and general manager of front-end technology development at Intel Foundry.

    Intel 14A builds on top of architectural foundations introduced with Intel 18A but incorporates several substantial enhancements. These include 2nd Generation RibbonFET 2 gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, PowerDirect backside power delivery (which delivers power right to the transistor source/drain regions without using intermediate connections like TSVs used by PowerVia), and Turbo Cells (high-performance standard cells designed to accelerate timing-critical paths in CPUs and GPUs), which provide chip designers with additional ways to increase performance and optimize power efficiency. Since Intel has previously outlined advantages of these technologies, the latest announcement does not provide updates regarding transistor performance, power consumption, or transistor density figures for Intel 14A.

    Beyond improvements to transistor, power delivery, and interconnect technologies, Intel is applying manufacturing experience gained during 12 months of Intel 18A production to accelerate maturation of 14A. Specifically, the company says it has increased investments in inline defect detection, modeling, and simulation to identify potential manufacturing problems earlier in the development cycle. These initiatives are intended to improve manufacturing yields, process variability, ultimately transistor performance, and reduce production cycle times. Intel also says it has introduced several strategic initiatives to accelerate technology development, although it does not quantify their impact.

    Another important change concerns Intel's relationships with equipment and materials suppliers. The company says it has revised its collaboration model to involve technology development teams and external suppliers earlier in the process development cycle. The goal of such close collaborations is to address manufacturing defects and improve equipment capabilities before they become obstacles for yield improvements after the technology enters mass production. Intel also conducts regular yield summit meetings with suppliers to accelerate progress on critical development objectives.

    Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

    "This has required evolving our collaboration model with equipment and material suppliers, and earlier engagement from our [technology development] leaders with suppliers to drive improvements in defects and equipment capabilities," Sell said.

    A bonus of such early collaboration is that equipment and materials suppliers may incorporate Intel's requirements into their standard products and development roadmaps. This could give Intel an advantage over competitors, which would have to either adapt their manufacturing processes to equipment optimized around Intel's requirements or work with suppliers to develop alternative solutions from scratch.

    Historically, Intel frequently set the direction for semiconductor manufacturing technologies as other chipmakers subsequently adopted similar approaches. One notable exception was immersion DUV lithography, which Intel adopted after TSMC, which led the development of immersion DUV lithography. By engaging equipment and materials suppliers earlier, Intel could regain some of its historical influence over the development of industry-standard manufacturing solutions, though the importance of this should not be overestimated.

    Meanwhile, Intel continues to expand the design ecosystem for its 14A technology. Cadence and Intel have established a design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) collaboration focused on next-generation AI-driven design tools and intellectual property, whereas Keysight, Siemens, and Synopsys have announced design-tool certifications for the process. Intel is also working with other software developers and IP providers to validate design flows and reusable building blocks required by prospective foundry customers.

    Intel says it is encouraged by customer feedback regarding the progress of 14A development. However, the company has not identified any customers that have committed to manufacturing products using the technology, disclosed customer tape-outs, or announced specific manufacturing agreements, which is normal for the foundry industry. For Intel Foundry, attracting external customers remains particularly important because development costs of modern leading-edge process technologies can only be recoupled when they are used to make hundreds of millions of chips, way more than Intel sells these days. Meanwhile, the commercial success of Intel Foundry with advanced manufacturing technologies depends not only on transistor performance and manufacturing yields, but also on its ability to deliver predictable development schedules.

    Looking ahead, Intel intends to continue improving performance, yields, variability, and manufacturing cycle times of 14A, though for now the company does not disclose any actual goals. Intel also plans additional process enhancements and performance refinements for 14A-E and 14A-P nodes after the initial technology becomes available. However, exact schedules for these nodes are not known at the moment.

    "Our next major milestone is the Intel 14A PDK 1.0, expected in the first quarter of 2027," said Ali Farhang, corporate vice president and general manager of Intel Foundry's design technology platform organization. "I am looking forward to sustaining this level of quality across future releases and continuing to earn our customers' trust by delivering on our commitments with a customer-first mindset."

    #10166. Indie games are missing launch dates because Steam is backed up

    Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

    Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

    Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

    One developer has been waiting for weeks on approval for a game it planned to release today.

    One developer has been waiting for weeks on approval for a game it planned to release today.

    Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

    If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

    Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

    Many indie game developers have recently posted on social media about unexpectedly long approval wait times for their game submissions on Steam, with some of the approvals causing developers to miss their planned launch dates.

    For example, Studio Daimon, the team behind an upcoming title called Food Devils, had planned to launch the game in early access today after submitting its build on October 12th. But the game is “still awaiting approval,” according to a post from game director Alfred Kamon. “Even now, we don’t know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game. We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored.”

    In October, publisher 2 Left Thumbs said it missed its planned launch of Wheel Make It “by nearly two weeks” due to the long wait for build reviews. You can read some details about the studio’s setbacks, including failing a review for a “one single option in the menu” not being accessible with a controller, in a Steam post. There are lots of other recent posts about review build waits as well.

    Valve says on a Steam developer website that a review of a game’s store presence “typically takes 3-5 business days to complete,” though the company suggests submitting a page for review “at least 7 business days before you want it live to account for potential changes you’ll need to make.”

    However, as of late, Steam has seemingly been grappling with a sharp increase in games; October’s Steam Next Fest had 7,240 games, a 65.2 percent increase over June’s Steam Next Fest, according to How to Market a Game. A Reddit user also found that 49.9 percent of all games released since Valve started asking developers in 2024 to label games that use AI now have an AI disclosure.

    Kamon and 2 Left Thumbs suspect the longer waits are due to “slop” slowing down the process. “We can only assume it’s because Steam’s review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers,” said Kamon.

    In a new post from Valve published after we first ran this story, the company acknowledged that following a “a significant increase in submissions for store and page review in recent months,” it’s “running a little behind right now” and taking “up to 12 business days” for reviews, saying that much of the delay is “having to re-review games.” It has updated its release checklist for developers, including requiring them to run a game through Steam for at least five minutes. Valve also says that further improvements are on the way for the build review process.

    Itch.io has also been dealing with a rise in games, with the platform saying last weekend that “The number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past 2 months.” Last night, the platform said it “Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop 😌”

    Update, November 3rd: Added new post from Valve.

    #10165. A 10-Point Checklist for Legacy Application Modernization

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    Legacy applications often support critical business operations, but keeping them running can become increasingly difficult. Outdated infrastructure, growing technical debt, security vulnerabilities, and limited integration capabilities can make these systems expensive to maintain and harder to adapt to changing business needs.

    Modernizing them involves more than upgrading technology. You need to understand what the existing application does, identify which components need improvement, and manage the transition without disrupting essential operations.

    This 10-point legacy application modernization checklist walks you through the process, from assessing your existing systems and selecting a modernization strategy to migrating data, testing applications, and measuring results.

    Legacy application modernization is the process of updating existing software applications, their architecture, infrastructure, or underlying technologies to meet current business and technical requirements.

    Depending on the application's condition, modernization may involve moving it to a new platform, improving its code, redesigning its architecture, or replacing it with a new solution.

    The goal is to improve performance, security, scalability, maintainability, and the application's ability to support future business requirements.

    Modernization isn't necessarily the same as cloud migration. Moving an application from on-premises infrastructure to the cloud changes where it runs, but it may leave its underlying architecture and technical limitations unchanged.

    An organization can modernize an application without moving it to the cloud or combine both approaches as part of a larger transformation.

    Use this checklist to track the ten essential steps involved in modernizing legacy applications.

    1. Define modernization goals: Identify business problems and establish measurable success criteria.

    2. Assess existing applications: Review infrastructure, technical debt, code quality, and performance limitations.

    3. Map application dependencies: Document critical workflows, integrations, and business rules.

    4. Choose a modernization strategy: Select an approach based on business value, cost, complexity, and risk.

    5. Develop a roadmap and budget: Prioritize activities, estimate costs, assign responsibilities, and establish milestones.

    6. Plan architecture and security: Design the target environment and address security, compliance, and availability requirements.

    7. Prepare data migration: Plan data transfer, integration changes, and validation procedures.

    8. Modernize incrementally: Validate the approach with a pilot and implement changes in manageable phases.

    9. Test and deploy: Verify functionality, performance, security, and data integrity before production rollout.

    10. Monitor and optimize: Measure results, support users, and continuously improve the modernized application.

    Let's examine what each step involves and how to determine whether you're ready to proceed.

    Before selecting technologies or planning development work, identify what the modernization initiative needs to achieve.

    Clear business objectives help prioritize investments, guide technical decisions, and establish whether the project delivers meaningful improvements.

    Start by examining the problems affecting your application's performance, reliability, or business value.

    For example, a legacy order management system might still process transactions reliably but require extensive manual work whenever the business adds a new sales channel.

    In this situation, improving integration capabilities may be more valuable than replacing the entire application.

    An application's age alone doesn't justify a major technology investment. Whether legacy modernization makes sense for your business depends on the problems the existing system creates, the cost of maintaining it, and whether smaller improvements could resolve those issues.

    Once you've identified the problems, translate them into measurable objectives.

    If slow performance is the primary concern, establish a target for response times or transaction processing speed. If maintenance expenses are rising, determine what reduction in operating costs would justify the investment.

    Relevant key performance indicators (KPIs) may include:

    These baseline measurements will help determine whether the changes deliver the expected results.

    Completion check: You have a documented business case identifying the problems to address, expected outcomes, measurable KPIs, and stakeholders responsible for approving success.

    A legacy application assessment provides a clear picture of your current technology environment.

    Without this assessment, teams may underestimate project complexity, overlook critical components, or choose a modernization approach that doesn't address the application's actual limitations.

    Begin by creating an inventory of your applications and their supporting technologies.

    Document each application's purpose, business owner, primary users, operating environment, programming languages, frameworks, databases, and infrastructure requirements.

    Also identify software versions, third-party dependencies, licensing restrictions, and components approaching or past their end-of-support dates.

    If your organization operates several legacy applications, use a consistent assessment framework. This makes it easier to compare their business importance, technical condition, and modernization urgency.

    Review the application's codebase to identify issues that make maintenance and development difficult.

    Look for tightly coupled components, duplicated logic, outdated libraries, insufficient automated tests, and undocumented configurations.

    Pay particular attention to areas where small modifications regularly cause unexpected problems elsewhere in the system.

    For example, if payment processing, inventory management, and customer records share tightly connected code, modifying one function could require extensive testing across the entire application.

    Your infrastructure assessment should also cover hardware limitations, database compatibility, backup capabilities, operating systems, and unsupported dependencies.

    Analyze how the application performs during normal operations and periods of increased demand.

    Review response times, database queries, resource utilization, transaction volumes, and recurring failures.

    Existing monitoring data and incident records can reveal problems that aren't immediately visible during routine use.

    Determine whether performance limitations originate from inefficient application code, infrastructure capacity, database design, or external dependencies.

    This distinction matters because adding computing resources won't necessarily resolve problems caused by poor application logic.

    Completion check: You have an application inventory and technical assessment report documenting major components, technical debt, operational risks, and performance limitations.

    Legacy applications rarely operate independently. They exchange data with other systems, support interconnected business processes, and often contain business rules that aren't fully documented.

    Understanding these dependencies is essential because changing one component can affect several other applications or workflows.

    Document the processes that rely on the application, including the steps users follow, the data they need, and the expected outcomes.

    Work with business users, application owners, operations teams, and developers familiar with the system.

    Identify processes that cannot tolerate significant interruption, such as payment processing, order fulfillment, customer authentication, or financial reporting.

    Don't overlook activities that happen less frequently. Month-end financial reports, annual calculations, and scheduled data exchanges may depend on functionality that isn't exercised during everyday operations.

    Map how the application communicates with databases, APIs, third-party services, and other internal systems.

    Include scheduled jobs, file transfers, message queues, authentication services, and reporting tools.

    Some legacy applications contain years of accumulated business logic.

    Rules for pricing, approvals, calculations, or customer eligibility may exist only in source code, database procedures, or undocumented workflows.

    Identify these rules before modifying the underlying implementation.

    Where possible, create automated tests that capture existing expected behavior. These tests can help verify that the modernized application preserves required functionality.

    Completion check: Critical workflows, system dependencies, integrations, and business rules are documented and reviewed by the relevant business and technical owners.

    The appropriate modernization strategy depends on the application's technical condition, business importance, budget, and future requirements.

    Not every application needs to be rebuilt. Some systems require targeted improvements, while others may be better replaced or retired.

    Common legacy application modernization strategies include:

    Different applications within the same organization may require different approaches.

    Evaluate each option against your technical constraints and business requirements.

    Consider implementation effort, expected benefits, ongoing maintenance costs, required expertise, and potential disruption.

    For example, replatforming may be suitable for an application that operates reliably but depends on aging infrastructure. Rearchitecting may be necessary when tightly coupled components prevent independent updates or scaling.

    A complete rebuild requires particular caution. Recreating undocumented functionality can be expensive, and important business rules may be lost if the existing system hasn't been thoroughly assessed.

    The right strategy should solve the identified problems without introducing unnecessary cost or complexity.

    Completion check: Each application has a selected modernization strategy, documented rationale, estimated effort, and an approved decision on whether to modernize, retain, replace, or retire it.

    Once you've selected a modernization approach, convert it into an actionable plan.

    Your roadmap should establish what will change, in what order, who will be responsible, and how progress will be evaluated.

    Prioritize modernization work according to business value, technical complexity, urgency, and dependencies.

    Applications with unsupported components or significant security risks may require early attention. However, starting with the most complex application isn't always the best choice.

    A smaller, lower-risk application can provide an opportunity to validate tools, workflows, and team capabilities before modernizing more critical systems.

    Dependencies also affect the sequence. For example, a shared authentication service may need to be updated before applications that rely on it can be migrated.

    Prepare a budget covering the full modernization process rather than development alone.

    Compare upfront implementation expenses with expected operating costs over time.

    A modernization approach with a lower initial cost may still require significant ongoing maintenance.

    Allow contingency for unexpected issues, particularly when legacy documentation is incomplete or system dependencies remain uncertain.

    Divide the project into phases with defined deliverables and approval requirements.

    Assign responsible owners for architecture, development, security, data migration, testing, and business acceptance.

    Establish how project risks will be reported and who can approve changes to scope, budget, or deployment schedules.

    Keep the roadmap adaptable. Findings from pilot implementations or migration rehearsals may require changes to the original plan.

    Completion check: Your modernization roadmap includes prioritized activities, estimated costs, responsible owners, dependencies, milestones, and approval checkpoints.

    The target architecture determines how the modernized application will operate, scale, integrate with other systems, and remain maintainable.

    Security and compliance requirements should be incorporated into the design from the beginning.

    Choose an architecture that fits the application's actual requirements.

    Possible approaches include a modular monolith, service-oriented architecture, microservices, or event-driven components.

    Microservices aren't automatically the best option. Although they allow independent deployment and scaling of components, they also introduce complexity in communication, monitoring, deployment, and data management.

    For smaller applications or tightly integrated business processes, a well-structured modular architecture may be easier to maintain.

    Document architectural decisions covering application components, data storage, interfaces, infrastructure requirements, and operational responsibilities.

    Identify security weaknesses that should be resolved during modernization.

    Review authentication, authorization, encryption, secrets management, logging, and access to sensitive information.

    Evaluate third-party dependencies and establish processes for vulnerability scanning, patching, and security testing.

    Regulatory and contractual requirements should also influence the target design.

    Security controls should be applied throughout development and deployment rather than added shortly before release.

    Define how the application will remain available and recover from failures.

    Establish recovery time objectives (RTOs) and recovery point objectives (RPOs) based on business requirements.

    Plan backup procedures, restoration testing, appropriate redundancy, and monitoring for critical components.

    Validate that the target environment can support the required availability and recovery objectives.

    Completion check: The target architecture has documented design decisions, security controls, compliance requirements, availability objectives, and recovery procedures.

    Data migration is one of the most sensitive stages of legacy application modernization.

    Legacy databases may contain inconsistent records, outdated formats, duplicated information, or relationships that newer systems handle differently.

    A migration strategy needs to explain how data will be transferred, validated, and made available without compromising business operations.

    Begin by reviewing the quality and structure of existing data.

    Identify missing values, duplicate records, inconsistent formats, obsolete fields, and relationships that could create migration problems.

    Document how existing data structures correspond to the target system.

    For example, a legacy customer database might store contact details in a single field, while the new application requires separate fields for email addresses and phone numbers.

    The migration process needs defined transformation rules to handle these differences.

    Determine which records must be migrated, archived, retained for compliance, or excluded.

    Choose a migration approach based on data volume, application availability requirements, and acceptable downtime.

    Depending on the system, this may involve a scheduled migration during a maintenance window, staged transfers, or synchronization between old and new environments.

    Identify integrations that will need modification.

    Where applications exchange information through APIs, files, or messaging systems, verify that the modernized implementation supports the required data formats and business behavior.

    If the legacy and modernized applications will operate simultaneously, define how data updates will be synchronized between them.

    Test the migration process using representative datasets before transferring production data.

    Validate record counts, field values, relationships, and critical business calculations.

    For sensitive or business-critical information, use appropriate reconciliation methods, including integrity checks where applicable.

    Document how inconsistencies will be identified and resolved.

    Also establish what happens if migration fails or the application needs to return to its previous environment.

    Completion check: Data mapping rules are approved, migration rehearsals have been completed, and reconciliation procedures can verify data accuracy.

    Modernizing an entire application in a single major release can increase project risk, particularly when the system supports critical business operations.

    An incremental approach allows teams to validate decisions, identify problems earlier, and limit the impact of failures.

    Select a manageable component or workload to validate your modernization approach.

    The pilot should test an important assumption, such as whether the target platform supports the application, whether a legacy integration can be replaced, or whether an architectural change improves performance.

    Define success criteria before implementation.

    A useful pilot should provide evidence that the approach is technically feasible and that the team can manage its operational requirements.

    Use the findings to improve estimates, identify missing skills, and refine the broader implementation plan.

    Divide the application into manageable migration or development units where its architecture allows.

    One approach is the Strangler Fig pattern, which gradually replaces legacy functionality while the remaining parts of the original application continue operating.

    For example, an organization might modernize customer notifications first, followed by reporting and then core transaction processing.

    This can reduce the risks associated with replacing an entire system at once.

    However, incremental modernization also requires careful coordination. Temporary integrations, duplicated components, and parallel systems can introduce complexity.

    Each phase should have defined boundaries, validation requirements, and completion criteria.

    Establish repeatable processes for developing, testing, and deploying application changes.

    Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines can automate builds, execute tests, and promote approved changes through environments.

    Use version control, consistent configuration management, and infrastructure as code where appropriate.

    Include security and quality checks in the delivery process to reduce the risk of introducing defects during frequent releases.

    Completion check: The pilot has validated the selected approach, implementation is divided into manageable phases, and repeatable build, test, and deployment processes are established.

    Modernization isn't complete when the new application runs successfully in a development environment.

    It must perform the required business functions, communicate correctly with connected systems, and meet operational expectations before production rollout.

    Develop a testing plan based on the application's critical workflows and identified risks.

    Automate repeatable tests where practical, especially for critical business processes.

    Compare results against the performance baselines and acceptance criteria established earlier.

    Business users should verify that the modernized application supports their actual workflows.

    User acceptance testing (UAT) should include routine operations, exception handling, reporting requirements, and tasks that depend on specialized business knowledge.

    Use representative migrated data during testing.

    Confirm that critical records, calculations, and reports remain accurate after the transition.

    Resolve issues affecting essential operations before approving production deployment.

    Prepare a documented deployment plan outlining the sequence of activities, responsible teams, communication channels, and expected service interruptions.

    Choose a deployment method appropriate for the application, such as a phased rollout, canary release, or scheduled cutover.

    Establish measurable conditions that would stop deployment or trigger a rollback.

    Rollback planning must account for data changes made after cutover. Restoring an earlier application version doesn't automatically restore database consistency, especially if new transactions have already been processed.

    Rehearse deployment and recovery procedures in a suitable non-production environment.

    Completion check: Required tests have passed, business owners have approved acceptance criteria, and deployment, cutover, and recovery procedures have been validated.

    The initial deployment marks the beginning of ongoing operation rather than the end of modernization.

    The application needs continued monitoring and maintenance to ensure that expected improvements are sustained.

    Compare post-modernization results against the baseline established at the beginning of the project.

    Track metrics linked to your business objectives, such as application availability, maintenance costs, response times, deployment frequency, security vulnerabilities, and user satisfaction.

    Use monitoring tools, logs, traces, and alerts to identify problems that may not be visible through basic availability checks.

    Review performance after deployment and at agreed intervals to determine whether the modernization initiative is meeting its objectives.

    Technical improvements may introduce changes to established workflows.

    Provide relevant training, updated documentation, and support resources for users and operational teams.

    Ensure that administrators and developers understand the new architecture, deployment processes, monitoring tools, and incident response procedures.

    Collect user feedback to identify usability issues or missing functionality.

    Use production data and operational feedback to guide further improvements.

    Optimization may involve updating dependencies, improving database queries, adjusting infrastructure capacity, strengthening security controls, or simplifying application components.

    Once replacement functionality is stable and approved, begin decommissioning components that are no longer needed.

    Before retirement, confirm that dependent applications have been migrated, necessary records are retained, and archival or compliance obligations have been met.

    Removing unused infrastructure and software can reduce maintenance costs and unnecessary security exposure.

    Completion check: Monitoring and support responsibilities are established, modernization KPIs are reviewed, and unused legacy components have an approved retirement plan.

    Organizations without the internal resources to manage legacy modernization may need support from an external software development company.

    Depending on the project, a development partner can assist with application assessments, code refactoring, architecture redesign, system integration, data migration, and implementation.

    Companies offering custom software development and application modernization services include:

    Idea Maker: Provides custom software development and legacy application modernization services, including application assessments, code refactoring, architecture redesign, and cloud migration.

    ScienceSoft: Offers custom software development, legacy software modernization, application reengineering, cloud migration, and system integration services.

    Itransition: Provides custom application development, legacy application modernization, system integration, software migration, and post-modernization support.

    Simform: Offers digital product engineering, software modernization, cloud and platform engineering, and data integration services.

    These are examples of providers rather than a ranked comparison.

    When evaluating a development partner, consider their experience with your existing technology stack, ability to handle complex integrations, approach to data security, and experience delivering projects with similar requirements.

    Ask prospective providers how they assess legacy systems, manage migration risks, preserve critical business logic, and validate application functionality before deployment.

    The main steps are defining business goals, assessing existing applications, mapping dependencies, choosing a modernization strategy, developing a roadmap, designing the target architecture, planning data migration, implementing changes, testing and deploying, and continuously optimizing the application.

    The exact sequence may vary depending on the application's complexity and business requirements.

    Start by evaluating the application's business value, technical condition, dependencies, and future requirements.

    Rehosting or replatforming may be sufficient when the application functions well and infrastructure is the primary concern.

    Refactoring or rearchitecting may be necessary when code quality or architectural limitations affect maintainability and scalability.

    Rebuilding or replacing becomes an option when the existing implementation no longer meets business needs or would be too costly to maintain.

    Compare expected benefits, implementation costs, risks, and ongoing maintenance requirements before making a decision.

    Common risks include undocumented dependencies, data loss or corruption, unexpected downtime, security vulnerabilities, integration failures, and loss of essential business functionality.

    Projects may also experience delays or budget overruns when technical complexity is underestimated.

    These risks can be reduced through early assessment, phased implementation, migration rehearsals, comprehensive testing, and validated recovery procedures.

    The timeline depends on the application's size, architecture, technical debt, data complexity, integrations, and selected modernization approach.

    A limited rehosting or refactoring project generally requires less effort than rebuilding a large application or modernizing several interconnected systems.

    A reliable estimate requires an initial technical assessment. A pilot or proof of concept can help validate assumptions about implementation effort and potential challenges.

    Measure success against the business and technical objectives established before implementation.

    Relevant indicators include application performance, availability, maintenance costs, security improvements, deployment speed, and user satisfaction.

    For example, if reducing maintenance effort was the primary goal, lower support costs and faster resolution of application issues may be more meaningful than infrastructure performance alone.

    Modernization success should be evaluated over time rather than only immediately after deployment.

    Legacy application modernization works best when it follows a structured plan based on business needs and the realities of existing technology.

    The ten steps in this checklist cover the key decisions and activities involved, from assessing legacy systems and selecting a modernization strategy to migrating data, validating functionality, and maintaining the resulting application.

    Careful dependency mapping, realistic planning, incremental implementation, and thorough testing help reduce risks throughout the transition.

    Start by assessing your existing applications and defining what modernization needs to achieve. Those findings will help you identify which systems deserve attention, where to invest resources, and how to approach modernization without introducing unnecessary complexity.

    #10164. From the Hugging Face Hub to robot hardware with Strands Agents and LeRobot

    A walkthrough of the LeRobot integration in Strands Robots - one agent loop, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot, with sim-to-real datasets in the same on-disk format and policies you swap with a string.

    You have a robot, a folder of demonstration data on the Hugging Face Hub, and a new task you want it to learn. Today that takes five separate tools: one to record new demonstrations, another to train, a third to test in simulation, custom code to deploy on hardware, and yet another to coordinate when you have more than one robot. The pieces work on their own. They don't talk to each other.

    Strands Robots is an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools that you compose into a single Strands agent. The integration is deliberately thin: LeRobot's own scripts handle hardware recording and calibration, and the Strands AgentTools come in for the parts an agent actually orchestrates. The simulation tool records LeRobotDatasets in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware. LerobotLocal serves policy inference behind one interface for GR00T, ACT, SmolVLA, and MolmoAct2 checkpoints. A peer mesh fans the agent out to remote robots. The dataset format stays exactly as LeRobot wrote it; the agent loop is the glue.

    This post walks you through five steps inside a single agent: build the agent over the LeRobot AgentTools, record a demonstration as a LeRobotDataset in simulation, run a policy on the same robot, deploy the same agent code to a physical SO-101 with one keyword argument change, and broadcast commands across a fleet over the Zenoh mesh. At the end, you can clone the working sample application from GitHub and run it on your laptop in simulation. No hardware, no GPU, no Hugging Face credentials needed for the default path. The runnable companion to this post lives at examples/lerobot/hub_to_hardware.py and hub_to_hardware.ipynb. The notebook is sim-only and Mock-policy by default.

    The Strands Robots SDK exposes the LeRobot stack as AgentTools that you compose into one Strands agent. The example agent in this post does four things: record new demonstrations in simulation, push the result to the Hub as a LeRobotDataset, run a policy in simulation against that same format, and deploy the same agent code to a physical robot with one keyword argument change. When you have more than one robot, the agent can coordinate the whole fleet through a built-in peer mesh. For hardware recording and calibration, LeRobot's own CLIs (lerobot-record, lerobot-calibrate) handle the bring-up; the agent picks up from there.

    Figure 1. Robot("so100") defaults to a MuJoCo-backed simulation; mode="real" returns a hardware robot driven by LeRobot. Both modes share the same DatasetRecorder and the same policy providers, so a dataset captured in sim and a dataset captured on hardware use the same on-disk LeRobotDataset format.

    Two design choices make this work. First, Robot("so100") returns a simulation by default (no hardware, no risk), and mode="real" returns a hardware-backed robot driven by LeRobot. The agent code is identical across both modes. Second, the DatasetRecorder that writes a LeRobotDataset is shared between the simulation path and LeRobot's own hardware recording, so a dataset captured in MuJoCo and one captured from a physical SO-101 are in the same format.

    The whole workflow in five lines of Python:

    What follows is what's actually happening inside that call, step by step.

    That's it. The example in this post runs end-to-end on a laptop with these three.

    Install Strands Robots and get the example files:

    Export your Hugging Face token if you want the agent to push datasets or pull policies from the Hub. This is optional for the default simulation path in this post; the example runs end-to-end with the Mock policy and writes the dataset to your local cache without needing Hub access.

    The runnable example lives at examples/lerobot/hub_to_hardware.py (Python script) and hub_to_hardware.ipynb (notebook), in the strands-labs/robots repository alongside the MuJoCo examples. The notebook is the recommended starting point: open it in JupyterLab and run cells top-to-bottom in simulation mode without any hardware connected.

    The simulation tool records LeRobotDatasets in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware. No hardware required. The Simulation tool's start_recording action writes through the same DatasetRecorder class: same parquet schema for joint states and actions, same per-camera MP4 layout. The agent prompt is almost identical:

    Figure 2. The recording scene in MuJoCo simulation: the SO-100 arm reaching toward a red cube on the ground plane, captured to a LeRobotDataset. No hardware, no GPU, no Hugging Face credentials needed for this default path.

    The Mock policy is intentional: it generates placeholder joint actions so the workflow runs end-to-end without a trained checkpoint. The robot moves through random motions rather than completing the grasp, and the recording is structurally complete (valid joint states, valid camera frames, a well-formed LeRobotDataset episode), but the demonstration itself isn't useful as training data. Step 3 below swaps in a GR00T checkpoint through LerobotLocal for real grasping behavior. To see actual cube-picking in this step, run --policy lerobot_local --checkpoint allenai/MolmoAct2-SO100_101 (a MolmoAct2 checkpoint, auto-detected from its config.json and routed through the LerobotLocal path); the prompt, dataset format, and agent code stay the same.

    The proof is what happens next. LeRobot's own dataset loader reads the sim-recorded data with no Strands-specific code path:

    This features dict is identical in shape to any LeRobot dataset on the Hub: same column names, same parquet+MP4 layout, same loader path. Training scripts that consume hardware-recorded data consume the sim-recorded data without modification. Datasets pushed from sim sit alongside hardware recordings in the same Hub repository if you want them to.

    A single episode from a recorded LeRobotDataset, played back from the per-camera MP4 the recorder wrote, the same on-disk video a training script reads.

    To record demonstrations on a physical SO-101 instead of simulation, use LeRobot's record CLI directly. The Strands integration doesn't wrap that command as an AgentTool because LeRobot already does the job cleanly:

    The dataset that lands on the Hub from this command is in the same format as the simulation recording. To fine-tune a policy on it, run LeRobot's training CLI (lerobot-train); training itself is out of scope for this post and follows the standard LeRobot workflow. From Step 3 onward, the agent picks up either the original or a fine-tuned checkpoint interchangeably. For full SO-101 hardware setup, calibration walkthroughs, and troubleshooting, see the README in the example folder.

    With the dataset on the Hub, the next step is to run a policy. The example uses the Robot() factory in its default sim mode and runs a GR00T checkpoint through the LerobotLocal provider, in the same process:

    Under the hood, the agent runs a run_policy action on the simulated robot with policy_provider="lerobot_local". The provider downloads the checkpoint from the Hub and loads it through LeRobot's GR00T policy in the same process. The simulation steps with the policy's action chunks, and a render of the result is available via Simulation.render. To run inference on a separate GPU host instead, start strands_robots.inference.server.PolicyServer there and use policy_provider="remote".

    Figure 3. With a trained policy (a GR00T or MolmoAct2 checkpoint), the agent drives the SO-100 to grasp the red cube in simulation, the behavior the Mock policy stands in for.

    The same provider loads any LeRobot checkpoint. A model ID under the lerobot/ organization routes to it by name:

    LerobotLocalPolicy supports ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, and π0.5, anything LeRobot's own policy registry can resolve from a config.json. Real-Time Chunking turns on automatically for flow-matching policies that ship an rtc_config (π0, SmolVLA).

    NVIDIA's recently released Cosmos 3 is also available as a policy provider behind the same interface, so the agent code stays the same whichever provider you point it at.

    Note: LerobotLocalPolicy loads Hugging Face models with trust_remote_code=True. Set STRANDS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE=1 to opt in, and only load checkpoints from organizations you trust.

    This is the same code as Step 3, with one keyword argument changed. The Robot factory returns a hardware-backed robot driven by LeRobot's make_robot_from_config:

    The same agent prompt now runs against a physical arm. The hardware path uses LeRobot's robot abstraction for joint commands and camera reads, and the same GR00T checkpoint, loaded in-process, generates the action chunks.

    Before this runs against your SO-101, calibration for both follower and leader has to be in place. Run LeRobot's calibration command (lerobot-calibrate) once per device; the files land under ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/calibration/ and any Strands code path that touches the hardware reads them from there. If a calibration is missing, the agent surfaces the error from the LeRobot driver layer.

    Up to now we've driven one robot at a time. The mesh is how Strands Robots handles more than one. Picture a leader arm on your desk teleoperating a follower arm in another room, or five SO-101s running the same warehouse task in parallel, or a humanoid coordinating with a mobile base. All of those are mesh patterns. The mesh is built on Zenoh, an open source peer-to-peer protocol, and you don't manage IP addresses, write discovery code, or pick a broker; new robots show up on the mesh the moment they come up, and the agent can talk to all of them at once.

    A Robot() or Simulation() joins a Zenoh peer mesh when you pass mesh=True, or set STRANDS_MESH=true; the mesh is off by default. The robot_mesh tool gives the agent a vocabulary for fleet operations such as discovery, structured commands, broadcasts, and emergency stop:

    By default, every physically-actuating mesh action pauses for a human approval interrupt before it runs: the fleet-wide broadcast and emergency_stop, plus the single-peer tell, send, and stop. You can tune this set with the STRANDS_MESH_HITL_ACTIONS environment variable (set it to all, none, or a comma-separated subset). The first time you run this example, you'll see a robot_mesh-broadcast-approval prompt in your terminal; type y (or yes / approve) to authorize the broadcast. The approval is delivered out-of-band of the LLM's tool arguments, so a prompt-injection attempt that tries to slip an approval flag into the command body cannot bypass the gate.

    The transport scales without touching agent code. The built-in Zenoh mesh is the automatic fallback: on the LAN, Zenoh peers find each other with no broker (gossip by default; set STRANDS_MESH_MULTICAST=true for multicast scouting), and adding the [mesh-iot] extra routes traffic through AWS IoT Core (MQTT5 with mTLS) for cloud fleets, with a BridgeTransport that fans LAN and cloud behind one API (select it with STRANDS_MESH_BACKEND=bridge).

    For production fleets, Device Connect, a device-aware networking layer developed in collaboration with Arm, handles discovery, presence, structured RPC, event routing, and safety. The same robot_mesh tool dispatches through Device Connect when it is available and falls back to the built-in Zenoh mesh otherwise, so the agent code in this post is unchanged either way. See the Device Connect documentation for setup and current availability.

    The full sample is on GitHub at strands-labs/robots in the examples/lerobot/ folder. It packages all five steps into a single CLI script (hub_to_hardware.py) and a notebook (hub_to_hardware.ipynb). The CLI defaults run end-to-end in simulation with the Mock policy. No GPU, no Docker, no Hugging Face credentials needed.

    The recorded dataset lands at ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/local/strands-cube-pick/. To push to the Hugging Face Hub instead of keeping it local, pass --hf-user after exporting HF_TOKEN with write scope. For real grasping behavior in Step 3, pass --policy lerobot_local --checkpoint nvidia/GR00T-N1.7-3B, or another Hub checkpoint. This needs a GPU and STRANDS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE=1.

    The notebook (examples/lerobot/hub_to_hardware.ipynb) walks through the same workflow cell by cell, with narration between each step. Open it in JupyterLab and run top-to-bottom in simulation mode.

    The code snippets shown in this setup represent a “hello world” example of setting up Strands Robots with HuggingFace. For more serious, production-ready use cases there are some important considerations users should be aware of:

    Supplying untrusted data into agents can lead to prompt injection, where untrustworthy context is treated as LLM instructions. Given the actuation of these robots in physical space, this is an important risk to track. To mitigate this behavior, developers should be careful to feed the robots only data that comes from a trusted source. If not all input data can be trusted, developers should restrict the tools available to the agent to prevent the robots from making safety-critical actions.

    The STRANDS_MESH_LOCAL_DEV=1 setting shared in the code snippets in this blog initializes the robot mesh without authentication or access controls. This means that any device on the same network can provide commands to the robot fleet. This is acceptable for trusted development environments, but is not suitable for untrusted networks or production environments. For these use cases, STRANDS_MESH_AUTH_MODE=mtls is required.

    The robot_mesh tool's physically-actuating actions affect peers on the network: broadcast and emergency_stop reach every peer, while tell, send, and stop reach a single targeted peer. To prevent an agent from issuing these commands autonomously (or under prompt injection), all five are gated behind a human-in-the-loop interrupt by default. When the agent invokes a gated action, the Strands runtime pauses the agent loop and asks the operator to approve out-of-band of the LLM's tool arguments. You can adjust the gated set with the STRANDS_MESH_HITL_ACTIONS environment variable (all, none, or a comma-separated subset). Per-action rate limits, command validation, and an audit trail run alongside the interrupt. Outside an agent loop (a bare script or unit test), the gated actions fail closed.

    The preceding workflow opens serial ports on hardware and writes a local dataset cache. To return your environment to a clean state:

    The integration's central design choice is that Strands Robots doesn't reimplement what LeRobot already provides. Hardware abstraction, calibration, and the dataset format stay upstream. Strands adds the AgentTool surface that makes them composable from natural language.

    Two consequences follow. For users, every dataset on the Hub is an asset an agent can extend, fine-tune from, and deploy against with no conversion step. For developers, simulation data and hardware data share a single file format, so training scripts written for one consume the other unchanged. The line between sim and real becomes a deployment detail, not an architectural divide.

    Figure 4. The Strands Robots catalog spans arms, humanoids, quadrupeds, and hands, all in the same MuJoCo simulation and behind the same Robot() factory. The SO-100 in this post is one of many supported embodiments.

    The full Strands Robots documentation covers the robot catalog, simulation, policy providers, the mesh, and Device Connect in depth. For larger workloads, Strands Robots also ships heavier simulation backends, Isaac Sim and Newton. Both backends plug into the same Robot abstraction shown in this post, so the agent code stays the same as you scale up.

    Contributions are welcome under Apache 2.0. If you build something with this workflow, open an issue with what worked and what didn't. The SDK improves fastest when developer feedback lands directly on the surface that needs it.

    Cagatay Cali is a Research Engineer at AWS focused on Agentic AI and robotics. He designs interfaces that connect AI agents to physical robots, enabling developers to control robotic systems through natural language and making agents and robotics development accessible to builders at any skill level.

    Sundar Raghavan is a Sr Solutions Architect at AWS on the Agentic AI Foundations team. He leads the developer experience for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, owning the SDK and CLI, and drives the framework and ecosystem integrations strategy. He focuses on how developers build, deploy, and scale production AI agents on AWS. He is currently extending that focus into physical AI, collaborating on Strands Robots to bring the same agent developer experience to robotics.

    Fantastic to see! The single-kwarg flip from MuJoCo sim to mode="real" (same agent code, same LeRobotDataset format end to end) is exactly the friction-removal that gets robotics agents into real labs. Work like this lifts all the ships: the easier and more open we make agent-to-hardware control, the faster the whole industry moves. The Device Connect team at Arm is excited to collaborate!

    #10163. Google will disable Search for students unless schools accept AI features in ‘Guided Learning’ push

    Google is today launching new AI settings for schools, but with the big catch that Search is fully disabled if AI features are turned off entirely.

    In a blog post today, Google says it is “focused on building technology responsibly to help students thrive” and, as such, will tailor its AI efforts to help students. “Guided Learning” in Gemini, Search, and Classroom will include helping students “work through problems without skipping straight to answers.”

    …if a student pastes a complex physics problem or asks for help writing a book report in Search, they’ll see prompts to help them think critically and work through the concepts, without going directly to the answer.

    That’s launching in a pilot program this month in select US schools, with Guided Learning in Google Classroom launching globally today. Google describes this as a “1-1 study tool, anchored in class material to help [students] stay on task” while also giving the teacher insights into how their class is handling the material.

    Beyond this new Guided Learning push, Google also says that it will now turn off “Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search” for K-12 student accounts by default “until school administrators explicitly turn them on.”

    As The New York Times points out, having those features fully off has a big side effect: it cuts students off from Google Search entirely.

    Google says that this is because Search and AI “are deeply integrated” and confirms that students in schools with AI features turned off (which, to reiterate, is now the default setting) “will not have access to search.”

    As a reminder, Google Search’s AI features can largely be turned off using a simple modifier.

    Google’s post says that the “goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit.” Yet, speaking to The New York Times, Google further explained that two options will be available to schools in “early 2027,” one that has AI Overviews and other AI features turned on, the other with Guided Learning in their place, leaving schools with no choice other than to accept AI features or give up access to Google Search for their students entirely.

    NYT points out repeatedly that Google’s prior AI pushes in schools have been met with fierce opposition from educators and parents alike.

    This move could help data centers operate sooner without waiting for the rest of the grid to catch up to its peak demand.

    When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

    Electricity consumption is one of the biggest concerns that residents bring up whenever a data center is proposed in their community, which is why OpenAI is taking steps to minimize its impact on the local electricity grid. According to the company, its Grid Protectors Program aims to reduce the power consumption of its data centers as local demand increases, ensuring that the grid is not overwhelmed during peak hours. Aside from ensuring that the lights remain on for everyone, it would also allow its data centers to connect to the grid and go online sooner instead of waiting for the additional power sources to come online.

    “Whether it’s heating homes during a northern cold snap or running air conditioning through a southern heat wave, families need reliable electricity. Our goal is to make campus flexibility a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most,” OpenAI said in its blog. It also added, “Through Grid Protectors, our ambition is to make this kind of flexibility a core part of how we build and operate future campuses. That means designing facilities to reduce electricity use when needed and working with utilities to agree on how much demand can be reduced, how quickly and for how long. The arrangements will differ by location, and we will share additional commitments as they are finalized.”

    OpenAI is testing the program in its planned Effingham County campus in Georgia, with the company saying that it has already signed a 3.2-gigawatt agreement with Georgia Power that included 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response. This ensures that if demand jumps on the hottest days of the year, there would be enough power to accommodate the hundreds of thousands of air conditioners keeping Georgians cool. With the average American home drawing around 1,200 kilowatts, the 1,000-megawatt buffer is more than enough to power around 800,000 households — nearly 20% of the state’s homes.

    This technology, called demand response, has been around for decades now, where large operators reduce their demand in response to a peak in demand from other consumers. Before automation, grid operators would manually call up industrial customers like steel mills and ask them to cut consumption to ensure the reliability of the entire grid. But with modern technologies and IoT, it can now be done automatically, allowing data centers to reduce their load in under a minute. In fact, Nvidia has already been experimenting with a similar system in the UK and has proven that it works.

    #10161. ChatGPT has hit roughly 20% of Google Search volume, OpenAI says

    According to OpenAI, ChatGPT has managed to grow its search use to around 20% of Google Search’s total volume, a staggering figure.

    Google Search has had a massively dominant lead in the search space, with Microsoft’s Bing a distant competitor with a single-digit share at any given time. But, following its push into AI-powered search about 2 years ago, OpenAI says that ChatGPT is catching up in a big way.

    Speaking at an OpenAI press event/chat yesterday, ChatGPT consumer product lead Adam Fry confirmed that search volume in ChatGPT is “roughly one-fifth (20%) of the volume of queries of Google.”

    There’s a lot of wiggle room there, as the source of Google’s search volume wasn’t revealed. OpenAI’s measurement of what a search query is boils down to when a user inputs a prompt/query that results in a web search – “Every time you ask a question and go search the web, that’s a search.” Again, a lot of wiggle room here.

    But, in any case, this would be the biggest rival Google Search has had yet, and certainly explains Google’s massive push to expand AI in Search. Google admits it is facing “lower monetization” with that push, something OpenAI is also surely dealing with in its own efforts. The Verge notes that Fry said that “most people do not seem to mind ads” in ChatGPT and that “we could be doing this more, actually.”

    Fry also said that “people really love” ChatGPT’s personalization and understanding.
